blogs.description: TypeSafe AI is an AI lab building machine-native intelligence infrastructure for automation, designed to make decisions within software. Try our first System One Model, Jev, in early access.
blogs.content: Jev: For the builders AND dreamers - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Company News Company News Jev: For the builders AND dreamers Oct 14, 2026 Oct 14, 2026 Oct 14, 2026 TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. 🔥 Our philosophy A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity. To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally. On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers. Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases! See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards. Composable Images Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love ( jev-1.13.0 ) was multimodal all along! Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets . You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state , instructions , or even criteria ! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve. As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot. TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images Types Beyond Decisions We’re introducing another new type as well: box . It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support. We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers). Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box Size does matter, apparently 💅 We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod. We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to: TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length Opt-in to help us We love the community’s desire to help make models better! We’ve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases. jev-1.14.0 We’re also releasing a new version of Jev under jev-preview ! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to everything . Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support. Model releases should generally also be strict improvements, but we’re well aware of how much developers hate updating their dependencies. jev-latest will be updated to jev-1.14.0 in a week. jev-1.13.0 will be available for a while. We intend to give 60 days warning before jev-1.13.0 is formally deprecated, and 30 days for jev-1.14.0 . We’ll release a deprecation policy prior to this. Measuring Intelligence As you all know, we dislike public benchmarks . However, we have our own internal best guesses on how to measure the form factor of intelligence that matters most for developers. We’re trying something new out here: we’re going to treat you guys like adults and share this with you all. Some nuance This measurement is our best guess and will continue to evolve. If ever we show you our internal numbers again, don’t expect them to be consistent. Don’t believe it entirely. Always favor your own experimentation and evals with your use cases. We’re including only open weight models because we guard our validation set very closely and are spooked out about the data policies of our model providers. This is likely biased towards our models. Feel free to ignore our model, and instead focus on the relative ranking of open source models. What’s next Lots of people love to ask what kind of sci-fi we’re releasing next. While we are working on some mindblowing stuff, expect most releases to be beautifully boring (like we think AI should be): small improvements across the board, better stability, and features for real deployment. ∵ ⩆ ⩆ ∵ TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility LinkedIn X TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility

blogs.description: TypeSafe AI is an AI lab building machine-native intelligence infrastructure for automation, designed to make decisions within software. Try our first System One Model, Jev, in early access.
blogs.content: How Jack & Jill Cut Candidate Screening Costs By 88% With Jev - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Case Study Case Study ')"> How Jack & Jill Cut Candidate Screening Costs By 88% With Jev Oct 7, 2026 Oct 7, 2026 Oct 7, 2026 We saved ~half a million dollars last week with Jev. And our products got much better at the same time. Matthew Wilson, Co-founder/CEO @ Jack & Jill View post on LinkedIn Background Jack & Jill is a talent marketplace brokered by AI agents. Jack is a career agent for top professionals and Jill is an agent for hiring teams. When Jack and Jill agree there is a mutual match, they introduce the candidate and the company directly, skipping the application altogether. To date, they’ve worked with over 5,000 companies and more than 400,000 professionals working in startups - and raised a total of $60M in the process. Within 10 days of their first test, Jack & Jill had fully rolled out Jev in production - replacing Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite for 100% of calls for a key stage in their candidate matching pipeline. Compared to Gemini, Jev maintained the same level of accuracy, with 88% lower cost and roughly 50% faster task completion time. Cost savings are projected to be $500K per year - and more importantly, new use cases have been unlocked across the product, such as showing candidates matched jobs immediately after signup. Impact Result Details ↓ $500K/year Absolute projected savings ↓ 88% cost BEFORE | $0.755 with Google Gemini AFTER | $0.092 with TypeSafe Jev Cost per 1,000 candidates scored 2x speed BEFORE | 20.3 sec AFTER | 10.3 sec Median time to screen each candidate No loss in quality BEFORE | 93.9% Baseline AFTER | 94.6% Candidates requested by hiring managers The challenge: expensive to screen a large volume of candidates with Gemini Before Jev Candidate pool. Every day, 6,000 candidates for every open role are pulled from the database Initial scoring. A low-cost model (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) scores each candidate and creates a shortlist of the top 2,000 candidates Close review. A higher-power model assesses the top 2,000 candidates, ending with a list of a few hundred candidates for the hiring manager Even with a “low-cost” model like Gemini Flash Lite, costs were adding up fast, due to the "Initial scoring" step that assessed 6,000 candidates for every open role. Results with Jev: Similar quality to Gemini at 88% lower cost With Jev Before switching, Jack & Jill tested both Gemini and Jev models on 150 live roles, and the same candidates for each role. For each role, they included: every past “winner”: a candidate a hiring manager later asked to meet a sample of remaining candidates (weighted to accurately represent the original 6,000 candidates retrieved for each role) The test counted how many winners each model kept on the shortlist. For example, a score of 95% means that for every 100 candidates that the hiring manager asked to be introduced to, the model correctly kept 95 of them in its shortlist. Ultimately, Jack & Jill found that Jev was able to maintain similar quality to Gemini, with 88% lower cost and half the median time to complete scoring. Overall, the team expects to save more than $500K based on projected volumes over the next 12 months. Quality: Slightly higher than Gemini (Recall and AUC) Jev kept slightly more winning candidates than Gemini (+0.7 percentage points), although the difference was not statistically significant (90% confidence interval of −0.4 to +1.8) Jev also performed slightly better on AUC, a measure of how often a model ranks a winner above a randomly chosen candidate with no recorded hiring manager selection. 1.0 is perfect and 0.5 is a coin toss. Jev’s score of 0.933 means it ranked the winner higher in approximately 93.3% of those pairings, compared with 92.4% for Gemini — aligning better with the recorded hiring manager selections. Measure Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Jev % winners kept in the Initial Scoring of 2,000 candidates 93.9% 94.6% Ranking quality (AUC) 0.924 0.933 Speed: Roughly twice as fast Median time to screen candidates dropped by 50% with Jev compared with Gemini. Measure Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Jev Median time to screen all candidates for a role 20.3s 10.3s Cost: 88% lower token cost, $500K in projected savings Jev's input price is a sixth of Gemini's and its output is free. As a result, the cost per 1,000 candidates with Jev is just 9 cents - compared with 76 cents with Gemini. Just at their current volume of roles, Jack & Jill will save $265K a year. Factoring in expected growth, the team expects to save $500K over the next twelve months. Measure Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Jev List price per million tokens $0.25 in, $1.50 out $0.042 in, output free Cost per 1,000 candidates screened $0.755 $0.092 Improving user experience by unlocking new features Jev’s usage has expanded across more than 15 workflows across Jack & Jill's product, ultimately powering a better product experience for users. For instance: Matched roles at sign-up. Every new candidate is checked against every suitable open role straight after onboarding, for under $0.10 per candidate. A near-instant profile check. The check candidates wait on after onboarding dropped from about 3.6 seconds on Gemini to about 0.2 seconds, with better accuracy. Checks across the product, including the CV editor, company classification and marketplace filtering. Savings from using Jev instead of Gemini in these additional features are excluded from the projections above. Conclusion Within just 10 days, Jack & Jill used Jev as a “drop-in” replacement for Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite - achieving comparable results on quality, with 88% lower cost and 50% median completion time. In addition, adopting Jev has unlocked new use cases that will power better user experience throughout Jack & Jill’s product, resulting in faster / better job matches for both hiring managers and professionals considering their next move. Methodology: Quality figures come from an offline test on live roles. The $500K figure is a projection based on expected growth in search volume (cost savings based on current volume = $265K). Gemini list prices are as published by Google at the time of measurement. ∵ ⩆ ⩆ ∵ TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility LinkedIn X TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility

blogs.title: Introducing System One Models & Jev - TypeSafe AI Blog
blogs.description: TypeSafe AI is an AI lab building machine-native intelligence infrastructure for automation, designed to make decisions within software. Try our first System One Model, Jev, in early access.
blogs.content: Introducing System One Models & Jev - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Company News Company News Introducing System One Models & Jev Sep 15, 2026 Sep 15, 2026 Sep 15, 2026 Diogo Almeida, founder, TypeSafe Models have been superhuman at chat for years, so where is all the automation? This has been my driving question for the last four years. At OpenAI, I helped build the methods that made language models useful at following instructions and talking with people. That work ended up as the research behind ChatGPT. At the time, I thought maybe chat models would lead to AGI, but despite the hype it became obvious to me that there was something really big missing. After two years in stealth, countless technical challenges, and research breakthroughs… I am beyond excited to announce that today, TypeSafe AI is releasing our first System One Model : a new class of frontier models built to make fast, structured decisions that software can use directly. We built a new stack entirely focused on automation: with a new model architecture, parallel sampler for maximum efficiency, and training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). Our first public model is Jev , available today in early access. Jev achieves similar levels of intelligence on System One tasks compared to existing LLMs, while being two orders of magnitude faster and more efficient. While Jev gives up string generation, it’s optimized for structured outputs and can’t hallucinate. Think of Jev as a frontier-intelligence function call: unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence so see below for the receipts. 💅 Frontiers, Old and New Existing LLMs System One + Jev Optimized with Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) / Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) Optimizes for Human preference: writeups and chat responses that human raters prefer. Verifiable rewards: outputs that can be programmatically verified. Calibrated decisions: answers with epistemically honest probabilities on System One tasks. Inputs Unstructured data (e.g. text) with an emphasis on sequential messages . Unstructured data (e.g. text) with an emphasis on structured program state . Outputs Strings / generated text. Strings are flexible and can be anything: chat responses, code, hallucinations, refusals, or even type-safe structured values. To be used by software, responses need to be parsed + validated. There is also always some risk that the AI goes off the rails. Type-safe structured values. Possible outputs and structure are defined in advance . The model never makes type errors. All answers are accompanied with calibrated probabilities and confidence scores. Sampling Sequential. Generates one token at a time, each conditioned on the last. Parallel. Generates all outputs in a single query. Incredibly efficient and hardware-aware. Cost Input tokens: from $0.20 to $10 / MTok. Output tokens: ~5x more expensive than input tokens. Input tokens: $0.042 / MTok ($42 per billion tokens). Output tokens: FREE (too cheap to meter). Speed End-to-end response time is 3 to 329 seconds for frontier models. Fast enough for interfacing with humans, but a big bottleneck when integrated in code. End-to-end response time is 70ms-500ms for TypeSafe. This can range from 40x-200x faster for the same levels of frontier intelligence for System One shaped queries. Confidence Even if prompted for a confidence estimate, models tend to be overconfident and inconsistent. If a model can do a task 95% of the time but doesn’t say when it’s in the 5%, it can’t automate that task. Always communicates confidence and uncertainty with every output. Calibrated: higher confidence means higher accuracy. More consistent: returns similar answers for similar inputs. Use cases Human-in-the-loop tasks (chatbots, copilots, coding agents). General and powerful, but requires human oversight because their freedom also means they might go off the rails. Verifiable problems (math proofs, kernel optimization). When correctness can be checked cheaply and automatically, LLMs can generate, test, and iterate until they find something that works. Demos. The flexibility of strings allows it to be incredible for quickly making prototypes that only work sometimes. AI-Powered Workflows / smart if-statements. Structured outputs slot into ordinary software as fuzzy decision rules: classify, route, score, extract, or branch where hand-written logic is too brittle. The surrounding code constrains their freedom, making them easier to compose into reliable systems. Map-reducing over big data. Turn petabytes of data into features and insights. Real-time applications. 100ms speeds means you can use AI in your applications where UX is critical. Verify everything. Score, judge, verify, guardrail, and detect jailbreaks of LLM prompts, reasoning traces, and/or outputs. Evidence / Technical Results We love skeptics, and are skeptics ourselves. There are some claims you can easily verify: Speed per call: We truly are that fast, though our published evals are generally run from our laptops on the West Coast (this is where our service is currently based). Cost per call: We make our pricing transparent. We can’t prove it isn’t subsidized; we’ll need the long-term to prove the sustainability of our pricing (which we expect to go down, not up). No type errors : This would be an easy thing to falsify with just a single counter-example, but it is mathematically impossible. For our bolder claims, we want to provide as much nuance as we can. Side-by-side demonstration Our side-by-side demo shows a key difference between our models and LLMs: Jev outputs all probabilities in parallel instead of autoregressively generating by token. Strings are extremely powerful and general, but costly. “Giving up” strings actually gives us a lot of superpowers! Nuance For people with early access to TypeSafe, here is the actual query . The query is highly simplified and questions were chosen to have descriptive, human-readable keys so that the output on the screen is understandable. The state is also a short, dense, and detailed paragraph, to emphasize the difference in sampling methodology. The relatively shorter input paints our model in an advantageous light. For the keen eyed, for the recorded run, the only disagreement with GPT-5.6 Terra is on “Churn likelihood level”. The actual answer seems genuinely ambiguous to us. We used GPT-5.6 Terra with default reasoning for this example, because we’ve found it to be the most comparable at intelligence to Jev on average. Fun fact: a similar demo was what convinced us to go all-in in the direction of System One Models! Workflow evals We made a new type of evaluation to measure how well AI works within code. We don’t optimize for a ground truth classification or allow the harness and model to change (potentially allowing for overfitting via harness engineering). Instead, we assume there is a correct compute graph (a “workflow” represented in code) and use the predictions of the largest, smartest, and most expensive external models as reference probabilities. Rephrased: every model gets the same workflow. We test how they compare to the average of the smartest models (in this case, Astra and Fable). Jev is off the charts – owning the Pareto frontier for almost 2 orders of magnitude. We also compare to models with a generated prompt doing all the logic in their chain-of-thought, but this tends to do significantly worse than using the workflow itself. Note that the calls here are significantly more complex than the side-by-side demonstration above. That’s because they’re more representative of the types of production workloads needed for true business automation. Below is the simplest of the 4 workflows we’re publishing: The most reliable real-world workflows tend to have many independent, decomposed questions, with fine-grained behavior that’s dependent on probabilities instead of discrete decisions. The end result is discrete branching, but how we get to a final answer involves a lot of domain-specific engineering that needs to be done highly consistently. See our workflow evals site for all the details: examples, disagreements, full queries, and each workflow. Nuance This is where the claims of 193.6x faster, 444.6x cheaper on our home page come from, and we expect that these are on the higher end of real world gains. The content of these workflows was not deliberately chosen nor constructed to make our model look good, and is not in our training distribution. However, they were made by individuals on our model capabilities team, so some bias could exist. We use the average of GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 as the reference answer, which biases answers towards OpenAI and Anthropic’s models. We likely underestimate the relative performance of our model and DeepSeek’s models. The LLMs use our System One LLM wrapper, which constrains LLMs to output structured decisions compatible with our API. We have found this to be the most accurate way to get decisions from LLMs, but this tends to be slower and more expensive than giving decisions without probabilities. Hallucination and Type-safety Hallucination and type-safety are intrinsically related, and we think the latter is table stakes for automation. Having a hallucinated tool call is inconvenient in an agent, but is an absolute deal-breaker if it’s part of a system with latency guarantees or it’s buried several layers deep in a dependency chain. Existing models, no matter how smart , still hallucinate and have type errors. Nuance The numbers for LLMs are from OpenRouter i.e., there almost certainly is bias here: more complex queries might be routed to better models. Our number is not empirical. Schema matching is guaranteed, thus we can confidently add 0% into the plots. Fun Demos Perhaps the most exciting part of our work is enabling new use cases. We have a lot more to show you, but here are a couple of the team’s favorites: Doom We love how this doomo doomonstrates real-time intelligence and what can be doone with code + AI. The engineer behind it was worried about making 10 queries a second (which ends up costing ~$7/hour), but the rest of us agreed that was lower than expected! This is so fun we intend to not only release an in-depth walkthrough, but also host some events to hack on this. Nuance The demo is on structured state as a data structure with text, not on images (yet…) A non-AI doom bot could play better, but we wanted a bot that was reactive to different representations of game state, and most importantly… following instructions was cool as heck! Wikiracing The objective of the game is to start on one Wikipedia page and reach a specific other Wikipedia page using only links you come across while traversing. Each step can mean choosing between hundreds to thousands of links! It’s a great playground for demonstrating not just intelligence-per-second, but also the compounding benefits of not hallucinating with high-cardinality choices. Nuance As far as we know, it was completely random that both the 2nd and 3rd challenges started with “Rubber Duck.” The author only noticed when the team pointed it out. Our speedups here tend to be a lot less than in previous demos. That’s because this is against the non-reasoning modes of the models (except Astra which was set to the lowest reasoning setting). This is also why Jev tended to finish in fewer steps (a sign of greater intelligence). This was to make the demo more bearable to watch. The LLMs look much worse at this task than with reasoning enabled. Jev supports a cardinality up to 255. For the higher cardinality choices, we do a two-stage system of scoring independently then making an explicit choice, hence the occasional slowdown. What’s next We’re still in Jev’s early days. We have a lot more in the pipeline and are so excited to keep on shipping 🔥. Today, we are opening early access and bringing developers off the waitlist as quickly as we can. We want to hear which decisions you need to automate, where Jev works, and where it falls short. Tell us what sci-fi you want to build!! We started TypeSafe because we believe that AI needs an interface software could depend on. We can't wait to see new use cases continuously diffuse through the community and economy. We Give A FAQ Where do the names “System One Models” and “Jev” come from? We were inspired by Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow . The model class name draws on the distinction between fast, intuitive System 1 thinking and slow, deliberate System 2 reasoning. “System 1 thinking” has also implied error-prone. For reasons we will get into in the future, we believe System One Models can be made more reliable than their alternatives. We named Jev after William Stanley Jevons. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar path to coal, after steam-engine efficiency led to an increase in demand. Every order of magnitude drop in the cost of intelligence unlocks orders of magnitude more use cases. Why was a new training algorithm needed? What use cases is Jev good for? Is Jev just a smaller LLM? How does Jev perform against public benchmarks? Where does our training data come from? These results are kinda crazy - how is it possible? ∵ ⩆ ⩆ ∵ TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility LinkedIn X TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility

blogs.description: TypeSafe AI is an AI lab building machine-native intelligence infrastructure for automation, designed to make decisions within software. Try our first System One Model, Jev, in early access.
blogs.content: Lies, Damned Lies, and Benchmarks - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Thoughts Thoughts Lies, Damned Lies, and Benchmarks Sep 11, 2026 Sep 11, 2026 Sep 11, 2026 Benchmarks got us to incredibly smart AI. What gets measured gets managed, and for years making lots of benchmark numbers go up generally made models smarter. I’m not arguing against benchmarks and their helpful contributions to progress. I’m against benchmaxxing. A benchmark inevitably gets “benchmaxxed” when people building the model can optimize for a public eval score[1]. You don’t have to train directly on a benchmark to benchmaxx it; you just have to train on similar data or try a hundred experimental settings, then compare how your model performs. The benchmark selects the model even if nobody intended to game it. Things were not great when benchmarks were an academic pursuit, but now that they are tied to enormous attention and funding , negative incentives to game them abound. Illustration of the Streetlight Effect - source The field wants to measure general intelligence, but can only optimize what it can see. Public evals are the streetlight. Post-training therefore pushes capability fastest in the illuminated areas, while reliability outside them can stay flat or even get worse. My claim is that many of the spikes in “jagged intelligence” are the benchmarks. Annotated version from source Everyone is cheating Models chase benchmarks. Meta’s Llama 4 allegedly ranked near the top of LMArena , but it turned out that not only was it not the public model, Meta was also caught testing 27 private variants before picking the best one, which had the unusually verbose and emoji-heavy style that Arena users rewarded. The ordinary version later landed far lower . Even Claude (normally the goody two-shoes), on a benchmark to simulate a vending machine and end with the most money, formed price cartels, lied to suppliers and promised customer refunds it never sent. Benchmarks chase users. When GPT-6 Astra launched, Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index had it tied with GPT-5.6 Sol , which clashed with the widespread belief that Astra was a major leap. The next day, a revised index put Astra four points ahead . Three days later, another revision tied it with Claude Fable 5.1 for first . I do not think Artificial Analysis rigged the index. The changes are defensible. But the sequence shows the feedback loop: people’s intuitions about which model is better help determine whether an eval looks valid. The point of external evals should’ve been to inform the population, not the other way around. People cherry-pick for their favorite narrative. When the Chinese open-weight model GLM-5.2 beat Fable 5 on one web-design leaderboard, it became evidence that Chinese models had caught the frontier. Design Arena’s own analysis was narrower: GLM used more repeatable templates, generated 25% more code, took twice as long, and still lost to Fable on several design categories. Benchmarks have been broken for a while. Unspecialized humans scored 34.5% on MMLU in the original paper , worse than many small old models. The OpenAI coup was partially a result of safety researchers seeing models surpass PhD level at Google-Proof Question Answering (GPQA - an extremely hard dataset) in 2023. Yet humans still do most of the world’s useful work. Source Everyone in the field knows they’re broken, but they still get quoted because everyone is competing for attention. What benchmarks should be The crux of the problem is (1) intelligence is hard to measure, (2) a (good actor) lab wants to say “we made the model smarter,” and (3) for it to be believed (to whatever extent is accurate). Benchmarks are a shortcut to get around the hard problem of trust. They seem like a magnifier of trust, but instead are a loan: bad actors can then exploit the trust projected on the benchmark. The way out is to be trustworthy in the first place. We need to stop outsourcing credibility to a leaderboard and just be honest. For labs, that means publishing caveats, disclosing cherry-picking, including the evidence that makes you look bad, and de-emphasizing benchmarks even when you’re ahead . Users have a responsibility too: run your own private evals, treat public ones with a grain of salt, and don’t amplify every number or plot you see. At TypeSafe, we’re making a new type of model, which means existing benchmarks don’t apply. We can start the race to the bottom with a wall of evals showing that we beat everyone else, or start from a clean maximally honest slate. We are choosing the clean slate: no standard benchmark table in our model releases. New evals will be dated snapshots and immediately retired once posted rather than hill-climbed. We will also publish our evolving internal evals as our current best guesses, alongside the caveats, any cherry-picking, and evidence that looks bad for us. 1. This is a form of p-hacking: try enough training choices, then report the result that looks strongest. ∵ ⩆ ⩆ ∵ TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility LinkedIn X TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility

blogs.description: TypeSafe AI is an AI lab building machine-native intelligence infrastructure for automation, designed to make decisions within software. Try our first System One Model, Jev, in early access.
blogs.content: The Bitterest Lesson - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Thoughts Thoughts The Bitterest Lesson Sep 10, 2026 Sep 10, 2026 Sep 10, 2026 TL;DR: Compute drives progress in AI, but what good is progress if you are not doing the right task! Rich Sutton’s bitter lesson states that compute beats algorithms. Researchers want to encode their clever ideas about intelligence into machines. Yet over and over, the approaches that win are the general ones which leverage more computation. Search beat hand-built chess knowledge. Neural networks beat hand-built vision features. The lesson is bitter because researchers love algorithms, yet cleverness matters less than scale. My experience is that Sutton’s bitter lesson is the tip of an iceberg of bitterer lessons: beyond compute and algorithms , there’s data and even picking the right task to do ML on. The bitterest lesson in ML is that doing the right task > data > compute > algorithms. Sutton’s bitter lesson is easiest to see in games because there are two major differences to the real world: the right task is obvious (follow the rules to win or maximize score), and data can be endlessly generated through self-play (through compute). It makes sense that the next most important thing is compute . At the end of the day, machine learning makes reward go up or loss go down. Someone still has to decide the objective to optimize though. Getting this right requires understanding the external system in which the model will operate. Without the right task, everything can work perfectly, with the most beautiful loss and scaling curves, but the model may still be useless! Unfortunately, ML research tends to attack these problems in the opposite order. Researchers love inventing algorithms. More recently, we have learned to love scaling curves. Meanwhile, data is messy. Choosing the right task often requires leaving the ML problem entirely to study users, products, organizations, or whatever part of the world is supposed to benefit. This is not an argument against scale. Once the task and data are right, scale is incredible. It is an argument against treating scale as the be-all and end-all. Bitter LLMs When life gives you LLMs... We learned this lesson at OpenAI when making InstructGPT/RLHF: GPT-3 was an incredible model trained to predict the next token on internet text, but people wanted something that followed instructions more than they wanted a super-powered autocomplete. GPT-2-sized models (>100x smaller than GPT-3) trained on the right task, 1 even with the dumbest algorithm 2 and barely any compute, destroyed GPT-3. Annotated from figure 31 from the InstructGPT paper Scaling pre-training would need to reach roughly GPT-7 level to beat even that baseline, and GPT-9 to beat InstructGPT built on GPT-3. 3 You get what you optimize for and the bitterest lesson in ML is that the most important part of it isn’t ML at all. ∵ ⩆ ⩆ ∵ TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility LinkedIn X TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility

blogs.content: The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Shapers The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived Category Shapers published Oct 13, 2026 author Team Legora Lydia Bugden and Paul Saunders have spent more than a decade pursuing a shared vision for Stewart McKelvey, just from different seats. As CEO and Managing Partner, Lydia oversees the firm's six offices in Atlantic Canada, more than 250 lawyers, and over 350 staff on any given day. As Chief Strategy and Innovation Officer and Partner, Paul co-chairs the firm's AI and Technology Steering Committee, drives strategy and innovation across the firm, and is now Managing Director of Stewart McKelvey’s newest venture: the Fortified Firm. Eleven years ago, the two of them made the case to the firm's partnership board for something no one at Stewart McKelvey had done before: a dedicated practice innovation function. Its job was to systematically improve how the firm practiced law, covering everything from process and pricing to technology and profitability. They made that call years before generative AI existed, which is largely why the firm was ready to move fast once AI arrived to the business of law in a substantive way. Two different starting points, one shared instinct Lydia's path to leadership ran through in-house roles first. Those years gave her an early look at how good businesses are run, rather than just the legal work layered on top of them. Sitting on the client side meant understanding different law firms' value for herself, and taking on project work that stretched beyond legal advice into the operational side of the business. "They always let me do a little bit more than just the law," she says. "And I enjoyed that quite a bit." She became CEO and Managing Partner in August 2015, and has since been balancing the collegiality of a partnership alongside the discipline of running Atlantic Canada’s largest law firm. Early on, she pushed back when a senior partner insisted the firm was a partnership, not a business, telling him they were "professionals in a big business." This ability to see what's working ‘under the hood’ is what took her from evaluating outside counsel to running a substantial business. Paul came to law with a background in finance and technology. "I just started to look at opportunities to systematize, improve processes, solve problems," he says, recalling his first summer at work. Lydia noticed early. "Paul was the young lawyer you'd have someone pitch a virtual data room to for 50,000 US dollars," she says, "and he'd come in on a Monday and say, if you don't mind, I spent 18 dollars on a license, and here's a secure data room we can use. He'd solve the problem, but he'd also build something everyone else at the firm could use." By his fifth or sixth year practicing, Paul took a secondment to work on technology projects, and a trip to a legal conference in Chicago sharpened his sense of urgency. "I just couldn't believe what some of the conversations about profitability and leverage and pricing were, things we just weren't exploring at that point," he says. He came back and, in the fall of 2015, not long after Lydia became CEO, the two of them flew to St. John's to pitch creating a practice innovation role to the partnership board. Paul left his practice to become the firm's first Practice Innovation Partner, building out document automation, process mapping, and checklists. "It wasn't a hard sell," Lydia says. "Paul said he wanted to devote 100 percent of his time to the firm, and it just mushroomed from there." Over the following decade, that function grew to include partner compensation redesign, strategy, financial dashboards, and change management, laying the groundwork for what would eventually become the firm's AI strategy. A culture of continuous improvement What Paul and Lydia played key roles in building, long before generative AI arrived, was a culture that could absorb change without resisting it. "You need to develop a culture of continuous improvement, learning, and change," Paul says. "That's actually the model of our practice innovation strategy, so that tools change, technology changes, processes change, but what remains constant is the ability to adapt." Getting there meant treating partners as owners who were consulted, not employees who could be told what to do. “To dictate how something is going to happen, and expect people to fall in line, has never been a successful strategy in any law firm,” Lydia says. The compensation system overhaul is the clearest example of this philosophy in action; instead of rolling out a new comp system in one year, Paul and his committee spent years building the tools and knowledge partners needed to understand how it would affect their own practice. Then they revisited it every year, through partner interviews and a formal debrief. "We've had comprehensive partner interviews at the end of every year," Paul says. "We conduct a debrief session, focus on what works, what doesn't work, what should change, and then implement changes every year to refine it and improve it." Lydia calls it one of the firm's most successful rollouts. "Taking the time and doing it that way meant partners had time to think about their own behaviors, rather than us just plunking in a system," she says. "That's some rigor we would not have had without that process improvement mindset." Why adoption came easily when Legora arrived That decade of groundwork is why Stewart McKelvey became the first law firm in Atlantic Canada to partner with an AI platform, adopting Legora on what Lydia describes as more of a conviction than a line item. "We had not budgeted for that expense when we came into that year's budget,” she says, "but it was a gut feel that this was the right thing to do at the right time." Lydia credits the AI and Technology Steering Committee, which Paul co-chairs, with backing the decision before it ever reached the wider partnership. "We had the confidence of our board and our team that if Paul was saying this is the time to make this move, and he'd worked it through with the committee, then we had the support, and we were able to go," she says. When Paul made the case at the firm's partner retreat, the response surprised even him. "We were kind of like: ‘We're in a new era of human history right now. We're moving from the digital era to the AI era, and everything is going to change,’" he says. "You just saw heads nodding all across the room. They were sold on it, because we'd made those investments over the last 10 or 11 years. This wasn't coming out of left field." The adoption numbers back that up. About two-thirds of the firm's lawyers use Legora at least five times a week. "That's really unprecedented on any major technology we've rolled out," Paul says. "I think the tool is great and intuitive, but I also think it's because we've done the heavy lifting over many years to get them there." Lydia points to a subtler reason it landed well: the rollout didn't require splitting lawyers up by practice group the way past systems did. "Normally we would roll something out and have to say, well, if you're in this group, you do this, and if you're in this group, you do this," she says. "For the first time, you can roll something out and, intuitively, each group will use the tool differently, but maximize the opportunity for their own practice." Rethinking how the next generation of lawyers learns Both Paul and Lydia see AI as changing something more fundamental than workflow: how junior lawyers develop expertise in the first place. "We don't have the privilege of them doing it the old-fashioned way, like Lydia and I learned, by reviewing hundreds of leases on large due diligence projects," Paul says. "Expectations from clients have shifted substantially, and lawyers across the firm are adapting to meet those expectations." He calls this tension the "AI training conundrum," and the firm's answer is to double down on mentorship rather than step back from it. Stewart McKelvey recently rolled out a lawyer skills database that lets every lawyer document their level of expertise across practice areas, along with where they want to build new skills, so senior and junior lawyers can be matched deliberately. "A junior might have stronger expertise in AI. They wouldn't have that substantial knowledge of the practice of law. You've got to connect them together," Paul says. Lydia adds that junior lawyers are watching their profession change quickly, and believes the firm's job is to meet that head-on rather than downplay it. "We recognize their fretfulness,” she says, “but we've decided to embrace the change rather than fear it.” That's part of why she leans on the firm's most senior partners to take an active role in mentoring and training the newest ones. "We’re at the age and stage in our partnership that, from our most senior partner down, everyone will be able to participate in the growth and development of our young lawyers," she says. The firm has also built out what it calls a profile of the AI-enabled lawyer, mapping the skills it expects lawyers will need three to five years out, many of which its lawyers are already building in Legora. "Some of the skills are totally brand new, like how you develop an AI prompt or set up an agent, or use the different context layers within an AI tool,” Paul says. "Some are exactly the same as they were 30 years ago, like being responsive to client needs and understanding your client's business." He likens the approach to a piece of hockey wisdom. "As Wayne Gretzky says, skate to where the puck is going to be, not where it is," he says. "We don't know exactly where it's going to end up, and it's going to change constantly, but that's why we need to get the reps in on that adaptation." Turning a decade of lessons into a new venture This accumulated experience, what worked and what didn't, has now become something new in its own right; Paul is Managing Director of the Fortified Firm, a new venture built to diversify opportunities by bringing Stewart McKelvey's approach to change management, pricing, and AI adoption to other law firms and clients. “It’s an opportunity to take everything Paul's developed, and everything we've all learned along the way, and launch something a little different,” says Lydia. Paul sees the timing as inseparable from the pace of change now facing the profession. "We're just in an era now, with generative AI, of constant change for the legal profession," he says. "Every industry in the world is going to be disrupted, and legal and private practice will probably be among the top industries to be disrupted. It becomes so important that law firms, and their clients, develop the ability to continuously improve and adapt. That's something that can be taught, but you need a consistent framework, a toolkit, and a methodology that can be applied and scaled out." For Paul, the underlying thesis is simple: "It's not about representing a client on a one-off matter anymore. It's about developing systems and collaborating with the client to solve multiple matters going forward," he says. "That's not just the practice of law; it's understanding AI, pricing, data, process improvement, and change management. That's really what the Fortified Firm is all about, how law firms and clients embrace not just AI, but all the other changes that have to happen along with it." The demand for this type of support existed long before the business had a name. Other firms had already started asking what Stewart McKelvey was doing, and whether Paul could help them do the same. Lydia remembers hearing from more than one firm that they were looking for their own version of him. "People recognized you needed a change agent," she says. "They didn't really know what the skill set was that they needed, but they were recognizing that times were starting to really change in the profession." It just took a few more years, and a name, to turn that recognition into an actual offering. Empowered by the future "Getting something done in a law firm can have its challenges," Paul says. "If you know how to get things done in a law firm, you can pretty much get things done anywhere." "What makes a good lawyer, what makes a strong firm, is all about client service, delegation, mentorship, and understanding your client's business deeply," he adds. "I think that hasn't changed at all, and it's even more important as a result of AI." "We're inspired by our history, but we're empowered by our future," Lydia says. "You don't want a service provider who's rooted in the past. You want someone thinking forward, evolving at the same pace, or slightly ahead, of your own business." Legora is the clearest expression of that so far. "It's a tool that's just there wherever you're working," Paul says. "I don't have to use this, but I want to, because it's going to produce a better quality output for the client." That's the real story behind the decade-long head start: eleven years spent building the discipline to stay ahead of the curve and thrive in an environment of constant change. blogs.content: Meet the Legora engineer catching any problems that fall through the cracks | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Legora voices Meet the Legora engineer catching any problems that fall through the cracks Meet the Legora engineer catching any problems that fall through the cracks Category Legora voices published Oct 7, 2026 author Team Legora Before becoming one of Legora's earliest engineering hires, Oskar Elvkull took a winding career path through auditing, energy tech, and backend development. Today, he's known at Legora for tackling the problems with no obvious owner, the unglamorous work that falls between the cracks but can make or break a company as it scales. Finding his way to Legora Oskar’s career started at EY, where he trained as an auditor before realizing that his real interest was in data. That led him to a Swedish energy startup, where he worked on building data infrastructure, and eventually into backend development. But Oskar's move to Legora was different. It wasn’t simply the role that convinced him to make the jump. It was the people and the way they thought. “It didn’t feel like a traditional interview. I was actually working on a coding problem, and it led to a really interesting discussion and sharing of ideas within the team. I knew after that meeting I had to be involved in building this company, and work alongside people who think the same way as me.” Being surrounded by people who are willing to question how things are done and figure things out together has continued to be a big focus when hiring new members of Oskar’s team as they scale. Scaling without losing the culture Oskar’s role has changed significantly over time as the company has grown. The engineering team has grown with it, but the culture that brought people together early on has remained remarkably consistent, with an emphasis on high standards, a willingness to take ownership and a shared appetite for constantly building. "When I joined, there were very skilled people, but the team was small. Now it's bigger, because the product's grown fast but the same energy is there. There's always someone to bounce ideas off, and that appetite for building hasn't changed." That growth is now happening across locations, too. Stockholm remains home to most of the engineering team, while the New York and London teams are beginning to expand. Oskar and other engineers now spend regular stints in the other offices to help build the team and establish the same culture on the ground. For Oskar, maintaining that culture comes down to being intentional about who joins the team. Legora keeps its hiring bar high, looking for people who share the same standards and excitement for building. “We keep the bar high when we hire. But in return we get this engineering culture with very high standards, which I think is really important if we’re going to succeed.” That same mindset extends to how the team works. Engineers are encouraged to go beyond their immediate remit and take ownership of problems that interest them. Oskar has had much experience doing exactly that, including when he picked up a platform stability issue that wasn’t technically his to solve, simply because he wanted to see if he could fix it. A deep dive behind the build "I noticed an opportunity to make the platform faster. The first step was understanding where the time was actually going. So I dug into the code to see exactly where it was being spent and where small gains were hiding. I didn't find one big lever to pull. Instead, I found hundreds of small operations, each taking milliseconds, sitting on a path that every user hits. Individually tiny, but across the platform they added up to a meaningful opportunity. I was excited to dig in. I started with caching and cutting out work that was being repeated unnecessarily. This is exactly why I love working at Legora. At a fast-growing company, it's easy to overlook what seem like small wins, but these small things are what make a product great. It wasn't technically my problem to solve, but I had the freedom to go find the opportunity anyway. Knowing leadership encourages that kind of proactivity and curiosity is exactly why we keep making this kind of progress on the product, and why I love what I do." Building for lawyers As part of Legora’s engineering team, Oskar builds the product, informed by feedback from legal teams. That means Legora’s engineers get a level of feedback you don’t always get in product development, as they hear directly from customers what is working, what isn’t and what they need next. One fundamental for Legora’s customers is security. As Oskar puts it: “Every company says security first, but we really mean it. Security isn’t something we can balance against speed. We have to write secure code and work in a secure way, while still keeping up the pace.” For Oskar, that's part of what makes the engineering challenge at Legora different. You're building quickly, but you're building for customers where the stakes are high. One thing Oskar says makes that easier is being in the office with the team five days a week. This allows people to solve problems together in the room rather than over Slack, catching issues faster, pairing through the hard problems, and keeping the pace up without cutting corners on security. This culture extends outside of the office too, and Oskar and his team now often go bouldering and running together outside work. For anyone thinking about joining, Oskar sees this as one of the real draws of the Stockholm office. As for the city itself, his firm recommendation is the Vasa Museum. “It’s just a ship, but it’s still cool,” he says. As for why someone should join the engineering team in Stockholm, his answer is simple: "If you like engineering, and want to work with smart people who are passionate about the same things, then come join us.” If you are an engineer who wants to be part of our team, check out our careers page: https://legora.com/careers Stay in the loop More stories Shapers Team Legora Oct 13, 2026 The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived Lydia Bugden and Paul Saunders have spent more than a decade pursuing a shared vision for Stewart McKelvey, just from different seats. blogs.content: Introducing Skills | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Product Updates Introducing Skills Introducing Skills Category Product Updates published Oct 5, 2026 author Team Legora Teach the Agent how you work. Skills let legal teams encode their standards, processes and preferences inside the Legora aOS™. Today we're launching Skills , available to all Legora customers. Skills enable lawyers to encode their ways of working so the Agent knows how to execute work to their standards. Every legal team knows the law. What sets them apart is how they practice it: the positions they take, how they structure their advice, the tone they strike with the other side. That way of working takes years to build, and it's what makes their work recognizably their own. Some of it sits in playbooks, or in precedents, or in the experienced heads of the lawyers who built them. Skills turns it into instructions the Agent can follow on every task. "What I find valuable about Skills is that it gives us a consistent process while still being flexible. It adapts to the information provided, asks questions when it needs more context, and helps us get to the result we actually need." – Kiren Bigwood, Senior Growth Manager, Hamilton Locke What are Skills? A Skill is a set of natural language instructions, saved as a Markdown file, that teaches the Agent how to approach a specific legal task. It captures three things: the standards your team holds its work to, the processes it follows, and the preferences that make the work recognizably yours. A Skill might set out how you review a supplier agreement against your playbook, including the fallback positions you'll accept on liability and indemnities. It might capture your process for building a trial bundle, or the way a partner likes a client advice note structured. Along with instructions, a Skill can hold reference materials, templates and past examples, including what the output should not look like. The Agent can invoke a Skill when a task calls for it, or you can tell it which Skill to use. You can read, edit, export and update any Skill as your work changes. " I think of a Skill as a packaged capability because it's a package, there's a lot you can put in it: structured instructions, reference materials, your templates, even other Skills ." – Timothy Besada, Software Engineer for the Agent. How Skills work Using a Skill starts the way any work in Legora starts: by prompting the Agent in the chat, in natural language. If a Skill already exists for the task, the Agent recognizes it and uses it automatically. You don't need to find it or name it. To pick a Skill yourself, type / in the chat and choose from the list. If no Skill exists yet, the Agent can build one from documents you've already produced, or by asking you a few questions about how you approach the task. When it's done, it asks whether you want to install the new Skill. Some lawyers spend time refining a Skill until it's exactly right. Others build one in five minutes, with the Agent doing most of the work. Take a litigation team working on a matter with a large case file. The Agent can move and rename files, so the team creates a Skill that sets out how every matter should be organized: the folder structure, the naming conventions, where pleadings and correspondence go. From then on, every new matter is set up the same way. More capable than a prompt. More flexible than a workflow. Prompts, workflows, and Skills all direct the Agent’s work, and each suits a different kind of work. A prompt is an instruction for the task in front of you. It's the quickest way to get work started, and you write it fresh each time. A workflow is a fixed sequence. You run it when a process needs to be followed the same way every time. A Skill is know-how the Agent keeps. You set it up once, and the Agent applies it whenever the work calls for it, adapting to the task at hand. Unlike a prompt, a Skill can carry files such as templates and examples. Unlike a workflow, it doesn't need you to start it. Skills can also be combined. You might have one Skill for how your team writes and another for a particular review process, and the Agent can draw on both for a single task. Each Skill stays focused, so you never need one long instruction that tries to cover everything. What it is Best for Prompt An instruction for the task at hand One-off requests and getting started quickly Workflow A fixed sequence of steps Processes that must run the same way every time Skill Know-how the Agent applies when the work calls for it The way your team approaches work it does again and again From personal to firm-wide A Skill can start anywhere in the organization. It might begin with a single lawyer capturing a tone of voice, a preferred way to structure a clause, or something they'd otherwise explain at the start of every session. From there, they can share it with a colleague, refine it together, and release it to their practice group or legal team. A Skill can also start at the top. Knowledge managers and innovation lawyers can build Skills around organization-wide standards, such as house style, document templates or negotiating positions, and make them available to everyone from day one. Most teams end up with both. And not everyone has to build Skills. Many start with a small group, such as innovation lawyers and a champion in each practice group, who create and test the Skills everyone else uses. One lawyer's expertise becomes a capability the whole team can use. A colleague who is better than you at something can teach the Agent how they do it, so you can work at that level too. The Skills Library Legora comes with a Skills Library of more than 250 Skills, built by our legal engineers across practice areas and jurisdictions. Whether you work in litigation, real estate, corporate or in-house, there are Skills ready to use as they are or adapt to how your team works. The Library is also home to every Skill you have access to: your own, your team's, and your organization's. Your personal Skills sit alongside those your colleagues have shared with you, and organization-wide Skills published by knowledge managers are available to everyone with access. The Library is organized by a clear taxonomy, so the right Skill is easy to find, and it's browsable enough that you might discover a capability you didn't know existed. Governance and trust You choose what the Agent uses. Sharing a Skill with someone makes it available to them, but their Agent won't use it until they install it. The same applies to Skills published across the organization, and to Skills you build yourself. Nobody can add a Skill to your Agent without you choosing it. Admins set the boundaries. Sharing a Skill across the whole organization requires a permission and isn't open to everyone by default. Admins can restrict sharing to specific user groups, and they can remove a Skill that shouldn't be in circulation. Every Skill can be read. A Skill only changes when someone edits it, and anyone it's shared with can see exactly what the Agent has been given. That matters most for the things you'd never want to change without your knowledge: your standards, your review process and your positions. Matter permissions still apply. The Skill holds the know-how, and the matter sets what the Agent can access. A Skill used on one matter doesn't carry information from that matter into another. How do you turn your team’s expertise into a Skill? Join us alongside a Legora design partner to see Skills in action. Can't make it live? Register and we'll send the recording. blogs.content: Your iManage, in Legora | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Product Updates Your iManage, in Legora Your iManage, in Legora Category Product Updates published Oct 2, 2026 author Team Legora Work with your iManage files directly in Legora, from finding the right document to saving your edits back. Your day-to-day work runs through iManage: the document you’re reviewing, the draft you’re working on, the documents for your current matter. With our new iManage integration, firms on iManage Cloud can access those matters, folders, and documents directly inside Legora. Find what you need, work on it with the Agent, and save the result back to iManage. No uploading. No downloading. No manual syncing. Why this integration is different Many integrations with a DMS work like a file picker. You browse to a document, pull a copy into the tool, and do your work there. That copy now lives outside the DMS. It drifts from the latest version, sits outside your firm's governance, and has to be manually synced back when you're done. The integration saves a few clicks, but the work still happens in two places. We built it to be better. Your documents stay where they belong. In iManage, fully accessible in Legora. You don't have to find the right file and hand it to the Agent. The Agent can search your iManage the way your firm has organized it, by client, matter, author, and your own custom fields. Then it reads what it finds, drafts from it, and puts the result back where it came from. That changes what the Agent can do for you. Finding documents, editing them, and saving the updated version used to be three separate jobs across two systems. Now they happen in one conversation. And because every step runs on the permissions and versioning your firm already relies on, you get the speed without giving up control of your documents. Legora + iManage Standard integration Documents stay in iManage Pulls a copy out of iManage The Agent searches by client, matter, author, and your custom fields You find the file and hand it over Saves back as a new version or new document Manually sync changes back when you're done Find, draft, and file in one conversation Work happens in two places What's new Connected files. Link an iManage matter to a Legora project and its folders and documents are right there. You can browse them, preview them, and bring them into your work without leaving Legora. Ask the Agent. You don't need document numbers or exact field names. Ask the Agent in plain language and it searches your iManage by client, matter, author, date, or recent activity. It understands your firm's own iManage fields, and every answer links back to the source document. Edit and save back. The Agent can draft from a precedent or revise a Word document, with every change shown as a tracked change. When you're happy with it, save it back to iManage as a new version or a new document. Built on your existing governance Everything runs on each user's own iManage permissions, so the Agent only sees what you can already see. It never saves anything on its own: you review the edits and decide what goes back. iManage stays your system of record. Try asking "What iManage documents did I work on recently?" "Find a precedent term sheet for a joint development deal." "Search across my matters for indemnification language." Getting started The integration is available now for iManage Cloud customers. Once it's enabled for your organization, each user connects their iManage account in Legora's integration settings. Talk to your Legora team to get it switched on. blogs.description: Teach the Agent how you work. Skills let legal teams encode their standards, processes and preferences inside the Legora aOS™.
blogs.content: There is no best model. Bet on the system. | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Product Updates There is no best model. Bet on the system. There is no best model. Bet on the system. Category Product Updates published Oct 1, 2026 author Team Legora There is no best model. The frontier is jagged. Advancements are constant, surprising, and uneven. Model advancements are uneven, surprising, and accelerating - just last week, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Muse Spark 1.3, Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra were all released. Every model has unique characteristics (or personalities, if you will) and they excel at different things. As such, no single model will be the best model for everything. But a system that takes advantage of each model’s unique strengths and mitigates its weaknesses can outperform any one model. The frontier is jagged The headline leaderboards models are measured against reduce their capabilities to a single dimension and, over time, make the frontier look like a staircase that’s slowly - or rather, very quickly - being climbed. However, vertical AI companies understand that their domains don’t reduce to singular dimension. Rather they understand that models are multifaceted: They have different characteristics, personalities, and they excel at different tasks. Some models need very specific instructions, while others can handle ambiguity. Some are quick to ask for help/clarification, while some are reluctant to ask at all. Some models are great at long-context reasoning, some are good at manipulating documents, and some are good at instruction-following for writing styles. And this dimension is only one of several. Models differ in cost and latency by a factor of fifty or more. Certain providers are very reliable while others often fail either generally or in odd, specific ways. On top of that there are differences in geographic availability and governance. This makes the frontier of intelligence jagged: different models drive the frontier in different aspects. The frontier moves quickly and unevenly Not only is the frontier jagged, it’s constantly changing. New providers are popping up with new models and even new versions of existing models often have vastly different characteristics than previous versions. And it looks like the rate of change is increasing. One year ago there were for all intents and purposes two labs: OpenAI and Anthropic. Now SpaceXAI, Meta Superintelligence, and Google look like serious competitors. Not to mention that Chinese labs like Z.ai and Moonshot have caught up rapidly with frontier closed-weight labs. The palette of potential models has never been more diverse or faster changing. Just last week, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Muse Spark 1.3, Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra were all released. Frontier leaderboards are changing weekly, and the pareto frontier is being pushed outwards along its entire curve: tiny, efficient models are being released for specialized workflows or certain intelligence-saturated tasks, while big models push the ceiling of intelligence and reasoning. And inference efficiency gains and/or open weights competition leads to frequent steep price cuts: recently OpenAI slashed prices by 80% for their Luna model. The best model is all the models Because models are different and the model landscape is changing so quickly, the best way to ensure optimal outputs for our users is to make sure the best possible model does any given job. Often “best” means that it completes the task at a high level of quality at the lowest possible cost and latency. Achieving this generally means decomposing the problem into constituent parts that different models tackle with their own context windows and specialized tools. Each model has strengths and weaknesses. A multi-model system can trace the outer envelope of them all - taking the best capability in each direction to create a whole that outperforms any individual model. Vertical AI companies are uniquely positioned to map the nuanced model map and spot “model arbitrage” opportunities - places where changing models gives more performance, lower cost, lower latency or the gain of other desired properties - that aren’t immediately clear from a public leaderboard. They can do this because they have two very valuable things: in-house expertise and valuable real-world usage.[1] Expertise creates high-quality evals at the level of “updating change-of-control clause in poorly-formatted Italian shareholder’s agreement” not just “good at legal”. Having in-house expertise means vertical AI companies can continuously revise evals and add more difficult, detailed cases as models improve and climb the scores. Real-world usage ensures that what’s being created by experts matches what’s valued by actual users. Without live usage, evals are best-guess, and value is bound to be left on the table. Live usage gives insights into long-tail failures and use cases that experts and product teams won’t consider a priori and creates a good environment to validate hypothesis and roll out improvements. The two feed each other. Usage shows where evals lack coverage; in-house experts turn gaps into detailed evals and failures into regressions as developers make harness tweaks to squeeze all possible performance out of each model. With any new model release, it runs against the suite, takes over the tasks where it wins, and a controlled rollout reveals new nuances to sharpen our understanding and advance the frontier. Bet on the system Every model on the board will be superseded, probably sooner rather than later. The harness will be changed as capabilities expand. The systematic analysis and model selection persists between it all - the expertise that encodes wanted behavior, the live usage that sharpens it. There is no best model. blogs.content: Legora for in-house teams: Webinar recording | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Events Legora for in-house teams: Webinar recording Legora for in-house teams: Webinar recording Category Events published Oct 1, 2026 author Team Legora What happens when the demands on a legal team grow much faster than the team itself? Legora hosted a webinar on how in-house legal work changes when teams rewire their operating model around AI, and what comes next on the product roadmap. In the past year, Legora grew its employee base by more than 5x, expanded from 3 to 18 offices, completed multiple acquisitions, and is now serving far more customers. Each milestone brought new complexity, risk, and pressure for a lean in-house legal team. In this session, General Counsel Emma Kadri Bergström shares how her team uses Legora day to day across commercial work, in-house M&A, and compliance monitoring. Then Adrian Parlow and Walter Myer walk through what’s ahead for in-house teams — including a live look at agentic intake — with time for audience questions. What this webinar covers During the presentation, we address how the legal operating model for in-house teams requires rethinking existing workflows around AI, and why speeding up individual tasks is insufficient. This includes a deep dive into the following topics: How Legora’s legal team applies Legora to commercial contracting, in-house M&A, and horizon scanning Where agentic legal work is headed for in-house teams — skills, automations, deeper integrations, and intake How intake can meet the business where it already works (Slack, Teams, email), and the how different use cases can be handled with a lawyer in the loop for revisions, or automated, to streamline and accelerate delivery of routine work Learn more & take the next step The session recording, including audience Q&A, is available below. Want to go deeper on how Legora supports in-house teams? Explore related product updates — including Walter Myer’s perspective on the real cost of legal intake . blogs.content: Autonomous Contract Management Is Now Generally Available - Spellbook spellbook.legal cookie bridge --> Webinar: The first-ever live demo of Spellbook ACM • Oct. 29 • Save your spot Product Solutions Resources Customers Careers Security Start your 7-day free trial Book a Demo Login Book a Demo Back to Blog Blog / Updates Last Updated on Oct 07, 2026 by Scott Stevenson ‍ Autonomous Contract Management Is Now Generally Available It's time for contracts to stop holding business back. Today, Autonomous Contract Management (ACM) is now generally available. It's the first AI system to power contracts from end to end. Spellbook ACM starts working the moment a deal lands in your inbox until the day it's due to renew. It keeps the work moving. Plus, if a team member needs to make a decision, they can jump in anywhere in the process. ACM helps remove handoffs between disconnected systems. It makes sure nothing slips through the cracks with always-on intelligence for the duration of a contract. Now, fewer contracts will sit around in a queue waiting for a go-ahead, less mornings can be spent sorting through what came in overnight, and more work handled before you've even poured your first cup of coffee (or tea). Here’s how Spellbook ACM works. Autonomous Intake Every contract is pulled in automatically from intake forms, Gmail, Outlook, and Slack. Spellbook captures each one, extracts and organizes the details, and routes it into the right pipeline and deal owner so nothing sits around waiting to be picked up. First-Pass Review Every contract gets a full diagnostic, including where it breaks from your playbook standards, where the risk sits, and what to do next. Routine agreements that come through clean get marked ready to approve, while everything else gets flagged for you with concise suggestions on how to navigate the remaining issues. Routing & Approvals Spellbook makes it easy to route agreements based on internal rules, run specific playbooks depending on the contract type, set up escalation protocols, assign contracts for review to other members of your deal team, and get issues quickly sorted and approved. Want to auto-approve contracts under $50K that pass all of your playbook rules? Just tell your agent to do so with plain language. Deal Workspace Work every deal from one place. Track all versions, compare contracts side by side, assign owners and approvers, and see all deal history and communications in the activity feed. Every redline that comes back from the counterparty gets reviewed automatically, so the deal never sits waiting on you. Human & AI Collaboration Collaborate with your team on the same document, with Spellbook working alongside you. Prompt Spellbook to redline or revise, and every edit shows up as a tracked change.
