blogs.content: The real cost of legal intake | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Product Updates The real cost of legal intake The real cost of legal intake Category Product Updates published Sep 15, 2026 author Walter Myer Giving lawyers new tools inside old processes only speeds up their work, but the real gains come from changing the process itself. Over the last few months I've had dozens of conversations with in-house lawyers about how they work. While every organization is different, three key roles have emerged as a common denominator: the requester, the lawyer, and the general counsel. The requester is someone on the commercial side. They're trying to get a deal signed, a supplier approved, a policy question answered. From where they sit, legal is a step in a process, and they want that step to be fast and low-friction. Then there's the lawyer fielding those requests. The lawyer is the person responding to those requests, for which they need the full context before they can do anything useful. They want to protect the organization from risk while also being commercial, acting as a partner to the business rather than being a blocker. Finally there's the general counsel. The GC cares about matching the team's expertise and capacity to the organization's most important legal needs. To do that job well, they need insight about the kind of work that comes in and how it gets completed. When these three roles slot together, the legal department works like a well-oiled machine. In most of my conversations, what I hear instead is a broken process that fails to protect a legal team's scarcest resource, the attention of its best people. Scoping the request A business stakeholder knows what they want to achieve. They may not know what a lawyer needs to help them get there, and we shouldn't expect them to. When a salesperson pings legal to ask for a quick look at a contract renewal, they attach what they have and assume that's enough. But often it’s missing key additional information, like schedule documents to which the contract refers, processes followed before deciding on the extension, and so on. Intake forms can help, because they steer the requester on what they need to provide. But a fixed set of questions often feels ill-adapted to the wide array of requests that can come through. Make the form too short and legal still has to fill the gaps. Make it too detailed and the requester simply sidesteps the intake form, or sometimes even the legal team altogether. According to Onit's 2023 Enterprise Legal Reputation Report , 67% of enterprise employees admit to bypassing legal, even when they know it breaches policy. The standard should be a flexible system that meets requesters where they are, asking only relevant clarifying questions to gather the context needed by the legal team and nothing more. Performing the work Legal work is not all the same. Some of it is routine and repeatable: standard NDAs, security questionnaires, basic compliance queries. This work follows predictable patterns. It draws on the same precedents every time. The legal judgment involved is real, but it doesn't vary much from one instance to the next. Research carried out by EY has found that 27% of in-house legal professionals' time goes to routine and low-value tasks, rising to 32% in larger functions. Work like this should be streamlined, and increasingly, it can benefit from automation. Other work is genuinely complex: an acquisition, a novel regulatory point, a counterparty pushing back on terms that matter. This work requires a lawyer's full attention. But it doesn't need to start from a blank page. As every lawyer knows, it’s far better to review a strong first pass than to start from scratch. That means resetting the default ways of working for lawyers. When a lawyer takes a first look at a request, it should contain all the context needed, and it should contain a draft response ready for their review. And in some cases, where the question is simple and the answer is clear based on trusted positions, it might not need their review at all. Understanding the workload A general counsel is expected to maximize the return on their team, explain where legal time is going, and make the business case for investment in headcount or tooling. All of that requires data: on volume, on turnaround time, on which types of work are consuming the most capacity. In most organizations, that data doesn't exist in any systematic form. Without that information, the GC is flying blind. They know the team is busy, but they don’t know where the bottlenecks lie or what to do about them. Decisions about hiring, about process, about where to focus improvement efforts rest on instinct rather than evidence. CLOC's 2026 State of the Industry Report found that less than a third of legal departments expect attorney headcount to grow, even as demand for legal support rises. Deploying a fixed headcount against a rising workload requires GCs to become more data driven in the way they work. What this costs There's a cost to all of this that doesn't show up in any report. It shows up in the relationship between legal and the rest of the organization. When the process makes it too hard to get a fast answer, the commercial org bypasses legal. On the other side, lawyers who spend their weekends working down a backlog of routine work feel demoralised and undervalued. That matters for retention, and for obtaining the right talent to match the legal requirements of the business. Giving lawyers a new tool inside the old process only speeds up the lawyer's work. The request still arrives incomplete, routine work still consumes senior time, and the GC still can't see where the hours are going. The gains that matter come from changing the process itself. That's why we are building Intake. It's the agentic legal front door that changes the process itself, so routine requests can be answered instantly, complex requests come with a first pass answer for review by counsel, and the GC receives actionable insights into the work carried out by their team. More to come soon. The author Walter Myer is a Product Lead at Legora. blogs.content: Ricardo Anaya on starting out as Legora’s first US legal engineer | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Legora voices Ricardo Anaya on starting out as Legora’s first US legal engineer Ricardo Anaya on starting out as Legora’s first US legal engineer Category Legora voices published Sep 9, 2026 author Team Legora Having worked as a lawyer, a client, and in legal technology, Ricardo Anaya was unusually well prepared for what he does today: translating legal workflows and judgment into effective ways of using Legora. That discipline has become known as legal engineering, and Ricardo was ideally placed to help establish it for Legora in the US. He studied law at Universidad del Pacífico in Lima, graduating top of his class, and worked at Baker McKenzie and PwC before landing an in-house role in private equity. But it didn't take long for frustration to set in. The work was repetitive and manual, and it rarely delivered the impact he'd gone into law to make. So he moved sides into investing. Within five months of joining Nexus as legal counsel, Ricardo had taught himself the investment business and earned a place on the deal team as the first lawyer in the firm's history to make that jump. He went on to become founding CFO of Olimpo, a sports betting business Nexus built from inside the fund. Then came Stanford where he earned an MBA. This was followed by a role at Responsiv AI, a legal AI company focused on regulatory compliance. "By the time I came to Legora, I'd been the lawyer, been the client, and worked on the product side," he says. "That's basically the job description for a legal engineer, though nobody called it that yet." Employee number seven in North America Ricardo joined Legora as the founding legal engineer for the US and became Lead about six months later. He was employee number seven in Legora's New York office, and roughly the 80th hire at the company globally, joining at a moment when there was no US legal engineering function and no playbook. This meant there was no local precedent to work from. A blank slate might seem intimidating, but Ricardo didn’t see it that way. "The appeal was that there was nothing here yet,” he explains. "Expanding from the ground up, in the largest legal market in the world, was exactly the kind of ambitious problem I wanted to be part of." Legora now has over 250 employees across the US and works with more than 100,000 legal professionals globally, a scale that makes those early days feel a world away. "I have never worked anywhere with this concentration of genuinely brilliant colleagues," he says. "The culture has a mix I hadn't come across before. Real competitiveness, paired with kindness and a default to helping each other. People want to win, and they want the person next to them to win too." The launch he's proudest of was at an AmLaw 50 firm, a project he steered from pilot through to implementation. From a standing start, more than 1,000 lawyers were using the platform within three months, with weekly active users above 70% of the licensed base. The generic workflow problem Ricardo’s biggest learning so far is that no firm works quite like another, however similar they may look from the outside. Two firms running the same deal type will structure it differently and rely on different precedents. Even what counts as a good first draft varies from one firm to the next. A generic workflow can be technically correct, and still go unused. "The fix was to stop building for the practice area and start building for the firm," he says. His team introduced use case discovery sessions as the first pillar of every rollout. "The first step is to understand how a firm actually does the work, where the judgment sits, and what they would never automate." From there, his team works around how the firm actually operates. This approach has a further payoff. The discovery sessions also identify the AI champions inside a firm. The people who get excited in the room are the ones who carry the rollout forward. Teaching the work, not the tool Understanding a platform and actually using it are two different things. Early on, Ricardo's team kept hearing the same thing. Training went well and people understood the platform, but then they went back to their desks and didn't use it. "The gap wasn't knowledge," he says. "It was that we were teaching the tool, not their work." So his team added a stage before training. Each practice area nominates champions, who identify the use cases their lawyers care about. Sessions then focus on just the top four or five. The first trial resulted in close to 500 weekly power users within three months. "Most adoption problems are diagnosis problems," he says, "and diagnosis doesn't happen over video. That’s why we go to them. Meeting lawyers where they are is a critical part of the job." Why New York New York is Legora's US hub for a reason. "That's where the lawyers are," Ricardo says, simply, "and it's the same story with the in-house teams we work with. It is a matter of density." A day can include breakfast with a knowledge officer, an afternoon in an attorney's office watching how they actually work, and an industry event in the evening. "I spend more time at our customers’ offices than my own," he says. "Being one call away isn't enough. I'd rather be on site, building the kind of rapport that lets you work through a problem with a customer rather than just report back on it." "The people who do well have three things," he says. "Real legal credibility, because you need to have felt the pain points to understand the workflow and how to improve it. Genuine curiosity about the technology, not just tolerance of it. And energy from customers, because this is a customer-facing role and a good amount of the work happens in other people's offices, solving other people's problems. The ones who thrive find that energizing, not draining." Measuring what matters Ricardo is now a senior leader within the North American legal engineering function that has grown substantially since he joined, with no signs of slowing down. The team are all former practicing lawyers, from firms including Latham & Watkins, Cooley, and Kirkland & Ellis, with law degrees from Harvard, Yale, and Columbia. "We’re focused on adoption and outcomes, not seats," he says. "It's easy to measure how many licenses a firm has bought. What matters is weekly active users as a share of the licensed base, and whether people are doing meaningful work with clear ROI, not just testing a tool." Asked what he'd tell someone earlier in their career, Ricardo points to what he had to unlearn as a leader. "When you've built something yourself, the instinct is to keep doing it because you're fast at it. That caps the team at whatever you can personally deliver." So he noted down what he knew, then let the team improve on it. That, he says, was the single highest-leverage thing he did last year. blogs.content: Creating more value in less time: How the Managing Partner of Harrison LLP became one of Legora's top power users | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Shapers Creating more value in less time: How the Managing Partner of Harrison LLP became one of Legora's top power users Creating more value in less time: How the Managing Partner of Harrison LLP became one of Legora's top power users Category Shapers published Sep 3, 2026 author Team Legora Matthew J. Madsen is the Managing Partner of Harrison LLP, a national law firm that focuses exclusively on helping clients define and achieve their private wealth goals. The firm now has more than 100 attorneys across 12 markets, and counts 14 Fellows of the American College of Trust and Estate Counsel among its ranks. Matthew has spent more than 25 years advising high-net-worth individuals and families on complex estate and wealth transfer planning, as well as charitable giving, and he continues to serve as outside General Counsel to the St. Louis Community Foundation alongside his leadership role. Inside his own firm, Matthew carries a specific title: Harrison LLP 's top power user of Legora. What follows is Matthew's account of the bet he made on AI, what being a power user actually requires, and how he's turned his own habits into a firm-wide strategy. Making innovation the centerpiece of firm strategy Innovation is a defining pillar of Harrison LLP’s direction, with AI emerging as one of its clearest expressions. “I remember when an associate told me about ChatGPT and I thought, 'This is going to change everything,'” Matthew says. Championing AI as managing partner meant owning the uncertainty it created. “An associate asked me, after hearing us talk about Legora, 'Is my job okay?'” Matthew recalls. His answer set the tone for how the firm would think about AI going forward: “If you're spending less time on routine work and more time in the meeting with the client, finding out why she's so passionate about how she wants to leave her legacy, that's more value for everybody.” Getting the rest of the firm on board took care. It started small, a beta test group that met periodically to trade tips and figure out what was actually working. “That group has since become our broader Legora users group,” Matthew says, “so the knowledge-sharing culture that developed early carried over into how we operate now.” The other piece is a nomination process: Legora users at the firm periodically identify a peer they think would genuinely benefit from the tool. “The thinking behind it is that seeing a colleague you respect use something effectively tends to move people more than any top-down push,” Matthew explains. What makes a Legora power user “I have great fun with Legora,” Matthew says. He explains how it isn't a tool he opens for a task and closes when it's done; it runs alongside everything he does. He uses it as an active thinking partner — for research, outlining, drafting, and testing arguments — not as a shortcut, but as a way to move faster toward stronger work. “The moments where I've felt the biggest impact have been in document-heavy situations where volume itself is the enemy,” Matthew says. “When you're reviewing twenty years of trust administration records, or trying to understand how a complex business interest interacts with a long-standing estate plan, everything is findable, eventually. The question is how long it takes, and what that costs.” “Getting there takes time no one can afford to waste,” he says. “Legora has surfaced things that I then confirmed were worth pursuing. In this work, that time doesn't disappear. It goes right back into the analysis that shapes the outcome.” “It's also great for client meetings,” he says, where the real advantage isn't preparation but responsiveness. “It just creates a much better experience. With Legora, you can check in real time and you have the answer.” Where judgment and Legora meet Matthew is careful to draw a line between the technology and the judgment that directs it. He stresses how private client work carries a heavy psychological and behavioral component. It’s as much about figuring out what a client actually wants, and sometimes helping them work that out for themselves, as it is about the law itself. “What you have to know is human psychology, behavioral economics, and how to be a counselor,” he says. “You have to know how to think. You have to know how to be creative in solving problems. If you're not learning those things, you're going to struggle practicing law.” The difficulty compounds with scale. “A single family might have business interests in three states, a foreign spouse, a charitable foundation, kids with very different relationships to money, and a trust drafted ten years before any of that existed,” Matthew says. “And ten years is forever. The amount of wealth changes. The types of assets change. The goals and values evolve. The humans these plans are built to protect and benefit evolve. The plan was right when it was written. The world just kept moving, and these families kept evolving with it.” “Legora has been quite valuable to me in those situations. When I'm working through a dense file, what I need isn't just to surface basic structural issues for confirmation. I need to probe for the interconnected layers that may no longer match present circumstances, the current goals, the current values, the current asset mix. It helps me do that faster and more systematically. The entire review of that material is guided by my judgment and by what I've learned working with these families over many years. Legora just makes sure I'm covering the ground I need to cover.” That judgment doesn't arrive on day one, which is why Matthew has taken a fairly unique approach to when AI is introduced to the firm’s lawyers. “We don't have associates using AI for the first three years. They do the work on their own first,” Matthew says. “Writing is thinking. The process of taking something complex and expressing it in a way a client can actually understand isn't a side skill you pick up later. It's central to how you develop as a lawyer, and it takes real repetition. Law school teaches you to write for professors and examiners, which is a different thing entirely. We worry that if you skip that early struggle, you lose something that's hard to get back.” What comes next for the profession “The thing I'm most interested in is what happens when AI is good enough to help us do the work we've always wanted to do but couldn't justify the hours for,” Matthew says. Private client lawyers, he argues, are often caught up in the details, too busy with the infrastructure. “Many of us turn down long-term trust administration roles, for example, not because we don't know how or shouldn't be in it, but because we're so busy with everything else,” he says. “The constraint has never been expertise. It's hours,” he says. “AI gives us those hours back, and when it does, that's not a marginal improvement. That's a real expansion of what we can deliver for families. And I think that's going to be true for every law firm in America.” Matthew has also noticed the shift on the client side of the table. “It used to be once or twice a year you'd hear 'AI said this,'” he says. “Now it's every single day. And you can tell when clients have put your own documents into their own AI: they're asking much more targeted, sophisticated questions. They got their basic questions answered before the meeting, and now we're having much more productive conversations. I always think: more value, less time,” he says. “How is that not a win for everybody?” When asked about what’s next, Matthew says: “The older I get, and the more experience I accumulate, the more I find myself thinking there is just so much I still don't know. That's always been true in this work. But it's especially true with AI, which is moving faster than any of us can fully track. We're trying hard to stay humble about it and treat everything as iterative. We're learning as we go, same as everyone else.” That combination, moving early and decisively, then staying honest about what's still unknown, is what's shaped Matthew's approach to AI at every stage: the early bet he made on it, the policy he built around it, and the discipline he brings as a power user. blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: Three in-house leaders share how they’re expanding their teams’ capacity while keeping lawyers’ judgment central to the work.
blogs.content: Insights How GCs are Rethinking Legal Work With AI Three in-house leaders share how they’re expanding their teams’ capacity while keeping lawyers’ judgment central to the work. by Harvey Team • Oct 16, 2026 In-house legal teams face a steady stream of work that varies in urgency, complexity, and the judgment required. AI can accelerate first drafts and other preparatory work, giving lawyers more room to focus on decisions that require their deep knowledge of the business. That raises an important question for legal leaders: Which work should the team take on vs. hand off to AI, and where can its lawyers add the most value? At Harvey FORUM in Sydney, Silv Roest, Group Chief Legal, Corporate Affairs, and Sustainability Officer at The Warehouse Group; Andrew Chivers, Regional General Counsel, APAC at Brambles Limited; and Georgette Apostolopoulos, General Counsel at The Star shared what they’re learning as AI becomes part of their teams’ day-to-day work. Their examples offer practical lessons for using AI to change how legal teams work, beyond accelerating individual tasks. Change How the Work is Divided At The Warehouse Group, one of the largest retailing groups in New Zealand, Roest is looking at how a four-lawyer team spends its time. First drafts, summaries, and issue tables are necessary work, but they can make it difficult to reach the questions that need the team’s judgment and knowledge of the business. That makes the division of work a useful place to start. Watch Video Apostolopoulos faced a different capacity challenge at The Star, one of Australia’s leading integrated resort companies. After the legal team downsized, it no longer had an in-house litigator to run an anti-discrimination matter. Her team used AI to help prepare the evidence before asking outside firms for quotes. By preparing the evidence in-house, the team could ask firms to price the work that remained, giving it a way to manage outside counsel costs. Watch Video Both examples start by breaking work into its component steps. Legal leaders can then identify what AI can help prepare, where their lawyers need to apply judgment, and when outside counsel’s expertise is needed. That gives a lean team a clearer way to allocate its time and scope external work. Make Existing Knowledge Easier to Use For a legal team supporting a global business, even a familiar question can take time to answer when the relevant guidance sits across different policies and jurisdictions. Global supply chain logistics company Brambles has 24 lawyers working across 60 countries. Chivers described how his team brought its policies together in an agent that people can query, reducing the need to search through documents each time a question comes in. Watch Video The example offers a useful starting point for teams with knowledge spread across many documents: look for questions that come up repeatedly and require lawyers to consult the same sources. Making those sources easier to use can help the team respond more quickly, while lawyers still assess how the guidance applies to the particular situation. Help Lawyers Evaluate AI Output Making information easier to access also changes the skills lawyers need to practice. Chivers noted that junior lawyers may be comfortable using AI while still developing the legal knowledge needed to challenge its answers. Familiarity with the tool is useful; the ability to spot a missing fact, weak inference, or incorrect conclusion takes training. Watch Video That training can happen in the course of real work. When reviewing an AI-assisted draft, a supervising lawyer can ask a junior colleague what they checked, where the answer came from, and why they agree with it. The discussion helps the junior lawyer develop judgment alongside their ability to use the tool. Apostolopoulos described a related challenge when colleagues bring Legal an answer they generated with AI. Before assessing it, her team has to understand what they were trying to do. “It’s been really important for us as an in-house team to go back to the business and validate the question. Not the answer, but the question: What problem are you trying to solve?” Clarifying that request gives Legal the context it needs to assess the answer. Look Beyond the Legal Team’s Workflow The next opportunity may be larger than improving a task inside Legal. Roest described a change in how she thinks about AI: a contract review is one step in a procurement process that involves people and decisions across the business. Improving that step can help, but the full process determines whether work moves more effectively from request to outcome. Watch Video For GCs, that means looking at who needs information before and after the legal team’s involvement. Where does work wait for a handoff? Which questions come back repeatedly? And would changing the legal step alone solve the problem? Those conversations can help teams choose AI projects that address how the business works, rather than adding tools to isolated tasks. The three leaders’ examples begin with immediate needs: evidence to prepare, policies to navigate, and answers to check. Starting there gives legal teams a way to learn what works. It can also reveal where a change to one task calls for a broader change in how lawyers, colleagues, and outside counsel work together. For more on how in-house teams are rethinking how legal work gets done with AI, read RSGI’s latest report, The New Economics of In-House Legal . After reviewing 151 applications from students at 61 schools, we are thrilled to announce Anthony Ross, a law student at the University of Missouri–Kansas City School of Law, as our first fellow. Anthony will spend the coming semester, tackling one of M&A’s most notorious workflows: disclosure schedules. With global transaction volumes surging 30% to $2.6 trillion in the first half of 2026, M&A is set for a record-breaking year. That increase in deal volume means a corresponding increase in contract volume. For most deals, preparing disclosure schedules means combing through every relevant contract a company has signed, one by one, to find what needs to be disclosed. It is grueling, high-stakes, needle-in-a-haystack work. But as Anthony put it, the actual lawyering involved is merely a "thin slice of judgment on top of a thick layer of hunting." Drawing on his experience as a summer associate at Polsinelli, Anthony plans to build an AI solution that cleanly separates those layers. His proposed tool will read the data room, surface candidate disclosures, and connect each result to its source language, leaving only the final judgment calls to the lawyer reviewing the results. Anthony will work alongside the Spellbook team to develop and test his idea. Congratulations, Anthony. We’re proud to have you as our first Spellbook Legal Fellow. blogs.content: Product Making Harvey the Orchestration Layer for Legal Work Legal Work Orchestration brings the phases, tasks, and reviews of a matter or project into the same place as the documents and the agents. by Harvey Team • Oct 15, 2026 Today, we’re launching Legal Work Orchestration , a new way to organize and manage legal matters in Harvey. It connects the phases, tasks, people, and review points within a matter so that agents can execute defined tasks, lawyers can review their work at designated gates, and everyone involved can see what needs to happen next. Watch Video Much of legal work follows a repeatable process. An M&A transaction, for example, moves through familiar phases, tasks, and review points. But the process itself often has to be reconstructed for every new matter from a checklist, a previous deal, or the knowledge of the people who have done it before. AI agents can already complete many individual steps within that process. What they often lack is the structure around the task: where it fits in the matter, which documents and instructions apply, who should review the output, and what happens next. Lawyers still have to provide that context, move the work between people and systems, and track its progress. Legal Work Orchestration brings that structure into Harvey, allowing lawyers and agents to work through a matter together in one place. How Legal Orchestration Works The same structure can support any matter or project a team runs more than once, from an M&A transaction to a quarterly compliance review. Legal Work Orchestration captures that process in a reusable template, carries the relevant context into each task, and coordinates reviews and next steps. Capture the Process in a Reusable Template Templates capture how your organization runs a recurring type of work. When an associate opens a new buy-side acquisition, the Space can already contain the relevant phases, tasks, playbooks, agents, collaborators, and review gates. Innovation and knowledge teams can define that structure once, helping teams follow a consistent process across matters without rebuilding it from scratch. Give Every Task the Context it Needs Each task includes its scope, inputs, and reviewer. An agent assigned a change-of-control review can therefore analyze the relevant contracts and produce a consent matrix without the lawyer having to assemble a new prompt and briefing for that step. Tasks can also be assigned to another lawyer or shared with the client while retaining the relevant matter context. The work no longer depends on one person manually carrying information from one step to the next. Keep Reviews and Next Steps Moving When the agent completes the review, Harvey notifies the designated partner that the consent matrix is ready. Once the partner approves it, the task is completed and the next step can begin. Updates can also be made from email. A lawyer can ask Harvey in a reply to close a task or begin the next one, while the Space maintains a current view of the matter’s progress. Partners can see where the work stands without asking an associate to reconstruct the status from email and separate checklists. The Future of Legal Work Orchestration Before the release of Harvey II in August, every step delegated to Harvey required a lawyer to gather the documents, write the instructions, and move the output to wherever it needed to go next. Legal Work Orchestration reduces that overhead by giving each task its inputs, instructions, and reviewer in advance. Today, lawyers still actively prompt the majority of steps in a legal workflow. We expect that balance to change rapidly. Over the next six months, we expect agents to take on an additional 20% of workflow steps. Within a year, we expect that share to triple. Lawyers will remain in control through defined review gates, and the work performed by agents will remain transparent and auditable. But as agents take on more of the execution, lawyers will be able to focus more of their attention on directing the matter, reviewing consequential outputs, and exercising judgment. Legal Work Orchestration, which includes tasks, commenting on tasks, and notifications, is rolling out across Harvey workspaces now. blogs.content: Legora AI Day at Bucerius Law School: preparing the next generation of lawyers | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Legora AI Day at Bucerius Law School: preparing the next generation of lawyers Legora AI Day at Bucerius Law School: preparing the next generation of lawyers Category published Aug 19, 2026 author Team Legora What does it mean to train a lawyer in the age of AI? That question sat at the heart of Legora AI Day at Bucerius Law School, the official launch of Bucerius's campus-wide Legora license and a signal of how seriously one of Europe's leading law schools is taking the transformation of the legal profession. The event brought together students, practicing lawyers, and legal innovators for a day of onboarding sessions and panel discussions about how AI is shaping the legal industry, and what that means for the people entering it. A profession in motion The legal market is changing faster than legal education has traditionally moved. Nathalia Schomerus, Legal Innovation Lead at Legora, explained: "I think students are not being prepared well enough for the age of AI. The way legal work is shifting means that the way we educate future lawyers has to shift as well." Florian Skupin, Executive Director of Legal Technology at Bucerius, agreed: "Legal education will need to adapt more to market realities. It's quite important that our students have AI experience during their studies." From the courtroom to the classroom The day featured practitioners who use Legora in their daily work, giving students a direct line to what AI-assisted legal practice actually looks like. Stefan Papastefanou, Associate at White & Case, made the point that law firms and their clients are already recalibrating expectations around efficiency: "Clients are starting to require you to showcase how much time you've saved." His message to students was to engage with these tools now, build a genuine understanding of what they can do, and come into the profession ready. Jonathan Cholewa, Partnerships and Digital Development at Otto Schmidt, brought a publisher's perspective. As a leading legal content provider, Otto Schmidt's goal is simple: to be present wherever legal research is happening next, and increasingly, that means AI platforms like Legora. It's a reminder that the shift extends beyond law firms and law schools. The entire legal information ecosystem is orienting around where AI-driven research happens. The next generation of lawyers If the practitioners were enthusiastic, the students matched them. "I'm using it on an everyday basis," one student said, when asked about Legora. "I have all of the material from the professors in there. I keep asking it questions and it's helping me so much." Another student added, "AI is becoming really important in the future, and I want to be on top of it." "I see a lot of opportunities," said another. "I want to work with it." That mindset is exactly what firms are looking for. Vadym Kuzmenko, Legal Engineer at Legora, pointed to the practical advantage students gain from starting early: "Coming in already with knowledge of how to use these tools is great for the law firms and the companies because you are quicker to be onboarded. You are quicker to actually deliver value." More than a license What distinguishes this partnership is the intent behind it. As Nathalia put it: "We're not just giving them licenses and then letting them run. I want to make sure that the lawyers we have in the future are the best lawyers." That means preparing students who don't just know how to use a tool, but understand when and why to use it, and how to critically evaluate what it produces. Legora AI Day at Bucerius was a starting point. The campus license means students will be working with Legora throughout their studies, building the kind of fluency that only comes from sustained, real-world use. The partnership signals a commitment by both Legora and Bucerius to raise the standard of legal work, and to equip the future generation of lawyers with the knowledge and skills to do so. blogs.title: KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen | Legora
blogs.description: Teach the Agent how you work. Skills let legal teams encode their standards, processes and preferences inside the Legora aOS™.
blogs.content: KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Perspectives KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen Category Perspectives published Oct 13, 2026 author Janusch Krasberg Anfang 2026 arbeiteten rund 3.000 Juristinnen und Juristen in Deutschland mit Legora. Bei der Eröffnung des Münchner Büros Ende September waren es bereits mehr als 13.000. Besonders stark wächst die Nutzung in Rechtsabteilungen: Dort hat sich die Zahl der Nutzenden seit Januar verachtfacht. Deutschland hat den Ruf, neue Technologien eher zögerlich aufzugreifen. Bei KI zeichnet sich ein anderes Bild ab: Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen setzen die Technologie mit bemerkenswertem Tempo ein. Für den deutschen Markt reicht es nicht, KI ins Deutsche zu übersetzen. Sie muss auf das deutsche Recht und die Arbeitsweise juristischer Teams ausgerichtet sein. In unseren Gesprächen mit Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz verändern sich die Fragen. In ersten Tests von KI-Lösungen für den Rechtsbereich ging es vor allem darum, wie verlässlich KI bei Recherche, Analyse und Entwürfen unterstützt. Inzwischen beschäftigen sich die Teams zunehmend mit der Auswahl eines passenden Anbieters, der Einführung im Team und der Einbindung in bestehende Arbeitsabläufe. Bei der Auswahl einer passenden Lösung zeigt sich in intensiven Pilotphasen, wie gut sie zum eigenen Arbeitsalltag passt. Teams bringen dafür ihre vorhandenen Unterlagen, ihr Wissen und ihre internen Vorgaben ein. Entscheidend ist, wie gut Legora diese Informationen nutzbar macht und sich an die Arbeitsweise des jeweiligen Teams anpasst: wie Ergebnisse aufbereitet werden, wie sie in die weitere Beratung einfließen und wie Kolleginnen und Kollegen damit zusammenarbeiten. Was deutsche juristische Arbeit von KI verlangt Wer Rechts-KI in Deutschland einführt, trifft auf konkrete fachliche Anforderungen. Das beginnt bei der Sprache. Eine juristische Stellungnahme auf Deutsch muss Fachbegriffe präzise verwenden, die relevante Fragestellung erfassen und eine nachvollziehbare Argumentation enthalten. Bei grenzüberschreitenden Mandaten kommen unterschiedliche Arbeitssprachen hinzu. Ein englischsprachiger Vertrag kann die Grundlage für eine deutsche Stellungnahme bilden, die anschließend mit einem internationalen Team abgestimmt wird. Eigene Vertragsmuster und frühere Stellungnahmen ermöglichen es Teams, Entwürfe in Legora an den fachlichen und sprachlichen Standards ihrer Organisation auszurichten. Ebenso entscheidend sind die Rechtsquellen. Gesetze, Rechtsprechung und Kommentarliteratur bilden zusammen mit dem Wissen der jeweiligen Organisation die Grundlage juristischer Arbeit. Für KI-Anwendungen bedeutet das: Der Zugang zu relevanten Inhalten, erkennbare Fundstellen und die Möglichkeit zur Überprüfung müssen im Arbeitsablauf mitgedacht werden. Deutsche Fachverlage spielen deshalb auch bei der Entwicklung von Rechts-KI eine wichtige Rolle. Wer Module von Otto Schmidt abonniert hat, kann diese direkt in Legora nutzen. Hinzu kommt der Umgang mit Daten. Kanzleien und Unternehmen benötigen konkrete Antworten darauf, wo Informationen verarbeitet werden, wer darauf zugreifen kann und wie ihre Verwendung geregelt ist. Datensouveränität und Vertraulichkeit gehören damit an den Anfang der Einführung. Wer Rechts-KI für Deutschland auswählt, sollte ihre Qualität an deutscher juristischer Arbeit messen. Gute Ergebnisse im britischen oder US-amerikanischen Rechtskontext lassen sich nicht ohne Weiteres übertragen. Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen sollten deshalb anhand eigener Fälle prüfen, ob eine Lösung relevante deutsche Quellen einbezieht, juristische Begriffe präzise verwendet und ihre Ergebnisse nachvollziehbar belegt. Ebenso muss sie die Anforderungen der Organisation an Vertraulichkeit und Zusammenarbeit erfüllen. Wie Rechtsabteilungen ihren KI-Einsatz weiterentwickeln Nachdem sich der Nutzen für einzelne Mitarbeitende bewährt hat, wird die Organisation der Zusammenarbeit zur entscheidenden Aufgabe. Die besonders stark wachsende Nutzung in Rechtsabteilungen lenkt den Blick auf deren Rolle im Unternehmen. Hier muss juristische Beratung Geschäftsbereiche und Länder miteinander verbinden und Entscheidungen im gesamten Unternehmen unterstützen. In Rechtsabteilungen kommen mehrere Anforderungen zusammen. Häufig betreuen vergleichsweise kleine Teams ein breites Aufgabenspektrum: Vertragsarbeit, gesellschaftsrechtliche Fragen, regulatorische Entwicklungen und die laufende Beratung des Unternehmens. Bei international tätigen Organisationen erstreckt sich diese Arbeit über mehrere Rechtsordnungen. In der Zusammenarbeit mit diesen Teams sehen wir, was die strategische Nutzung von KI konkret verlangt: Bewährte Anwendungen sollen für weitere Kolleginnen und Kollegen nutzbar werden. Bereits erarbeitete Einschätzungen sollen leichter auffindbar sein. Wiederkehrende Aufgaben sollen nach gemeinsamen Standards bearbeitet werden. Zeitersparnis bei einzelnen Aufgaben ist ein zu enger Maßstab für den Nutzen von KI. Kürzere Abstimmungswege, weniger doppelte Arbeit und leichter zugängliches Wissen schaffen Raum für Aufgaben, bei denen juristische Erfahrung und Urteilsvermögen besonders gefragt sind: komplexe Risiken bewerten, Handlungsoptionen abwägen und wichtige Geschäftsentscheidungen frühzeitig begleiten. Wie dieser Freiraum genutzt wird, ist eine Führungsaufgabe. Die Leitung der Rechtsabteilung muss Prioritäten setzen und die gewonnene Zeit gezielt einplanen: für die engere Zusammenarbeit mit den Geschäftsbereichen, die Begleitung strategischer Vorhaben oder rechtliche Fragen, die im Tagesgeschäft bisher zu kurz kamen. Der Erfolg von KI zeigt sich damit auch daran, welchen Beitrag die Rechtsabteilung zu den Entscheidungen des Unternehmens leisten kann. Wie Teams Wissen bündeln und Entwicklungen einordnen Für diese Beratung muss das Wissen einer Organisation über einzelne Teams und Standorte hinweg nutzbar sein. Legora unterstützt Teams dabei, Wissen aus Verträgen, internen Richtlinien und früheren Einschätzungen zusammenzuführen. Kanzleien können so vorhandene Erfahrung für neue Fragestellungen nutzen; Rechtsabteilungen erhalten eine gemeinsame Grundlage für die Beratung über Geschäftsbereiche und Länder hinweg. Neben dem vorhandenen Wissen müssen Teams auch neue regulatorische Entwicklungen berücksichtigen. Dabei geht es darum, deren Auswirkungen auf interne Richtlinien und strategische Vorhaben des Unternehmens einzuordnen. Mit Legora Monitors können Teams relevante Entwicklungen verfolgen und als Ausgangspunkt für die weitere Analyse nutzen. So kann Rechts-KI dazu beitragen, Zusammenhänge früher sichtbar zu machen: Welche Veränderung betrifft mehrere Gesellschaften? Wo entsteht gemeinsamer Handlungsbedarf? Welche Erkenntnisse sind für eine Investition oder den Eintritt in einen neuen Markt relevant? Damit dieses Potenzial im Alltag wirksam wird, brauchen Teams gemeinsame Arbeitsweisen und klare Zuständigkeiten. Sie müssen festlegen, wie Wissen bereitgestellt, Ergebnisse geprüft und neue Abläufe übernommen werden. Hier setzt die Zusammenarbeit mit unseren Legal Engineers an. Wie Legal Engineers die Einführung begleiten Unsere Legal Engineers bringen eigene juristische Praxiserfahrung mit. Sie verstehen die Anforderungen an eine belastbare Analyse und kennen die Abläufe in Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen. Gemeinsam mit dem Team klären sie, welche Aufgaben sich für den KI-Einsatz eignen, wie sich vorhandene Abläufe sinnvoll weiterentwickeln lassen und welche Unterstützung die Mitarbeitenden benötigen. Die Begleitung entwickelt sich mit dem Team weiter. In der Einarbeitungsphase stehen das Ausprobieren, der sichere Umgang mit der Plattform und die Bewertung der Ergebnisse im Vordergrund. Wenn der individuelle Nutzen belegt ist, unterstützen Legal Engineers dabei, bewährte Anwendungen zu gemeinsamen Standards weiterzuentwickeln und im Team zu verankern. Warum die Präsenz vor Ort zählt Mit unserem Büro in München bauen wir diese Zusammenarbeit in der DACH-Region weiter aus. Der Standort bringt uns näher an unsere Partner und an juristische sowie technische Fachkräfte. Viele dieser Partnerschaften bestanden schon vor der Eröffnung. Auf ihnen bauen wir auf. Persönlicher Austausch erleichtert es, Arbeitsweisen zu verstehen, Anwendungen gemeinsam zu entwickeln und Erfahrungen aus der Praxis aufzunehmen. Mit unserem Team in München erhält diese persönliche Begleitung nun eine dauerhafte Basis vor Ort. Gerade wenn Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen ihren KI-Einsatz ausweiten, gewinnt diese Begleitung an Bedeutung. Wir erwarten, dass KI in den kommenden Jahren zu einem selbstverständlichen Bestandteil juristischer Arbeit in der DACH-Region wird. Mit der breiteren Nutzung werden die Erwartungen steigen: Gefragt sind Lösungen, die das Wissen einer Organisation erschließen und ganze Arbeitsabläufe unterstützen. Entscheidend wird sein, wie gut Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen diese Möglichkeiten in ihrer täglichen Arbeit verankern. English Legal AI in the DACH region: What matters now to law firms and legal departments At the start of 2026, around 3,000 lawyers in Germany were working with Legora. By the time our Munich office opened at the end of September, that figure had already passed 13,000. Growth is particularly strong in legal departments, where the number of users has increased eightfold since January. Germany has a reputation for taking its time with new technology. With AI, a different picture is emerging: law firms and legal departments are adopting it at a remarkable pace. Legal AI for Germany needs more than a German-language interface. It must be built around German law and the way legal teams work. The questions we hear in conversations with law firms and legal departments in Germany, Austria and Switzerland are changing. Early trials of legal AI focused mainly on how reliably AI could support research, analysis and drafting. Legal teams are now increasingly considering how to choose the right provider, introduce AI across the team and integrate it into existing workflows. When choosing a suitable solution, teams use extensive pilots to assess how well it fits their everyday work. They use their existing documents, knowledge and internal guidelines as the basis for these pilots. What matters is how effectively Legora puts this information to use and adapts to the way each team works: how findings are presented, how they inform subsequent advice and how colleagues use them together. What legal work in Germany demands of AI Introducing legal AI in Germany means meeting specific professional requirements. Language is the starting point. A legal opinion written in German must use technical terms precisely, address the relevant legal question and present a clear line of reasoning. Cross-border matters add different working languages to the mix. An English-language contract may form the basis of a German legal opinion that is then discussed with an international team. Teams can use their own contract templates and previous legal opinions to align drafts in Legora with their organisation’s legal and language standards. Legal sources are equally important. Legislation, case law and legal commentary, together with an organisation’s own knowledge, form the foundation of legal work. For AI applications, this means that access to relevant content, clear source references and the ability to verify results must be built into the workflow. German legal publishers therefore also play an important role in the development of legal AI. Subscribers to Otto Schmidt modules can use them directly in Legora. Data handling is another consideration. Law firms and businesses need specific answers about where information is processed, who can access it and how its use is governed. Data sovereignty and confidentiality therefore need to be addressed from the outset. Teams choosing legal AI for Germany should judge its quality against German legal work. Strong performance in UK or US legal contexts does not automatically translate to German practice. Law firms and legal departments should therefore test solutions on their own matters: do they draw on relevant German sources, use legal terminology precisely and provide traceable support for their findings? They must also meet the organisation’s requirements for confidentiality and collaboration. How legal departments are developing their use of AI Once AI has proved its value for individual team members, the key task becomes organising how the team works together. The particularly strong growth in adoption among legal departments draws attention to their role within the business. Their legal advice needs to connect business units and countries and support decisions across the organisation. Legal departments face several demands at once. Relatively small teams often handle a broad range of work: contracts, corporate law matters, regulatory developments and ongoing advice to the business. In international organisations, this work spans multiple jurisdictions. In our work with these teams, we see what the strategic use of AI requires in practice: proven use cases need to become available to more colleagues. Previous assessments need to be easier to find. Recurring tasks need to follow shared standards. Time saved per task is too narrow a measure of AI’s value. Smoother coordination, less duplication and easier access to knowledge create room for work that draws most on lawyers’ experience and judgement: assessing complex risks, weighing options and helping shape important business decisions from the outset. How that capacity is used is a leadership decision. Legal department leaders need to set priorities and deliberately allocate the time gained: to closer collaboration with business teams, strategic projects or legal issues that previously received too little attention amid day-to-day demands. AI’s success should therefore also be measured by the contribution the legal department can make to business decisions. How teams bring knowledge together and assess new developments To provide this advice, teams need to be able to draw on their organisation’s knowledge across teams and locations. Legora helps them bring together knowledge from contracts, internal policies and previous assessments. This allows law firms to apply existing expertise to new questions and legal departments to develop a shared basis for advice across business units and countries. Alongside existing knowledge, teams also need to account for new regulatory developments. This involves assessing their implications for internal policies and the company’s strategic initiatives. With Legora Monitors, teams can track relevant developments and use them as a starting point for further analysis.In this way, legal AI can help teams identify connections earlier: which changes affect several group companies? Where is a coordinated response needed? Which insights are relevant to an investment or entry into a new market? To realise this potential in everyday work, teams need shared ways of working and clear responsibilities. They must agree on how knowledge is made available, results are reviewed and new processes are adopted. This is where their work with our Legal Engineers begins. How Legal Engineers support adoption Our Legal Engineers bring their own experience of legal practice. They understand what robust analysis requires and how law firms and legal departments operate. Together with the team, they identify which tasks are suited to AI, how existing workflows can be developed further and what support team members need. This support evolves with the team. During the initial learning phase, the focus is on experimentation, using the platform confidently and evaluating results. Once the value for individual users has been demonstrated, Legal Engineers help turn proven use cases into shared standards and embed them across the team. Change management also means listening to questions and concerns, involving those responsible and using feedback to guide further development. This creates an ongoing dialogue about what works in practice and where more support is needed. This close collaboration also shapes the expansion of our presence in Germany. Our Munich office allows us to deepen this collaboration across the DACH region. It brings us closer to our partners and to legal and technical talent. Many of these partnerships were already in place before the office opened. We are building on them. Face-to-face conversations make it easier to understand ways of working, develop use cases together and learn from practical experience. With our Munich team, this personal support now has a permanent local base. This support becomes increasingly important as law firms and legal departments expand their use of AI. We expect AI to become a routine part of legal work across the DACH region over the coming years. As adoption broadens, expectations will rise: teams will look for solutions that make organisational knowledge accessible and support entire workflows. What will matter is how effectively law firms and legal departments embed these capabilities in their everyday work. blogs.description: How legal teams are transforming their departments with Harvey to better serve the enterprise and help the business move faster.
blogs.content: Insights Building a Frontier In-House Organization How legal teams are transforming their departments with Harvey to better serve the enterprise and help the business move faster. by Matt Zerweck and Gabe Pereyra • Oct 13, 2026 Satya Nadella describes the frontier firm as a company built around intelligence on demand, where people and agents work side by side. Inside most companies, the legal department is where that shift arrives first. For the general counsels we work with, the question used to be how to get lawyers to use AI. Now it’s how to run the department on it. Behind that shift are four challenges we hear from in-house teams: Legal as the bottleneck. Lawyers spend too much time on work that doesn’t need legal judgment, instead of working at the top of their license. Rising volume, flat headcount. Demand for Legal grows with the business but headcount and budgets do not. Reactive instead of proactive. Regulatory change and contract risk surface late, when they’re already problems. No portfolio visibility. Contract history, obligations, and outside matters are scattered across systems, inboxes, and law firms. None of these problems stay in one lane. A single contract can be a bottleneck, a capacity problem, and a visibility gap at once. And when requests queue up and the business can’t see where they stand, employees bypass Legal and take legal questions to general-purpose AI tools, outside Legal’s controls. Banning that doesn't work. The frontier move is to give the business a better place to ask, with Legal in control of the answers. The Platform for a Frontier Legal Department Figure 1. The legal department of a frontier firm with everything in one place. We’re building Harvey as one platform for the business, its legal team, and outside counsel. It connects every request, contract, and matter with the documents, conversations, and context behind it. That knowledge, including the department’s policies, prior decisions, and outcomes, is codified in one legal brain that people and agents draw on as they work. Legal decides what agents can handle and where people should make the call. Legal puts that knowledge to work across requests, contracts, and matters. It sets what agents can handle, where people make the call, and when to involve outside counsel. Past matters, outcomes, and invoice data help Legal choose the right firm for the work. Requests come in and follow-up questions, updates, and completed work go back through the channels the business already uses. Each outcome adds to the department’s knowledge, informing the next decision. Figure 2. The platform architecture. Connected systems feed a shared model of the department’s work, with source permissions preserved. Harvey’s products and agents draw on that same model. If a sales lead asks whether a customer deal can include a new AI-use clause, Harvey can pull up the original request, the department’s position on AI clauses, the terms the company has agreed to before, and the EU rules that apply, all in one answer. We've built that connectivity with partners over several years. Harvey runs on Microsoft Azure and works inside Microsoft 365 , from Word to Copilot Cowork. It connects to LexisNexis for primary law, to Docusign and Ironclad for contract workflows, and through the Connector Library to the rest of the systems the department already uses. Resolve Requests Wherever the Business Works Intake extends the department’s legal front door across email, chat, and business systems, including Outlook, Gmail, Slack, Teams, Jira, ServiceNow, and Salesforce. Harvey gathers context, then routes and assigns work by type, risk, and department. Agents and lawyers send follow-up questions, updates, and completed work back through the same channels. Figure 3. Three paths for a request, with Legal setting the rules. Answers and completed work return to the business. Adapted from Winston Weinberg’s FORUM New York in-house keynote. Legal decides how each request is handled and when to escalate: Deflect routine work. Approved agents answer questions or complete work within Legal’s rules, without adding it to the team’s queue. Prepare work for judgment. Harvey gathers context, researches, drafts, and flags issues so the assigned team can make the call. Bring in outside expertise. Work routes to the firm Legal designates, with the request and relevant company context prepared in a Shared Space. Legal sets what agents may resolve and when review is required. A full audit log records every agent and human action and decision. Advice and outcomes feed back into the department’s knowledge, helping Legal improve responses and identify more work to deflect. Move Negotiations Faster and Put Every Agreement to Work Contracting is where most in-house work gets lost. Legal moves contracts through every negotiation round by hand, where history and next steps are scattered across email threads, systems, and people. Contract Intelligence , which we launched in May, is the contracting layer for the department. We’re building agents to carry contracts from request through multi-turn negotiation, approvals, and signature, then track what the company has committed to in order to proactively manage commitments and mitigate risk for the business. It works seamlessly alongside existing CLM and procurement systems, so the team can move deals faster without reconstructing their history at every step. As an example, say a salesperson forwards a counterparty’s marked-up agreement. Harvey connects it to the deal, prior drafts, and related agreements, reviews the changes, and prepares the response. Across each round, it carries forward agreed positions, routes exceptions for review according to rules set by Legal, and coordinates the next steps toward signature. Figure 4. Contract Intelligence brings contracting work across the business into one platform, with a shared record of agreements and decisions. “ When you’re in the kind of sustained, high-growth environment we’ve experienced at GE Aerospace over the past five-plus years, the pressure to move faster on contracts while protecting your people from overburden is real. Harvey’s Contract Intelligence has been one of the most impactful tools we’ve deployed to tackle both challenges simultaneously and upholding our world class contracting standards. ” John Cooke Senior Director, North America Contracts Leader, GE Aerospace Every review depends on the department's judgment, and historically most of it has lived in individual lawyers' heads. Two reviewers could give the same contract two different answers. Playbooks and Contract Review Agents standardize and ground reviews in the department’s documents, precedents, and historical judgment. Every decision adds to that history: what Legal changed, what the counterparty accepted, and what was signed. Future reviews learn from those outcomes, while Legal decides which lessons become updates to its standards . Put Signed Agreements to Work Before a renewal, an account manager can ask Harvey, “What mattered most to this customer last time?” Harvey brings together the agreement and negotiation history to show what the customer pushed for, what the company agreed to, and which commitments the team needs to honor. That context helps the business better serve the customer and prepare for the next negotiation. Across the portfolio, that same history helps business teams compare concessions and gives Legal visibility into where unusual terms and risk are accumulating by showing what the business is negotiating and agreeing to. We’re extending that work into obligation management , with owners and deadlines so teams can act before a missed commitment or unwanted renewal becomes a cost. Turn Regulatory Change Into Action Contract Intelligence helps teams get ahead of what they have agreed to. Horizon Scanning helps them respond to what changes outside the company. A global company answers to regulators in every market it operates in, and the rules change every week. Most legal departments find out late, then scramble to work out what a change touches. Horizon Scanning monitors the topics, regions, and regulators a team wants to follow, drawing on more than 12,000 sources across over 100 jurisdictions. Teams can assess relevant changes and use Harvey to draft policy revisions, guidance, and next steps. Figure 5. Horizon Scanning: connect a development to affected policies and agreements, then coordinate the response. We’re connecting those developments to the department’s contracts, policies, open requests, and past decisions. A new rule should not only inform them of the impact but should reveal which agreements may need amendments and which advice needs revisiting, with work assigned to Legal, HR, or Compliance and a record of what was completed to ensure the risk has been mitigated. Deutsche Telekom already uses Harvey across its German legal, compliance, and data protection teams, turning regulations such as the EU Batteries Regulation into actionable summaries in minutes. Give Outside Counsel the Context to Move Faster Most legal departments struggle to say what their firms are working on right now. The work sits in each firm's own systems, and the department sees it mostly through invoices. Harvey already works with both the legal departments and their law firms. Connecting the two means outside counsel can start with the business context and work the legal department has already done. In Shared Spaces , legal teams and firms work on the same matter with permissions on both sides. Each firm sees its own work and relevant context; Legal sees progress across matters. Deutsche Telekom and Gleiss Lutz are setting the direction here: after years of using Harvey separately, they brought their collaboration into the platform, on a foundation of shared context, security, and trust. Figure 6. In-house teams and their law firms collaborate on shared matters in Harvey, while each organization retains its own workspace. We’re building toward better decisions about who should do the work. Matter history, performance, and invoice data can help Legal understand scope, quality, speed, and cost across its firm relationships. When work goes to outside counsel, Harvey can prepare a Shared Space with relevant documents, prior advice, and business context from the department’s internal systems, reducing initial context sharing and cold start problems folks have struggled with in the past. With that shared context, outside counsel can build on the department’s work and tailor its advice to the company’s priorities. That can make outside expertise worthwhile on work once kept in-house because it was too slow or costly to send out. Firms can deliver new services to more of their clients, while departments get more from their outside spend. Putting Legal at the Center of Agent Governance Running this across an enterprise requires permissions, approved agents, and a record of their actions. Command Center helps the people leading the deployment understand usage, find gaps, and assess where to expand. The platform’s security controls protect sensitive work, and we do not train models on customer data. The next shift may be the most important. The policies Legal helps the company follow will also need to govern its agents, from sales drafting order forms to procurement onboarding vendors. Legal, Compliance, Risk, and IT/Security will share that responsibility. We’re building Command Center as their common platform, with Legal at the center: policies turned into rules agents are checked against, limits on what each can do, monitoring of every run, and exceptions routed to accountable owners. Figure 7. The enterprise governance vision: check agents against company policies and the law, monitor their work, and route exceptions to accountable owners. A More Profitable Business The case for a frontier in-house organization isn't a smaller legal department. It's a faster, safer, more profitable business. Faster contracts bring revenue and suppliers online sooner. Timely answers keep business teams moving. Acting earlier on obligations and regulatory changes reduces exposure to disputes and avoidable costs. Better allocation across agents, the internal team, and outside counsel gives Legal more capacity to advise on strategy, products, and growth. In RSGI’s research , 92% of surveyed in-house teams using Harvey report faster turnaround for the business, 91% save time on contract review, and 88% spend more time with the business on higher-value work. In its latest report , nearly half describe Harvey as foundational to how they deliver legal services. Built for Every Industry Every frontier in-house organization will look different, because every industry does. The platform underneath will be the same. The priorities vary by industry: regulatory work at a bank, commercial contracts and product counsel at a technology company, suppliers and workforce issues at a consumer business. Each department brings its own context and standards. Harvey works with five of the Fortune 10 and one in five of the Fortune 500, across more than 1,600 in-house teams. Some of the largest run it across the whole function. The Adecco Group’s legal and compliance department has more than 300 professionals, and over 80% of its lawyers report better quality and speed. It’s also spreading beyond Legal: Repsol’s legal department reached 96% adoption, and its tax and labor departments have since adopted Harvey too. Frontier Research for In-House Work This vision depends on agents doing the work reliably. In June we added 500 in-house contracting tasks to our open-source Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), across ten contract families. Each tests whether an agent can advance a negotiation from a given point, with every criterion required to pass. In Artificial Analysis’s launch evaluation of LAB , the leading model setup fully passed just 14.2% of tasks. Reliable legal work remains a hard research problem. Harvey is model-neutral: We work with models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google , route each task to the model system that handles it best, and train our own. Harvey Tenet is our first model post-trained for long-horizon legal work. It completes nearly twice as many held-out LAB tasks as the model it started from, and about 20% more contracting tasks. We are also working to make reliable legal work more economical. Post-training improves how efficiently models use tools and reason. Figure 8. Quality and cost on LAB: Contracts. LAB and Harvey Tenet use synthetic matters, public legal data, and expert review. Customer data is not used to train the models. Figure 9. How Harvey Tenet is trained and measured, with results on held-out LAB tasks and LAB: Contracts. Source: Harvey Tenet research. What Comes Next A legal department can start with one repeatable workflow: define the risk it is willing to delegate, connect the relevant context and channels, and measure whether the business gets good work back faster. Legal reviews the results, improves its guidance, and expands from there. We’re extending Intake into more of the places the business works, Contract Intelligence across the deal lifecycle, and search and models around the department’s own work. The business gets answers and completed work where it operates, backed by the department’s judgment. We’ll show more at a live demo for in-house teams on October 29 and at FORUM Chicago on November 5. The legal departments we work with are already building this. If you’re building it inside your company, we’d like to build it with you. blogs.content: Company Harvey to Open Tokyo Office by Harvey Team • Oct 12, 2026 Harvey will open an office in Tokyo in early 2027, deepening our commitment to supporting law firms and in-house legal teams in Japan. Trust is earned over time through close collaboration and consistent support. As we grow in Japan, we are investing in a local presence to build lasting relationships, listen to our customers, and ensure their needs guide how we continue to build and grow here. Our Tokyo office will support our growing customer base in Japan and deepen relationships with law firms including Mori Hamada & Matsumoto and Nagashima Ohno & Tsunematsu, and in-house legal teams, including Mitsubishi Corporation. A local presence will help us work more closely with these teams and strengthen the support we provide. We are also building Harvey to better support work in Japanese and reflect the needs of legal professionals in Japan. This includes our partnership with Legalscape for Japanese legal research. Working with local experts and listening to customer feedback will help guide how we develop our product and support its use. “Japan is a critical market for legal and home to many exceptional law firms and companies. With the government investing in AI acceleration country-wide, there’s no better time to bring Harvey to Tokyo,” said Winston Weinberg, Harvey’s Chief Executive Officer. “Having a team in Japan will help us better understand the needs of legal professionals in Japan and make their experience central to how we build and grow here.” Koji Toshima, Partner and CFO, Mori Hamada & Matsumoto, said, “Since establishing our partnership with Harvey in 2024, we have worked closely together to explore how AI can enhance the quality and efficiency of legal services in Japan. Harvey’s decision to open a Tokyo office is a very welcome and significant milestone, demonstrating its strong commitment to the Japanese legal market. Building on our collaboration to date, including our recent support in bringing about the partnership between Harvey and Legalscape, we look forward to further strengthening our collaboration with Harvey to advance the development of innovative AI solutions tailored to the needs of Japanese legal practice and deliver even greater value to our clients in Japan and around the world.” Tokyo will expand Harvey’s existing presence across Asia-Pacific, alongside our teams in Sydney, Singapore, and Bengaluru. Globally, more than 3,500 customers in over 85 countries use Harvey. We are grateful for the trust our customers in Japan have placed in us and look forward to building on our work here, alongside the lawyers and legal teams we serve. Harvey、東京オフィスを開設へ Harveyは2027年初頭に東京オフィスを開設し、日本の法律事務所および企業法務部門へのサポートをさらに強化してまいります。 信頼は、緊密な連携と継続的なサポートを通じて、時間をかけて築かれるものです。日本での事業拡大にあたり、当社は国内での体制づくりに投資しています。お客様と長期的な関係を築き、その声に耳を傾けながら、お客様のニーズを踏まえて、今後の日本でのプロダクト開発と事業展開を進めてまいります。 東京オフィスは、日本で増え続けるお客様をサポートします。また、森・濱田松本法律事務所、長島・大野・常松法律事務所などの法律事務所や、三菱商事などの企業法務部門との関係をさらに深めていきます。東京に拠点を置くことで、お客様とより緊密に連携し、サポートの充実を図ってまいります。 あわせて、日本語での業務への対応を強化し、日本で法務に携わる皆様のニーズに応えるべく、Harveyの開発を進めています。その一環として、日本法に関するリーガルリサーチ分野でLegalscape（リーガルスケープ）と提携しています。今後も国内の専門家と連携し、お客様からのご意見を取り入れながら、プロダクト開発と活用支援を進めてまいります。 当社の最高経営責任者（CEO）であるウィンストン・ワインバーグ（Winston Weinberg）は次のように述べています。「日本は法務分野において極めて重要な市場であり、数多くの優れた法律事務所や企業が拠点を置いています。政府が国を挙げてAI活用の加速に投資している今こそ、Harveyを東京に展開する絶好の機会です。日本にチームを置くことで、法務に携わる皆様のニーズをより深く理解し、その経験を日本でのプロダクト開発と事業展開の中心に据えることができます。」 森・濱田松本法律事務所 パートナー兼CFOの戸嶋浩二氏は、次のように述べています。「2024年にHarveyとのパートナーシップを締結して以来、当事務所はHarveyと緊密に連携し、AIによって日本のリーガルサービスの質と効率をいかに高められるかを探求してまいりました。このたびの東京オフィス開設は、日本の法律市場に対するHarveyの強いコミットメントを示すものであり、大変喜ばしく、意義深い節目と受け止めています。先般のHarveyとLegalscapeの提携実現に向けた支援をはじめとするこれまでの協業を礎に、Harveyとの連携をさらに強化し、日本の法実務のニーズに即した革新的なAIソリューションの開発を推進することで、国内外のクライアントの皆様に一層の価値をお届けしてまいりたいと考えております。」 現在、Harveyは世界85か国以上で3,500社を超えるお客様にご利用いただいています。東京オフィスの開設により、シドニー、シンガポール、ベンガルールの既存拠点に加え、アジア太平洋地域におけるHarveyのプレゼンスがさらに拡大します。日本のお客様からお寄せいただいている信頼に心より感謝申し上げるとともに、今後も弁護士や法務チームの皆様とともに、日本での取り組みを一層発展させてまいります。 Next Up Harvey to Open Boston Office The Ultimate Guide to Landing a Job at Harvey Y Combinator-Backed Benchmark Joins Harvey
