blogs.content: Product Introducing the Motion to Dismiss Workflow, Co-Developed With LexisNexisⓇ Draft a fully researched, citation-backed motion to dismiss in Harvey, grounded in the LexisNexis collection of U.S. case law, statutes, and Shepard's® Citations Service. by Harvey Team • Oct 7, 2026 In June 2025, we announced our strategic alliance with LexisNexis® to integrate LexisNexis AI technology, primary law content, and Shepard's® Citations within the Harvey platform, and to jointly develop advanced legal workflows. Since that announcement, we introduced Ask LexisNexis to bring citation-backed answers grounded in LexisNexis primary law content directly into Harvey. Today, we're introducing the first of our co-developed workflows: a drafting agent for an entire Motion to Dismiss (MTD). From Weeks of Associate Time to a Single Review-and-Approve Loop Drafting a motion to dismiss is one of the most time-intensive tasks in early-stage litigation. Typically, an associate has to read the complaint, spot viable grounds for dismissal, research each ground in the right jurisdiction, check for adverse authority, and draft 20–30 pages of intensely researched arguments. This multi-step process commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work. The new MTD workflow streamlines this entire process — just upload the complaint, approve the strategy, review the research brief, and watch Harvey prepare your first draft. How it Works The MTD workflow is agentic: a series of specialized agents plan, research, and draft in a review-and-approve loop, with human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer's judgment matters most. This loop breaks down into four stages: Harvey reviews the complaint and proposes a set of ranked arguments for dismissal The lawyer approves or adjusts the plan Multiple agents conduct in-depth research on each approved argument A final agent drafts the motion A planning agent reads the complaint and proposes a strategy. Harvey starts by identifying the forum and the governing law, then runs an initial research pass with LexisNexis US primary law to surface up to eight candidate grounds for dismissal. Harvey checks each ground against the specific elements of the claims pleaded — a missing element of a cause of action, a jurisdictional defect, a timeliness issue — while weighing the authority honestly and factoring in choice-of-law issues. Harvey rates each ground by strength, so the lawyer can see at a glance where the complaint is vulnerable and where the motion may be strongest. It then produces a proposed strategy: a ranked set of arguments the lawyer can build the motion around. The lawyer reviews and approves the plan. Each proposed argument is presented with its strength rating and a short explanation of the basis for each rating. From here, the lawyer can approve the plan as-is or give feedback to add or drop arguments before deep research and drafting begin. This is the point in the process where the attorney's judgment has the most influence over the final motion.› Parallel research agents run LexisNexis searches for each approved ground. Agents use jurisdiction-filtered, boolean queries tuned to find cases at the motion-to-dismiss stage. Where state authority is thin, they supplement with federal decisions applying that state's law. This research comes back as a memo for each argument, containing the applicable legal standard and the three to five of the strongest cases. Each case includes a full Bluebook citation, a direct link to the opinion on Lexis+® with Protégé™, its key holding, and how it applies to the specific allegations at issue. The memo also analyzes how the case law supports the theory, including the weaknesses the plaintiff is likely to raise, plus key adverse authority and how to distinguish it. Cases are validated through Shepard's ® Citations, with the Shepard’s Signal™ reported alongside them. A drafting agent assembles the motion. The agent drafts argument sections that weave the complaint's allegations together with the authority that the research agents retrieved, in both federal and state court. For a state-court complaint, it detects the caption and confirms the correct procedural vehicle for that forum — a demurrer in California, a CPLR 3211 motion in New York, preliminary objections in Pennsylvania, and so on. For a federal complaint, it drafts to the Rule 12(b)(6) standard — accepting the well-pleaded allegations as true and testing whether they state a plausible claim under Twombly and Iqbal — and addressing any other threshold 12(b) grounds available on the face of the pleading. Throughout the draft, every factual assertion is cited back to the complaint, and every legal proposition is cited to case law, so each statement is checkable against the record and the authority behind it. The result is a motion drafted end-to-end, complete with a Table of Contents and Table of Authorities, the forum-specific pleading standard, and motion-appropriate formatting. How to Get Started Instead of an associate spending days on research and a first draft, Harvey produces both in a matter of hours, with the lawyer's review built into the process at each stage. The time saved can go toward refining strategy, addressing edge cases, or simply moving the case forward faster. The Motion to Dismiss workflow is available to all Harvey customers who have access to Ask LexisNexis, and Harvey customers who are also Lexis+® with Protégé™ customers, whether or not they use the Ask LexisNexis integration. What's Next This is the first of two co-developed workflows we are building with LexisNexis, and a Motion for Summary Judgment workflow is next. Ready to see the MTD workflow in action? blogs.content: Amy Conroy: From joining Legora as the first UK hire to driving adoption at scale | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Legora voices Amy Conroy: From joining Legora as the first UK hire to driving adoption at scale Amy Conroy: From joining Legora as the first UK hire to driving adoption at scale Category Legora voices published Aug 11, 2026 author Team Legora Before joining Legora as its first UK employee, Amy Conroy’s career had already taken a somewhat unconventional path for a law graduate. Amy studied law at the University of Bristol, where her final-year research explored AI and the right to be forgotten, specifically the extent to which personal data can be removed from machine learning algorithms. “I was still interested in becoming a solicitor, but I was also really interested in the tech side of things,” she says. Amy followed up on her law studies with a conversion course in computer science and kicked off her career with a role at a document automation start-up, before moving into a position as a data scientist at one of Legora’s UK clients, Mishcon de Reya. By early 2024, she was ready for a change. “One thing I really missed about working at a start-up originally was that you’re all working towards the same goal: to have the best product and to make sure that it’s fully adopted by all of your clients.” Building from scratch Amy met Legora’s Co-Founder and CEO Max in July 2024, and was flown to Stockholm to meet the wider team, which consisted of around 15 people at the time. The pitch was clear: help Legora build a UK customer base that includes some of the biggest law firms in the world. When she started, there were around 30 people globally and 12 in growth. She has now helped to scale the UK office to almost 100 people, and now leads on driving adoption among UK clients. Amy spent her early days meeting prospective clients, supporting pilots, and converting early interest into long-term partnerships. “As the company has scaled, my remit has narrowed and become more specialised. Originally, it covered sales, legal engineering, and customer success too. It was a lot of fun, and I learnt a lot!” What does client adoption actually take? Amy describes her role as “the orchestrator of the account.” Her role is now focused on driving adoption among clients, running training and adoption programmes across Legora’s biggest accounts where platform features aren’t being used as deeply as they could be, and pulling in colleagues from legal engineering, product, and support as needed. “There is a real opportunity to drive usage of the platform. Legora evolves so quickly that there are always opportunities to go back into firms and teach them what’s new and how they can use it. Especially with generative AI, something that didn’t work a month ago will work now because the models are improving so rapidly.” One example she’s particularly proud of involves a law firm that rolled out Legora in 2024, where adoption of newer features had plateaued. Amy and her team designed a re-engagement programme. Unlike a routine training programme, they identified two to three high-performing users within each of the client’s practice areas to demonstrate back to their own teams how they had been using the platform in their day-to-day work. “It drove monthly adoption up by 10%. Not only had users gained practical knowledge of the features, but they’d seen colleagues demonstrate how much of their manual work could be handled through AI.” A consistent theme in the feedback from Legora’s earlier clients, Amy says, has been to preserve what attracted them in the first place: the partnership aspect. “They look at us like an extension of their team, not just another vendor. All of our engagement managers have smaller client portfolios, which means we can maintain those deep relationships with them. We’re constantly on site with them, and that is something we continue to make a priority. That’s one of the things that makes being right in the City of London so great!” Growing leaders, not just headcount Amy’s team now includes a number of associates who are new to careers in legal technology. Around a year ago, roles like this at Legora were few and far between. Hiring exceptional young talent has become a major focus for Legora as the company has scaled. Developing that talent in the London office is something Amy takes pride in. “What’s really exciting is seeing them try out different parts of their role and starting to understand what they’re really interested in, as well as growing into their specific skillset.” Her approach to leadership is grounded in honesty and perspective. “In the first instance, I like to make sure that I’m calling out what has gone well. That’s important, especially as we’re moving so quickly. We have to make sure we keep recognising great work when everything around us is moving at such pace.” When things don’t go well, Amy emphasises the importance of centring feedback on personal growth and opportunity rather than blame. “It’s never personal; it needs to be framed around where things could have gone better and understanding the scope for growth. I like to highlight that things like that will happen in your early days. Things will go wrong; they have for almost all of us. What matters is how you approach it.” Maintaining autonomy through growth Something that remains integral for Amy at Legora is the autonomy to act when spotting a gap. After Legora’s London Precedent event in May 2026, where a suite of new features was unveiled, Amy realised the team’s approach to client training needed to evolve. Together, Amy and one of Legora’s legal engineers redesigned a series of training programmes so that they could be delivered to clients. “We invited people to give us a lot of feedback, and then also enabled the wider engagement and legal engineering teams to make sure that they had what they needed to hit the ground running with clients when features were launched.” “One thing I love about working at Legora is that if you spot these gaps, you are given the space to run at them and take ownership,” she says. “That’s really fun and it’s hard to come by. It’s about figuring out what you enjoy, because that’s what you want to come to work to do each day.” Bridging the classroom and the courtroom Outside Legora, Amy sits on the University of Bristol’s legal technology industry board. Once a year, she meets with lecturers to share what’s happening in the industry, helping ensure the curriculum reflects the reality students will face when they enter the workforce. She also delivers an annual lecture on legal technology. As part of the Legal Technology in Practice module, the university gives students access to Legora itself during her lecture, so they can see first-hand what those in the profession are using. It’s a connection that feeds back into her work. Understanding what the next generation of legal professionals expects from technology, and from employers, sharpens her thinking about how Legora trains clients and develops its own people. What’s next? When thinking about what excites her most about the future at Legora, Amy points to the moments she gets to see her work pay off for clients. “I love the autonomy here: spotting a gap and being able to just try your hand at fixing it. But the best part is when that turns into real impact for a client, and you actually see it show up in their adoption. That’s what makes it feel worthwhile.” “We’re growing so quickly, especially in the UK office, and that means there’s always a new gap to spot, a new client problem to solve. Having a team around me that makes the work fun as well is what keeps me going,” she says. blogs.description: Three law firm leaders share how they use AI to assess potential cases, explore more options for clients, and build adoption without large innovation teams.
blogs.content: Insights How Smaller Law Firms are Using AI to Meet Client Needs Three law firm leaders share how they use AI to assess potential cases, explore more options for clients, and build adoption without large innovation teams. by Harvey Team • Oct 1, 2026 Watch Video Smaller law firms often work with leaner teams and fewer dedicated resources for adopting new technology. They can also make decisions quickly and stay close to the work they want to improve. That closeness to the work helps smaller firms spot where AI could make a difference, test it quickly, and put what works into practice. At Harvey FORUM in Sydney, Grant Guenther, National Managing Principal Lawyer at Macpherson Kelley; Ben Phi, Managing Director at Phi Finney McDonald; and Samantha Hocking, Chief AI & Knowledge Officer at Gilchrist Connell, discussed how their boutique firms are putting AI to work. Their clients have different expectations, but each leader is working through the same practical question: Where can AI make the biggest difference, and how do you bring lawyers along? Start With the Work That Needs Attention The best place to start depends on the firm’s clients and the work they need done. Hocking said some insurance clients now expect her firm to use AI for initial drafts and are questioning how much they should pay for work that AI can help complete faster. For Phi, speed matters early in a class action. His team needs to assess potential cases, explore different approaches, and decide which are worth pursuing. AI helps lawyers work through possibilities and narrow the field, even when they’re up against much larger legal teams. The analysis still needs careful verification, but the firm can get to the questions that require legal judgment sooner. In both cases, the opportunity is tied to a specific demand on the firm’s time. That makes it easier to see where AI helps and where lawyers should focus their attention. Look Beyond Time Saved Faster work doesn’t always mean fewer hours on a matter. For Guenther’s team, AI can make it practical to consider questions they might previously have set aside because the time required would have been hard to justify to a client. “I’m not entirely sure that it’s shrinking what we’re spending time on, but I do think it’s reallocating what we’re spending time on,” he said. “ I do think [AI is] reallocating what we’re spending time on. It is letting us do things that perhaps we wouldn’t have done previously. ” Grant Guenther National Managing Principal Lawyer at Macpherson Kelley That can mean exploring another approach or examining an issue in greater depth before deciding how to advise. Many of the businesses his firm serves have small in-house legal teams or none at all. They come to outside counsel with a problem rather than a prescribed way to solve it, so the value may lie in the additional possibilities their lawyers can consider within the time available. Hocking described a different use of that time. After a senior associate drafted questions for construction experts, she put the draft through Harvey for feedback. The response flagged where questions might be leading or moving from objective inquiry toward advocacy. Hocking shared that feedback with the associate as an opportunity to learn from the review, as well as improve the questions at hand. Make Adoption Part of the Work Smaller firms may be able to make decisions quickly, but they still have to find time to put those decisions into practice. Building a useful workflow with AI takes input from lawyers who know the work: examples of a good result, feedback on the output, and revisions when the first attempt falls short. Practice leaders need to review and refine those workflows alongside their client work, which can slow the rollout. The firm also needs to decide where people can experiment safely. Hocking described a targeted rollout that let her team manage risk and assess results before expanding access. Phi emphasized protections for client data and privilege , then put the goal plainly: “Establish a safe space within which you can then put this tool into the hands of your employees and let them experiment.” Importantly, lawyers still need to verify the work produced within those boundaries. Learning from colleagues can help a small team make progress without a large innovation function. At Gilchrist Connel, Harvey users share prompts and examples in an internal chat. Lawyers can see how others are using the tool, ask questions, and build on what early adopters have learned. Smaller firms are close to their clients and the work their lawyers do every day, giving them a clear view of where AI might help. By starting with one problem and involving the people who know it best, they can learn what works and build from there. — Learn how Harvey helps boutique, specialty, and mid-sized firms drive outsize impact. blogs.content: For the complete documentation index, see llms.txt . This page is also available as Markdown . Copy On this page Product Updates & Release Notes Review the latest Vincent updates. This guide provides information on our update cadence and links to vLex release notes so you can learn about new Vincent features. Summary Browse a chronological log of every major Vincent and Vincent Studio release, so you always know which AI workflows, integrations, and platform updates are available to your firm right now. Content Verified as of August 18, 2026. This log covers all major releases through today, including Conversation Statuses. For anything announced more recently, check "How to Stay Informed" below. Why This is Important Vincent is engineered for lawyers, and that engineering never stops. New workflows, model upgrades, and integrations ship continuously, often without a firm-wide memo to announce them. Reviewing this log regularly ensures your team isn't manually working around a limitation that a recent release already solved, and helps you plan training and rollout for the capabilities that matter most to your practice. Our Update Cadence Vincent receives updates at the speed of AI. Our product and engineering teams work in a continuous development cycle, which means updates and new features land every month. We are also continuously evaluating and implementing the latest-generation models from leading providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, so Vincent's responses stay clear, precise, and analytical. Learn more in Understanding the AI Models Used by Vincent . There's also a recurring 'Release Report' published roughly monthly on the Enterprise blog, a great secondary source for screenshots and deeper detail on anything below. See all Release Reports August 2026 Vincent Conversation Statuses August 18, 2026 Every conversation in your history now carries a status indicator, in Vincent so you can see what is still running and what is ready for you without opening anything. Five statuses are available: In progress , Completed & Unread , Completed & Read , Action Required , and Error encountered . Understanding Conversation Statuses July 2026 Skills Skills in Vincent (Standalone) Reusable instructions that tell Vincent how your firm handles a given task, applied automatically in every relevant conversation going forward. Skills use three roles, Publisher, Builder, and User, to control who creates, edits, and publishes them firm-wide, and you can install ready-made skills from the Skills Library or build a custom one by writing it directly or letting Vincent guide you through setup with questions. What are Skills in Vincent? Vincent Persistent Memory Vincent now retains your preferences and prior work across sessions, following your account's data retention policy. Memory works on two layers: User memory (your standing drafting style, tone, and formatting preferences, which apply across every matter) and Conversation memory (decisions and confirmed facts from your current session, which get carried forward into your user memory). Retention is rolling and applied per-memory, based on when each one was created — check with your firm administrator to confirm your account's retention period. It reads the active document in full, including comments and existing redlines, and proposes edits using native Word Track Changes, so you can surface risks or draft from a blank page without leaving Word. Vincent always checks vLex's authoritative sources first, and any web-sourced material is labeled separately in the Cited Sources Tray so you always know where an answer came from. Toggle it on or off per conversation, and firm admins can control it at the firm level. Web Search with Vincent AI Vincent Full-Length Translation Vincent can now translate complete documents rather than short excerpts, as part of the same May update wave. Integrations Document Management System (DMS) Integrations Mar 9, 2026 Pull files directly into Vincent from your firm's existing folder structure in iManage, NetDocuments, SharePoint, or Google Drive, so sensitive documents stay in your secure environment and never touch local hardware. blogs.title: How We Built Harvey’s Connector Library to Work Across External Tools
blogs.author: Chenghao Wang
blogs.description: Building the Connector Library meant making external tools available to agents while enforcing permissions and accounting for differences between providers.
blogs.content: Technical How We Built Harvey’s Connector Library to Work Across External Tools Building the Connector Library meant making external tools available to agents while enforcing permissions and accounting for differences between providers. by Chenghao Wang • Oct 1, 2026 A law firm runs on a stack of services such as Outlook or Gmail for client communication, iManage for documents, and data rooms for transactions. Harvey's Connector Library is built for exactly that scenario: an admin enables a connector, a user connects once, and the services the firm already relies on become usable inside Harvey. Today, users hold more than 110,000 individual connections across these sources, and agents make tens of thousands of connector tool calls a week. Making those services available to an agent creates a recurring engineering challenge. For every tool call, we need to know whether the user can use the tool, whether the result stays within their permissions, and whether the call is trustworthy. A single request may involve several calls, so those checks must hold at every step. This post explains how we enforce those boundaries and how we handle the differences between vendors without passing that complexity on to the agent. The Connector Architecture: From a Tile to Tools in the Agent's Hands A connector in the library is a vendor-level object: a tile in the catalog, one permission, one admin toggle, backed by one or more members that each provide part of the integration. A member is either a native integration or an MCP connector (a server the vendor operates, which Harvey calls over the Model Context Protocol ). Everything that defines a connector is collected in one registry that lives in code: what the connector is, which capabilities its native and MCP members provide, its permission, and the routing note written for the agent; the rest of the backend is an extension of this registration. That is what makes onboarding cheap — since Early Access opened, new connectors have entered the catalog one after another. When a user works with the agent, the client sends their selected connector and tools with the request. The backend resolves that selection into the connector’s native or MCP members and their tool configurations. Unknown connector types and tool keys are rejected. Resolution happens once per turn. The resulting configuration travels with the run and is reused as the agent works. The selected tools are registered into the model through Harvey's own adapters, and the agent decides, within that selection, what to call at each step. These tool requests still clear one more set of machinery and are allowed or refused. An allowed call goes out with the connection's own credential: for sources holding personal data that is always the asking user's own grant, and the source system returns only what that user may see under its own ACLs. In the results, documents retrieved by native members are presented to the user with inline citations, while MCP members' output enters the model context as plain text. The Trust Architecture: Approval and Call Safety Connector security starts before a tool reaches users and continues when the agent calls it. Before launch, our security team reviews threats such as prompt injection, misuse of write capabilities, credential compromise, cross-tenant leakage, and supply-chain risk. At runtime, each call must still pass the applicable permission and policy checks. When a connector is introduced, our security team validates it against Harvey's bar for security, assessed against a set of core threat scenarios: prompt injection, abuse of write capabilities, credential compromise, cross-tenant leakage, and supply-chain risk. A native member is a wrapper we wrote around the vendor's API, and it goes through the same security review: which of the vendor's APIs we call and which scopes we request are what the security team signs off on. An MCP member's server is operated by the vendor, so the review has to judge a system someone else runs, and it gets an extra layer of admission. The vendor submits its full tool list and capability scope, hosting and auth details, data-processing regions, and test credentials, and the security team reviews the tools one by one, deciding for each whether it is approved and assigning its risk level. This way, approval is a hard gate before engineering integration begins. Those decisions land in a registry that ships with the code: a structured URL matcher, the vendor's full advertised tool list, the subset that may be invoked, and a hand-written risk and capability annotation for each. With this information in hand, we add a further layer of runtime controls for MCP. It shapes what the agent can even see, and tools outside the approved set never appear in the model's list. We designed our own module for this, the MCP policy engine . Each time the agent wants to call a tool, it checks that the tool is still on the approved list, that the risk and capability annotation written at review time is still there (a missing one is an outright refusal), and that the workspace and user settings allow it. The engine's rule layer is written in Rego (Open Policy Agent's policy language), with the interpreter embedded in-process. The input that reaches the rules is deliberately data-blind: only the tool’s identity, risk level, capability flags, and the names of the run’s prior MCP calls cross over, a user's arguments and free text never do, and a rule-evaluation error fails closed. We also keep our own fingerprint of each approved tool, pinning its description and input schema at review time and comparing them on every tool discovery, and a change or a disappearance alerts the team. Tool results still pass through sanitization, including detection of mixed-script confusable characters, to catch as much encoding- and rendering-level disguise as possible. The aggregate telemetry along this path holds the same line: tool arguments, result contents, server URLs, and user identifiers never appear in our health events and metrics. Beyond what Harvey enforces, we hand controls to the customer. A workspace admin can disable or enable, for their own users, a specific connector, a specific member (native or MCP), or a single MCP tool; users can tighten further on top of the admin's settings. Together these controls compose into one intersection: the MCP tools the model can see = advertised by the vendor ∩ reviewed by Harvey ∩ allowed by the effective workspace and user settings ∩ explicitly selected for this request, when a selection is present. But as we support more and more connectors, additional problems appear. Platform Differences: Keeping Each Vendor's Quirks Inside the Adapter We kept finding that vendors behave differently, and the differences turn into concrete problems. For example, a valid token gets thrown away as invalid, a user is asked to re-authorize for no visible reason, or a tool schema the vendor declares legal is rejected by the model. The MCP authorization spec is still evolving, and the servers we integrate support different versions of it. The expected flow involves protected resource metadata discovery (RFC 9728), authorization server metadata (RFC 8414), dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, and resource binding (RFC 8707). In production, servers follow that flow differently. Some never send the 401 challenge that should start discovery. One token endpoint returns a valid token with 201 Created, and servers interpret the same scope declaration differently. Our authorization layer has to accommodate those differences for each server we integrate. Token handling differs too. Several providers issue single-use refresh tokens, while frontend prechecks, scheduled syncs, export jobs, and background renewal can all want the same user's token at the same time. This layer serves roughly 13 million credential reads a day. The same goes for tools. Client registration alone has three paths: the 2026-07-28 spec revision makes CIMD (Client ID Metadata Documents) the recommended path and deprecates Dynamic Client Registration, keeping it for backwards compatibility, while in production some servers we integrate only support dynamic registration and others only work with a client Harvey pre-registers. A tool's schema also passes through three hands, the MCP server, the agent SDK, and the model API. We handle these differences in an adapter layer. For authorization, we follow the behavior a server actually exposes: we can discover metadata directly when it does not send a challenge, accept valid tokens returned with either 200 or 201, and request the scopes it advertises. We also use conditional write-backs to handle competing token updates without locks. At discovery, we normalize tool schemas before registering them with the agent. If the adapter encounters behavior it does not recognize, it alerts the team so we can investigate and update the integration. Building on a Consistent Foundation Each new connector brings another set of vendor behaviors to account for. Keeping those differences in the adapter lets us expand the library while applying the same approval, permission, and runtime checks to every tool call. The Connector Library is now live. Explore the connectors Harvey has reviewed and approved, connect the tools your team uses, and start working with them in Harvey. If you'd like your service connected to Harvey, use the Connector Library intake form . And if these sound like the engineering challenges you'd like to work on, we're hiring . blogs.description: See how litigation teams draft Rule 26(a) initial disclosures from the complaint and case file, identify witnesses and documents, and calculate damages.
blogs.content: Insights How to Draft Rule 26 Initial Disclosures From the Complaint and Case File See how litigation teams draft Rule 26(a) initial disclosures from the complaint and case file, identify witnesses and documents, and calculate damages. by Harvey Team • Oct 1, 2026 Rule 26(a)(1) makes initial disclosures look deceptively straightforward: identify relevant people, documents and electronically stored information (ESI), damages computations, and insurance agreements. However, the harder work is deciding what belongs in each category when the information is spread across pleadings, correspondence, contracts, client records, and other case materials. A useful initial disclosure should be traceable to the operative pleadings and the case file, not assembled by dropping names and document categories into a boilerplate form. The goal should be to create a draft that reflects the information reasonably available at that stage of the case and makes it easy for the reviewing lawyer to understand why each person, document category, and damages figure appears. What Rule 26 Initial Disclosures Require Rule 26(a)(1) generally requires parties to provide initial disclosures without waiting for a discovery request, unless an exemption, stipulation, or court order applies. Parties must base those disclosures on the information reasonably available at the time. An incomplete investigation does not, by itself, excuse the obligation to disclose. Individuals likely to have discoverable information: Identify each individual likely to have discoverable information that the party may use to support its claims or defenses, along with known contact information and the subjects of that information. Connecting each person to the facts they may help establish produces a more useful disclosure than a standalone list of names. Documents, ESI, and tangible things: Disclose a copy (or a description by category and location) of documents, ESI, and tangible things in the party's possession, custody, or control that it may use to support its claims or defenses. The objective is to identify the materials that connect to the issues in the case with enough specificity to make the disclosure meaningful. Computation of damages and supporting materials: Provide a computation for each category of damages claimed and make the nonprivileged supporting documents or other evidentiary materials available for inspection and copying. Building the computation from source records helps the team identify unsupported assumptions, missing evidence, and figures that might need to be supplemented as the case develops. Insurance agreements: Identify insurance agreements under which an insurer may be liable to satisfy all or part of a possible judgment or to indemnify or reimburse payments made to satisfy it. Confirming this information directly with the client helps avoid assuming that the existing case file contains every responsive agreement. When are Rule 26 Initial Disclosures Due? The default deadline for Rule 26 initial disclosures is at or within 14 days after the parties' Rule 26(f) conference , unless a stipulation or court order sets a different time or a party properly objects to initial disclosures during the conference. A party first served or joined after the Rule 26(f) conference generally has 30 days after service or joinder, subject to a different deadline by stipulation or court order. However, teams should always check the scheduling order and case-specific requirements instead of calculating the deadline from the complaint filing date. Start With the Complaint, but Don’t Stop There Think of the complaint as the map and the matter record as the evidence layer. The operative pleadings establish the claims, defenses, and factual allegations that organize the case, but they rarely contain everything needed for complete initial disclosures. People with relevant knowledge, supporting records, damages evidence, and factual context often appear somewhere else in the file. An effective process uses the pleadings to define the issues, then tests those issues against the matter record to determine what should actually appear in the disclosure. Parse the operative claims, defenses, and factual allegations Break the operative complaint, answer, counterclaims, and other relevant pleadings into the claims, defenses, and material factual allegations that shape the case. This creates a structured framework for connecting each issue to potential witnesses, documents, and damages evidence. Turn each material allegation into an evidence question For each material allegation, ask what information would support or rebut it. Who has relevant knowledge? What records bear on the issue? Does it connect to a claimed category of damages? Turning allegations into concrete evidence questions makes gaps easier to spot before drafting begins. Resolve conflicts between the pleadings and the case file Compare the pleadings against the underlying records for discrepancies in dates, names, events, amounts, and other material facts. Flag conflicts for attorney review rather than silently choosing one version, so the disclosure reflects deliberate legal judgment rather than an unexamined inconsistency. Seven-Step Workflow for Drafting Initial Disclosures From the Case File A structured workflow turns the Rule 26 requirements into a repeatable drafting process. Each step should narrow the distance between the allegations in the pleadings, the evidence in the case file, and the information that ultimately appears in the disclosure. 1. Identify the Operative Pleadings and Governing Requirements Start by confirming which pleadings actually govern the case , including any amended complaint, answer, counterclaims, or amended responses. Then confirm whether Rule 26(a)(1) applies and review the scheduling order, applicable local rules, stipulations, and other court-specific requirements that may alter the default scope or timing. Rule 26 itself exempts certain proceedings from initial disclosure, so applicability should not be assumed. This step prevents the team from building its disclosure around superseded allegations or procedural requirements that do not govern the case. 2. Build a Claims-and-Defenses Matrix Create a working matrix that maps each claim or defense to its material factual allegations , potential individuals with relevant information, supporting documents or ESI, and any damages implications. Include source references where possible so the team can move directly from an entry in the matrix to the pleading or case-file material supporting it. The matrix exposes gaps and overlaps before they become drafting problems, while simultaneously giving the team a common structure for assembling each disclosure category. 3. Identify Potential Witnesses Across the Matter Record Search beyond the pleadings for individuals who appear in correspondence, agreements, business records, interview notes, prior statements , and other case materials. For each person, record the subject of their likely knowledge and the source material that explains their connection to the case. Then apply Rule 26's scope to focus on individuals with discoverable information that the party could use to support its claims or defenses (instead of treating every name in the file as automatically disclosable). This process makes the final disclosure more precise and reduces the risk of overlooking someone who never appeared by name in the complaint. 4. Map Supporting Documents and ESI to the Issues in the Case Identify the documents, ESI, and tangible things the party may use to support its claims or defenses , then connect each category to the relevant issue in the claims-and-defenses matrix discussed above. Group materials into meaningful categories and identify their location rather than relying on vague descriptions like “relevant correspondence” or “business records.” This gives the reviewing lawyer a clearer view of both what the category contains and why it matters. Apply privilege and work-product protections before service rather than treating everything surfaced during the review as automatically disclosable. 5. Build the Damages Computation From Source Materials List each category of damages the party claims and trace the amount back to invoices, financial records, contracts, payroll information, medical records, or other applicable source materials. Document the calculation method, relevant time period, inputs, and assumptions so other lawyers can still follow how the figure was reached. Where the available record does not yet support a complete calculation, identify the missing information instead of filling the gap with an unsupported estimate. This creates a cleaner baseline for later supplementation as additional information becomes available. 6. Confirm Insurance Information With the Client Ask the client directly about insurance agreements that may respond to the action instead of assuming that the litigation file contains all relevant coverage information. Confirm the responsive agreement and collect the materials needed to satisfy the disclosure requirement. If the file and the client’s information conflict, resolve that discrepancy before finalizing the draft. Direct confirmation reduces the risk that an applicable agreement gets missed just because it was never included in the original matter materials. 7. Verify Every Entry Before Service Trace each disclosure entry back to its source before service. Confirm individuals and their subjects of knowledge, document categories and locations, damages calculations, and applicable insurance information. Resolve inconsistencies and conduct the appropriate privilege and work-product review rather than relying on the first-pass draft. Rule 26(g) requires an attorney of record (or an unrepresented party) to sign the disclosure and certify, after a reasonable inquiry, that it’s complete and correct as of the time it is made. A source-traceable drafting process makes that final review more efficient while at the same time creating a stronger foundation for updating the disclosures as the matter develops. AI is Changing the Initial Disclosure Workflow Any general-purpose AI model can reproduce the four Rule 26(a)(1) headings. This by itself doesn’t produce a useful initial disclosure. The more meaningful use of legal AI is to work across the operative pleadings and matter record, connect proposed disclosures to their supporting sources, and produce a draft organized for attorney review. We recommend that you: Ground the draft in the complaint and matter documents: AI can analyze the complaint alongside answers, correspondence, contracts , client records, and other case materials rather than drafting from the pleading in isolation. This keeps the disclosure tied to the factual record that supports the claims and defenses. Extract witnesses and evidence with source references: AI can surface people, documents, and other evidence across a large matter record and connect each proposed entry to the materials where it appears. Source references make it easier for the reviewing lawyer to verify why an item belongs in the disclosure instead of retracing the analysis manually. Surface gaps and conflicts instead of inventing missing facts: AI can compare pleadings against the underlying case materials to flag inconsistent names, dates, amounts, or factual accounts. A review-ready workflow should mark missing or conflicting information for attorney resolution rather than infer an answer that the record doesn’t support. Standardize the process without standardizing the substance: A repeatable AI workflow can apply the same sequence of steps, inputs, and verification checks across matters while grounding each output in that case’s specific pleadings and evidence. Harvey Agents are designed around this distinction so teams can encode repeatable legal processes and organizational standards while supplying matter-specific context for each run. Keep attorney review at the point of legal judgment: AI can handle first-pass extraction, organization, comparison, and drafting so attorneys spend more of their review time on questions that require legal judgment . The lawyer still determines scope, resolves ambiguity, assesses privilege, and decides whether the disclosure satisfies the reasonable-inquiry standard. Common Rule 26 Initial Disclosure Mistakes Several recurring problems arise when teams treat initial disclosures as a form-filling exercise instead of a matter-specific disclosure process. These include: Treating initial disclosures as a boilerplate form: Reusing a prior disclosure can save drafting time, but it might also carry over generic categories or assumptions that don’t fit the current case. Use precedent for structure, then rebuild the substance from the operative pleadings and current matter record. Disclosing everyone who might know something instead of applying the rule’s scope: A broad name search can produce a list of everyone mentioned in the file, which is not the same as applying Rule 26(a)(1)’s standard. Focus on individuals with discoverable information that the party may use to support its claims or defenses. Naming witnesses without describing their subjects of knowledge: A name alone doesn’t satisfy the rule’s requirement to identify the subjects of the individual’s information. Tie each disclosed person to a concise description of the relevant facts or issues they may know about. Using vague document categories that cannot be traced to the matter: Descriptions like “relevant emails” or “business records” could obscure what the category actually covers. Define categories around the facts and issues in the case, and identify their location where required. Deferring the damages computation without analyzing available evidence: Teams might postpone damages analysis because discovery is incomplete, but Rule 26 requires disclosure based on information reasonably available at the time. Build the computation from the records already available, identify what remains unsupported, and update it when additional information changes the analysis. Forgetting that the disclosure must reflect a reasonable inquiry: Rule 26(g) ties the signed disclosure to a reasonable inquiry and certification that it is complete and correct as of the time it is made. A defined process for checking the pleadings, case file, client information, and source materials makes that inquiry easier to document and defend. Treating the first disclosure as final: Initial disclosures capture what is known at an early stage of the case, not a permanently fixed factual record. Rule 26(e) requires timely supplementation or correction when a disclosure becomes materially incomplete or incorrect and the new information has not otherwise been made known. What Happens if Initial Disclosures are Incomplete? An incomplete initial disclosure doesn’t automatically lead to sanctions, but failing to provide or timely supplement required information can create meaningful consequences. Under Rule 37(c)(1), a party generally may not use an undisclosed witness or information on a motion, at a hearing, or at trial unless the failure was substantially justified or harmless. On top of this, the court can also impose additional remedies. At the same time, the answer isn’t to disclose everything in the file. A better approach is to conduct a defensible inquiry based on the information reasonably available, document how the disclosure was assembled, and supplement it as the case develops. That keeps the process aligned with Rule 26 while reducing the risk that an important witness, document, or damages component falls through the cracks. Turn Rule 26 Initial Disclosures Into a Repeatable, Reviewable Workflow Effective Rule 26 initial disclosures depend less on memorizing the four required categories than on reliably connecting the operative pleadings to the people, documents, damages evidence, and other information in the case file. A structured workflow can reduce the manual work of assembling that information and make it easier to identify gaps, resolve inconsistencies, trace proposed entries to their sources, and conduct the reasonable inquiry behind the Rule 26(g) certification. Harvey helps litigation teams analyze complaints and other case materials, extract case-critical information, identify inconsistencies, and generate first drafts grounded in matter context. By combining those capabilities with repeatable agents , teams can move from a scattered case file to a review-ready starting point while keeping attorneys focused on the legal judgments that determine the final disclosure. blogs.content: Back to Blog GLM-Legal: Advancing Agentic Legal Intelligence Model By AutoClaw Team Oct 13 2026 Built on GLM-5.3-Flash, GLM-Legal matches frontier models on mainstream legal benchmarks.Designed for real legal workflows: contract review, evidence analysis, compliance, and more. Join the GLM-Legal Beta Whether you are a law firm, a legal tech company, an in-house legal team, or an independent practitioner, we invite you to experience GLM-Legal. - Apply for API access: https://z.ai/consultation/legal - Try AutoClaw: https://autoclaw.z.ai/ Large language models are shifting from single-turn code generation toward broader professional collaboration (Professional Cowork). Real-world knowledge work introduces distinct requirements: models must digest fragmented source files under concrete objectives and tight delivery constraints, structure specialized knowledge into cohesive analysis, and maintain domain rigor across the full execution lifecycle. Legal work concentrates on these challenges, providing an ideal stress test for training models to operate in high-stakes professional environments. Legal practice demands an unbroken chain between facts, statutory doctrine, analytical reasoning, and client-ready work product. When given a professional task, an agent must extract core issues from source documents, build defensible arguments, and format its findings to exact task specifications. Simultaneously satisfying all of these constraints is the true benchmark for domain-specific models. We evaluated GLM-Legal across three axes: complex task execution, specialized legal reasoning, and real-world legal workflows. GLM-Legal achieved a 19.2% all-pass rate on Harvey LAB, while matching frontier closed-source models on LegalBench and PLawBench despite running on a significantly leaner parameter footprint. Benchmark Highlights Across complex execution, legal reasoning, and real-world drafting, GLM-Legal matches frontier-tier performance while maintaining high inference efficiency: Harvey LAB (19.2% All-Pass Rate): In real-world law firm workflows across 24 practice areas, GLM-Legal scores 19.2% and improves on its base model by 12.5 percentage points. Under Harvey's strict all-pass grading, this confirms reliable end-to-end task execution without intermediate degradation. LegalBench (Domain Reasoning Parity): Parses specialized contracts, merger filings, and judicial opinions with the precision of top closed-source frontier models, despite operating on a significantly leaner parameter budget. PLawBench (Chinese Localized Practice): Achieves parity with leading frontier systems on Chinese legal consultation, case analysis, and document drafting under fine-grained rubrics. The results on the Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark and LegalBench were independently evaluated by Vals. See https://www.vals.ai/models/zai_glm-legal. Training Methodology GLM-Legal prioritizes training efficiency. Built on the lightweight GLM-5.3-Flash foundation, it scales domain competence through specialized mid-training coupled with high-efficiency post-training. By tying foundational pre-training directly to downstream task execution, we train the model to parse source records, apply doctrine, structure arguments, and maintain output quality through final delivery. 1. Mid-training: Solidifying Domain Foundations Mid-training establishes a systematic legal foundation. We expanded the volume of high-quality legal corpora, allowing the model to learn legal concepts, statutory rules, and interpretive frameworks within dense domain context. This stage strengthens deductive connections between facts, rules, and conclusions, providing the knowledge substrate required for complex downstream execution. 2. Post-training: Co-evolving the Model and Agent Harness Post-training translates domain knowledge into task execution via reinforcement learning across tens of thousands of realistic legal environments. The model learns to plan analysis, advance workflows, and generate deliverables under concrete constraints. In this setup, the Harness serves as the runtime orchestration framework. It manages task context, connects toolsets, and routes execution feedback: Co-iterative optimization: Harness architecture and model training iterate in lockstep. Task structuring, context ingestion, and runtime feedback loops collectively govern agent exploration. Bi-directional learning: Edge cases surfaced during model training pinpoint architectural bottlenecks in the harness. Conversely, harness refinements expose the model to realistic execution constraints, training it to retrieve relevant context, adapt via intermediate execution signals, and meet production-grade standards from prompt ingestion to final sign-off. 3. Production Feedback Loops Real-world workflows and practitioner feedback set our optimization roadmap. In production, legal professionals evaluate outputs against concrete criteria: Are all critical issues and edge cases addressed? Are arguments well-substantiated and citations legally sound? Does the deliverable strictly adhere to the matter brief? Can downstream teams use the output immediately without manual rework? These requirements turn subjective quality into concrete engineering loss signals. When diagnosing issues such as missed facts, shallow analysis, or format deviations, we inspect the entire execution pipeline, isolating the contributions of raw model intelligence, context staging, and workflow logic. We feed these findings directly back into task environments, evaluation rubrics, and harness design for subsequent training cycles, validating improvements against production benchmarks. This tight feedback loop between practical requirements, task environments, the harness, and model training ensures algorithmic progress translates directly into production reliability. Bringing GLM-Legal to AutoClaw You’ll soon be able to put these capabilities to work in AutoClaw, our desktop-native agent platform. The examples below illustrate how GLM-Legal can help with three common legal tasks: reviewing a contract, preparing a case, and planning a cross-border launch. 1. Contract Review: Making the Exit Clause Work for the Client Task: Review a software services contract for a client switching provider, focusing on termination and handover. GLM-5.3-Flash Termination and handover The contract allows the client to terminate on 60 days’ notice and provides a 30-day cure period for material breaches. Consider shortening the notice period to give the client more flexibility. On termination, require the provider to return client data and completed deliverables for which the client has paid. Add a duty to cooperate with the replacement provider, including reasonable access to documentation and assistance with the handover. Confirm outstanding payments and any charges for transition support. GLM-Legal Termination and handover Reduce the client’s convenience-termination notice from 60 to 30 days . Remove the cure period for breaches of IP, confidentiality, or data-security obligations so the client can terminate immediately . Section 4 already assigns the work product to the client: require return of all deliverables and work in progress, whether or not paid for . Add up to 90 days of transition assistance covering source code, documentation, data, and knowledge transfer to the client or its successor provider, at the provider’s then-current rates. When changing providers, your team needs an exit clause that protects the handover. GLM-Legal turns that goal into specific terms for immediate termination after serious breaches, return of work product, and up to 90 days of transition support. AutoClaw puts those edits into the Word document with tracked changes and comments, ready for your team to review and negotiate. 2. Evidence Analysis: Connecting the Documents to a Case Theory Task: Analyze 40 documents from a software project dispute to identify contradictions in the provider’s progress reports. GLM-5.3-Flash External reports and internal records The September 30 client report states that the project is on track and 60% complete (BR-000024), while the internal snapshot records approximately 41% completion (BR-000027). The internal emails also discuss architecture risks and instructions about client communications (BR-000014; BR-000015). These documents may support the client’s position that progress was overstated. Review the reporting history, invoicing records, and contract terms to determine whether the statements were misleading and what further evidence is needed. GLM-Legal External reports and internal records The September 30 “ON TRACK – 60% COMPLETE” report (BR-000024) should be read against the September 8 warning that the milestone could not honestly be met (BR-000014) and the internal ~41% snapshot (BR-000027). The CEO’s instruction to suppress the risk and continue invoicing (BR-000015) links that internal knowledge to a disclosure decision. MSA §§2 and 5 state that payment does not waive rights and warranties survive payment (BR-000001), so continued payment alone does not resolve the dispute. These links support a concealment theory; reconcile the completion measures and test the remaining claim elements before drawing a final conclusion. In a project dispute, the key is to connect the progress reports with what the provider knew internally. GLM-Legal pairs external statements with conflicting records, cites the source documents, and explains their potential legal significance. The contradiction map helps your team assess the evidence and decide what to investigate next, while keeping facts and inferences distinct. 3. Compliance Research: Identifying Pre-launch Privacy Priorities Task: Plan privacy compliance for a website launching in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia, with tracking, email marketing, and overseas cloud storage. GLM-5.3-Flash Pre-launch priorities Before launch, publish a privacy notice explaining collection, use, sharing, and overseas storage. Review whether cookies and analytics need consent, include an unsubscribe option in marketing emails, and ensure vendors provide suitable data-protection safeguards. Check the applicable privacy laws in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia and confirm any local requirements. The launch plan should address notices, consent, marketing, and transfers, with responsibilities assigned to the relevant teams and outstanding legal questions reviewed before the website goes live. GLM-Legal Pre-launch priorities P0 — recommended before launch: Publish English and Indonesian privacy notices covering purposes, transfers, rights, and complaints. Use opt-in for non-essential analytics and advertising, keep consent records , and separate marketing permission from registration. Make unsubscribe requests feed a suppression list . Map cloud, payment, email, analytics, and CDN vendors to their data destinations, then confirm the contracts and transfer safeguards required in each market (SG PDPA s26; MY PDPA s129; ID PDP Law Arts 55–56). Use these shared controls as a conservative launch baseline, while checking each market’s specific requirements. A cross-border launch needs a plan your team can act on. GLM-Legal breaks privacy requirements into practical steps for tracking consent, marketing permissions, and overseas data transfers, with legal references for each market. The prioritised checklist helps your team implement shared controls and identify country-specific questions to confirm before launch.

blogs.content: Insights How AI-Powered Regulatory Horizon Scanning Helps Lawyers Move From Regulatory Change to Action Legal teams can use regulatory horizon scanning and AI agents to monitor regulatory change, assess impact, and turn updates into actionable legal work. by Harvey Team • Sep 30, 2026 Legal teams face a steady stream of new rules, proposals, guidance, enforcement activity, and supervisory priorities. The difficult task is determining whether this development matters to your organization or clients. What does it affect, and what legal work needs to happen as a result? Effective regulatory horizon scanning helps teams answer those questions earlier. Instead of treating regulatory intelligence as a feed of alerts, legal teams can use it as the starting point for applicability assessments, obligation mapping, policy and contract reviews , gap analysis, stakeholder communications, and other tangible actions. The goal isn’t just to know that something changed, but to create enough context and lead time to respond effectively. Regulatory Horizon Scanning for Modern Legal Teams Regulatory horizon scanning is the systematic process of identifying and assessing emerging laws, regulations, guidance, enforcement trends , and other developments that could affect an organization or its clients. As legal teams operate across more jurisdictions and regulatory regimes, horizon scanning helps spot relevant regulatory changes, evaluate their potential impact, and prepare before new requirements become urgent compliance issues . Types of Regulatory Developments Tracked by Horizon Scanning Legal teams need visibility into developments at different stages of the regulatory lifecycle so they have enough time to assess potential consequences and prepare a response. These might include: Proposed legislation and rulemaking: Bills, proposed regulations, and rule changes that could create new requirements or modify existing ones. Consultations and draft rules: Consultation papers, exposure drafts, requests for comment, and other preliminary materials that indicate how regulation may develop. Regulatory guidance: Interpretive guidance, regulatory guides, information sheets, rulings, and other materials that clarify how regulators expect organizations to comply. Technical standards: Detailed standards or specifications that translate broader regulatory requirements into operational or technical expectations. Enforcement actions: Investigations, settlements, penalties, and other enforcement activity that can reveal how regulators interpret and prioritize existing rules. Supervisory priorities: Published agendas, examination priorities, speeches, and similar signals that indicate where regulators plan to focus their attention. Legislative reforms across jurisdictions: Changes occurring at the national, state, provincial, territorial, or other jurisdictional level that may create overlapping or divergent obligations. Developments from named regulators: Updates from specific agencies or authorities that oversee the organization’s industry, activities, products, or markets. Regulatory Horizon Scanning vs. Regulatory Monitoring vs. Regulatory Change Management Although these concepts are closely related, they serve different objectives. Horizon scanning looks ahead to what may be coming, regulatory monitoring tracks relevant developments as they occur, and regulatory change management turns those developments into assessed obligations, owners, deadlines, and implementation work. Area Question Being Answered Regulatory horizon scanning What’s coming? Regulatory monitoring What has changed or is currently binding? Regulatory change management What do we need to change internally, who owns it, and by when? Why Regulatory Horizon Scanning Matters for Legal Teams Legal teams need to keep pace with regulatory developments that can emerge from different regulators, jurisdictions, and stages of the legislative or rulemaking process. For organizations operating across different markets, a single development may affect different entities, products, or activities in different ways. Waiting until a rule takes effect can leave too little time to interpret requirements, update policies or contracts, coordinate stakeholders, and implement necessary changes. Modern regulatory horizon scanning systems give legal teams more lead time to identify which developments deserve attention and begin the appropriate analysis sooner. They also support a more consistent process for connecting external regulatory change to internal obligations, policies, controls, and business activity. All of this makes horizon scanning a critical part of proactive legal and compliance work instead of just another research task. More Regulatory Alerts can Create More Noise More alerts don’t necessarily produce better regulatory intelligence. When every consultation, proposal, guidance document, and enforcement action reaches the legal team with the same level of urgency, lawyers still have to spend manual time and effort separating meaningful developments from background noise. Effective horizon scanning therefore depends on prioritization just as much as coverage. Teams need to be able to evaluate developments against their regulatory perimeter, determine why they’re relevant, and identify which ones require analysis or action. The useful output isn’t a longer feed of updates; it’s a shorter, more relevant set of developments with enough context to decide what happens next. Identifying a Change is Just the Beginning Once a regulatory development is identified, the substantive legal work begins. Lawyers still need to determine whether the change applies to the organization or client — which entities, products, jurisdictions, and activities fall within scope, and what new obligations, thresholds, or deadlines it may create. The next question is what the change means for the organization’s existing operations. Legal teams might need to compare current policies against new requirements, review contracts for compliance, identify gaps or inconsistencies, update procedures or playbooks , create implementation checklists, and prepare guidance for stakeholders. They should also determine who owns each action, who needs to be informed, and what should happen by when. How Does the Regulatory Horizon Scanning Process Work? The exact methodology and steps will vary by organization, but effective regulatory horizon scanning usually follows a repeatable process of defining what matters, monitoring the right sources, separating meaningful developments from noise, assessing their impact, and turning that analysis into concrete work. 1. Define Your Regulatory Perimeter Start by defining the regulatory universe your team actually needs to monitor. Scope can include relevant jurisdictions, regulators, business areas, practice areas, legal entities, subsidiaries, products, activities, and regulatory topics. For example, a financial services company operating across several markets might need separate coverage for different entities or regulatory regimes instead of a single broad feed. A well-defined perimeter makes the rest of the process more useful by reducing irrelevant updates and focusing resources on developments that could affect the organization or its clients. 2. Monitor the Right Regulatory and Legislative Sources Once you’ve established the perimeter, identify authoritative sources that provide reliable visibility into relevant developments. Primary sources (such as legislatures, regulators, government agencies, courts, and other official bodies) are especially important because lawyers need to understand what the issuing authority actually published, not a third-party interpretation of it. The goal isn’t to assemble the longest possible source list, but to make sure that the monitoring process consistently covers the sources most likely to produce consequential developments. 3. Filter and Prioritize Developments for Relevance Not every development within the regulatory perimeter deserves the same level of attention. Legal teams should evaluate updates based on relevance, urgency, materiality, effective dates, consultation deadlines, and other time-sensitive requirements. A proposal with a long implementation horizon may require monitoring but minimal immediate action, while new guidance affecting an active business process could warrant rapid assessment. Prioritization helps teams direct lawyer time toward the developments most likely to create meaningful legal or operational consequences. 4. Assess Applicability and Potential Impact A relevant development still may not apply to every organization, client, or business unit. Lawyers need to interpret the rule in context, considering factors such as entity type, regulated activity, jurisdiction, thresholds, exemptions, product characteristics, and the client’s specific circumstances. This is where legal judgment becomes critical — the key question shifts from “What changed?” to “Does this change create an obligation for us?” 5. Map Change to Obligations, Policies, Contracts, and Processes Once applicability is established, translate the regulatory development into the areas of the organization it may affect. This might mean separating a regulation into discrete obligations and deadlines, comparing existing policies against new requirements, reviewing contracts for compliance , or identifying procedures and controls that need to change. This mapping makes your regulatory intelligence more operational by showing where gaps exist between the new requirement and current practice. 6. Assign Next Steps, Owners, and Deadlines Horizon scanning should produce work, not another newsletter that lawyers read and file away. For each material development, teams need to identify the required action, assign an accountable owner, establish key deadlines, and determine which stakeholders should participate or receive an update. Depending on the issue, that work could involve revising a policy, reviewing contracts, changing a control, preparing employee guidance, briefing leadership, or coordinating with outside counsel . Clear ownership turns early regulatory awareness into an implementation advantage. 7. Preserve Citations, Reasoning, and an Audit Trail Legal teams also need to be able to verify how conclusions were reached. Regulatory assessments should preserve the underlying source material, supporting citations, analytical reasoning, and a record of subsequent decisions so lawyers can review the analysis before relying on it. Our approach to legal AI emphasizes verification-first workflows . This is because AI can accelerate research and analysis, but lawyers need to have the ability to inspect the sources, evaluate the reasoning, and retain control over the final work product. Harvey Agents support this framework by backing up claims with citations and logging steps for review and auditability. How AI Solutions Like Harvey Agents are Changing Regulatory Horizon Scanning AI-powered systems are expanding horizon scanning from a primarily manual monitoring exercise into a more connected process for identifying, evaluating, and responding to regulatory change. The most useful platforms do more than just collect information, they help legal teams determine what matters and accelerate the analysis and work that follows. From manually checking sources to continuous monitoring: Instead of repeatedly checking regulator websites, government publications, and legal databases, AI solutions can monitor a defined regulatory scope and surface new developments as they appear. This gives lawyers more time to assess the substantive implications instead of spending their time finding the update in the first place. From alert overload to relevance-based prioritization: AI can help evaluate developments against a team's defined scope and surface those most likely to require attention. This shifts the objective from collecting the highest number of alerts to identifying consequential changes with enough context to understand their relevance and urgency. From reading regulatory text to structured impact assessment: AI can also help transform dense regulatory materials into structured analysis by identifying affected parties, key requirements, deadlines, and potential areas of impact. Lawyers can then spend more of their time validating applicability and exercising legal judgment instead of manually extracting each requirement from the source text. From a regulatory update to review-ready legal work: The biggest shift actually comes after the initial analysis. Harvey Agents can take on multistep work like researching the development, comparing it with internal policies or other materials, assessing implications, organizing obligations, and producing cited, review-ready output for a lawyer to refine. What Should Legal Teams Look for in Regulatory Horizon Scanning Tools? The best regulatory horizon scanning solutions for legal teams should do more than simply aggregate alerts. They need to help teams move from monitoring to prioritization, legal analysis, verification, and action. We recommend prioritizing platforms that provide: Customizable regulatory scope instead of a fixed feed: Look for tools that let teams define monitoring by jurisdiction, regulator, topic, entity, or business activity rather than relying on a generic feed. For example, Harvey lets users create tailored Horizon Scans in plain language around the areas most relevant to them. Coverage across the jurisdictions and regulators that matter to you: A strong solution should cover the jurisdictions and authorities relevant to your organization or clients. Harvey Horizon Scanning draws on more than 12,000 sources across 100+ jurisdictions. Relevance and materiality assessment: The platform should separate consequential developments from routine updates by assessing relevance, urgency, and potential impact. Harvey surfaces higher-priority developments with relevance assessments to help teams focus their attention. Source-grounded answers and verifiable citations: Legal teams need to be able to trace analysis back to the underlying authority. Harvey grounds regulatory analysis in source material with citations lawyers can review and verify before relying on the output. Applicability and impact analysis: A useful solution determines whether a development applies to specific entities, activities, jurisdictions, or thresholds and what it may affect. Harvey supports this analysis by helping teams assess applicability, map obligations, and identify affected policies, contracts, and processes. Connections to internal policies, contracts, precedents, and knowledge: Regulatory developments need to be assessed against the organization’s existing materials. Harvey can connect external regulatory intelligence with internal policies, contracts, precedents, and other knowledge to help teams identify what may need to change. The ability to take downstream action without changing systems: The best legal platforms let lawyers move directly from an update into memos, policy reviews, implementation plans, or client alerts. Harvey supports this progression within the same platform and through connected systems. Human review, governance, and auditability: Look for clear citations, review checkpoints, logged activity, and governance controls so lawyers can inspect and approve AI-assisted work. Harvey’s verification-first approach keeps human judgment at the center of the process. How Harvey Turns Regulatory Horizon Scanning Into Actionable Legal Work Harvey connects regulatory monitoring with the legal analysis and follow-up work required to respond, helping teams move from identifying a development to producing review-ready outputs. Use Agents to turn an update into a legal deliverable: Harvey Agents can take on multistep work such as researching implications, comparing internal materials, organizing obligations, and producing cited, review-ready memos or other legal outputs. Tailor Agents to your organization's regulatory methodology: With Agent Builder , teams can create agents that reflect their own playbooks , templates, knowledge, and preferred approach to recurring regulatory work. Schedule recurring regulatory reports and reviews: Scheduled Agents can run recurring reports, updates, and reviews automatically, helping teams make regulatory monitoring and follow-up work more consistent and repeatable. Harvey Horizon Scanning helps teams surface and assess relevant developments, while Agents can carry out the research, comparison, synthesis, and drafting required to turn those developments into review-ready legal work. Lawyers remain responsible for validating the analysis and applying the judgment that determines the final response. For law firms , that could mean tracking regulatory developments across a practice area, assessing the implications for clients, updating existing guidance, and drafting a client alert when new guidance lands. For in-house teams , it might mean monitoring developments across operating jurisdictions, identifying affected entities and internal policies, preparing an implementation plan, and briefing business stakeholders on required next steps.
