Learn More Resources RESOURCES Customer Stories Resource Hub Blog What's New Pricing Events & Webinars Guides Legal AI Assistant Guide AI Contract Review Guide Legal Matter Management Guide Contract Guides Learn More Company Company About Us Careers Newsroom Learn More Sign In Book a Demo Product Solutions Resources Company Sign in Book a Demo BLOG Industry Insights On AI, Creativity, and the Work Beneath the Work Last updated: August 26, 2026 Written by: Daniel Lewis, J.D. , Global CEO Many in-house legal teams are navigating the same pressures: more work, higher stakes, and technology that is changing fast. In this series, LegalOn CEO Daniel Lewis sits down with in-house legal professionals to talk workload, tools, trade-offs, and what it means to be a lawyer today. Christine didn’t grow up planning to be a lawyer. Originally, she wanted to design ships. Law came later, and at first it didn’t feel like an obvious fit. The formalities of legal practice didn’t excite her. But when she began practicing in M&A and finance, she found a kind of creativity based on depth of knowledge that had been missing before. At her company, a large financial institution, Christine’s role as Counsel for Product Development spans the globe, and that distinction still shapes how she thinks about legal work today. The value is not in the formality, but in the creativity. She sees things changing now, for both better and worse, with AI. As a self-described technology enthusiast, Christine is both curious and fluent when it comes to AI. With AI becoming part of the legal environment at her company, she and those around her are experimenting, testing, and trying to understand where various tools can help. But knowing which tool to use, when to trust it, how to test it, and how to build it into daily work takes time and requires training and experimentation. Even for Christine, it’s hard to keep up. The tools develop quickly, at a pace she hasn’t seen before. The constant change can create paralysis when it comes to choosing one and investing the time to learn it. Six months later, something better or different might come along. Christine is navigating this challenge by not trying to do everything at once. Instead, she is picking specific projects that can be tackled with technology that works today. The Concerns Beneath the Excitement Christine’s excitement about AI comes with concerns. Too many lawyers are using AI without critical thinking and evaluation, communication is worsening, and the depth of knowledge is getting shallower. She sees work that can look complete on the surface while lacking the analysis underneath. “AI becomes a problem when users stop interrogating the output." For Christine, the problem isn’t that AI sometimes gets things wrong. That’s to be expected. It becomes a problem when users stop interrogating the output. Bad translations get passed along. Weak analysis sounds polished enough to survive. Embarrassing mistakes slip through because no one has slowed down long enough to ask whether the result is actually right. Fortunately, that isn’t the case all the time. There are still lawyers who are curious, who dig deeper, who read past the first answer and test whether an analysis holds. But Christine worries about the essential lawyering skills that may be degraded without such diligence—analyzing, challenging assumptions, and understanding what matters that make lawyers who they are. Can Four Lawyers Do the Work of Ten? Still, Christine is not pessimistic about the future of practice. She can picture a world in which, with the right tools, a team of four may be able to do work that once required ten. But that depends on the tools working inside the way lawyers work. If systems are disconnected, lawyers spend time moving information instead of using it. If tools are too restricted, they can’t reach the work where they would be most useful. And if users accept outputs without scrutiny, speed becomes a risk rather than an advantage. When the tools do work, and when lawyers use them with care, the promise is real. Smaller teams will be able to do higher-quality work with less wasted effort. As those gains are won, you may find Christine enjoying the extra time where she likes to spend it, roadtripping. blogs.description: IP litigation spans patent, trademark, copyright, and trade secret disputes. See how legal teams review a complaint faster and shape a first response to it.
blogs.content: Insights Using Legal AI to Assess IP Complaints and Litigation Risk IP litigation spans patent, trademark, copyright, and trade secret disputes. See how legal teams review a complaint faster and shape a first response to it. by Harvey Team • Sep 14, 2026 A litigation team opens a newly served IP complaint. It runs dozens of pages, dense with technical allegations, a list of asserted patents or marks, and counts that each demand a response by a set deadline. Before anyone argues strategy, the team has to understand exactly what is being alleged and where the other side is exposed. The comprehension work is the slow part. Someone has to read the complaint, cross-reference every asserted right against the record, and map each allegation to a possible response. That takes hours, and it happens under a clock while the client waits for a first read of the case. The gap between a complaint landing and a working counterargument is where an IP case is shaped early, for better or worse. When the read-and-respond work drags, strategy starts late and deadlines close in before the argument is ready. This article examines where legal AI changes IP litigation first, how it handles a dense technical record, and how litigation teams keep a lawyer's judgment at the center. The Scope of IP Litigation IP litigation is the process of resolving disputes over intellectual property rights, including patents, trademarks, copyrights, and trade secrets, through the courts or administrative forums. It covers infringement claims, validity challenges, and misappropriation, and it often turns on dense technical records and expert testimony that shape how each side argues its case. Each type of dispute has its own shape. Patent cases turn on whether an accused product practices the asserted claims and whether those claims are valid. Trademark cases center on consumer confusion and the strength of a mark. Copyright cases weigh protectable expression and fair use. Trade secret cases ask whether information was secret, valuable, and taken by improper means. These disputes have grown as people move between competitors, and they often turn on what an employee took and how it was used. Most IP suits proceed in federal district court, while patent validity is frequently contested before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB). Import-related patent disputes can move quickly at the International Trade Commission (ITC), and patent appeals run to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. The United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) sits behind much of this as the office that granted the rights in dispute. Within a case, the phases are familiar even when the technology is not. Pleadings frame the claims, claim construction fixes what the patent terms mean, the legal discovery process surfaces the evidence, dispositive motions test the theories, and trial resolves what remains. What a party stands to win or lose gives these cases their weight. Remedies can include injunctions that stop a product from being sold, along with damages that run to significant sums in patent and trade secret matters. Because a single ruling can reshape a product line or a market position, both sides tend to invest heavily from the first filing. Many disputes settle before trial once the shape of the case is clear, which puts even more weight on getting the early reading right. How do You Respond to an IP Complaint? The first hours after a complaint arrives go to comprehension and response, well before strategy. The team has to know what each count alleges, which patents or marks are asserted, and where the allegations are thin, and only then can it decide which arguments to run. Under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure , a defendant generally has a short window to answer or move against a complaint, which is one reason the early reading cannot wait. That early reading is the slow, unglamorous work that sets up everything after it. This is the part of IP litigation where legal AI changes the work first. Platforms like Harvey can summarize and analyze an incoming complaint, pull out the asserted claims and the factual allegations behind each count, and draft counterarguments that a litigator then evaluates and sharpens. The lawyer still decides the theory of the case. What changes is how quickly the team gets from a stack of allegations to a structured first response it can test. In a patent case, a response often runs on three tracks at once. One argues that the accused product does not practice the asserted claims. Another challenges the validity of those claims based on prior art. A third raises affirmative defenses that limit or bar recovery. Sorting which of these to pursue, and in what order, is the judgment that follows the reading. The response also takes a procedural form. A team may move to dismiss where a count is legally deficient, or file an answer that admits, denies, and raises defenses count by count. Either way, the work starts from the same close reading of what the complaint actually alleges. The value shows up most clearly on a real matter. As noted in the report, The Accelerating Impact of AI , a litigation partner brought a case file into Harvey, using it to surface factual holes in the opposing side's case that reframed the dispute, and the matter resolved within a week. What stands out is the sequence. The team reached the decisive weakness early and spent its judgment on how to use it. A counterargument that comes out of an AI tool is a starting point. A qualified lawyer reviews every assertion, confirms it against the record, and decides whether it belongs in the response. Handled this way, the early read becomes a fast, deliberate first pass that the litigator controls, with the deadline still in view. How do Litigation Teams Read a Patent Record? An IP record is dense in a way that few other civil disputes are. A single patent case can involve several asserted patents, each with its own claims and specification, alongside prior-art references, technical drawings, product documentation, and competing expert reports. A large matter can grow to tens of thousands of pages once discovery opens, with the decisive facts scattered across them. All of it has to be read against everything else before a coherent case theory can form. Expert reports add another layer, because each side's technical expert reads the same patents and reaches opposite conclusions that have to be compared line by line. This is where an in-house IP team gets concrete value from legal AI. Bayer's legal team uses Harvey to analyze patent portfolios, draft claims, and generate claim charts, and its case analysis work summarizes facts and builds chronologies out of a large record. For a group whose work is driven by research and a deep patent portfolio, that turns a slow manual read into a faster, structured one the lawyers can build on. A claim chart is worth naming, since it recurs throughout patent disputes. It maps each element of an asserted claim against an accused product for infringement, or against a prior-art reference for invalidity, so the argument can be seen element by element. Building one by hand is exacting and slow, which is why getting a well-structured first version quickly matters. Two tasks make the record especially demanding. Claim construction, settled at what is often called a Markman hearing, fixes the meaning of disputed patent terms, and that meaning can decide the whole case. Prior-art analysis asks whether someone else disclosed the invention first, which means reading older patents and publications against the asserted claims. Both reward careful, structured reading, and both are places where a faster first pass frees the lawyer to focus on the close calls. The record work and the argument are the same effort seen from two ends. A clean chronology shows when each relevant event happened and who knew what. A mapped set of claims shows exactly where infringement is alleged and where a claim may be vulnerable. Those two artifacts are what a counterargument is actually built on, which is why speeding up the analysis speeds up everything that follows. Where Litigation Teams Gain the Most From AI Across an IP matter, much of the time goes to the work that surrounds the argument. Drafting motions and correspondence, running legal research , preparing for depositions, and writing internal memos all take hours, and all of it pulls attorneys away from the strategic questions only they can answer. Litigators tend to feel this acutely, because their days are built from exactly these tasks. That is why litigation teams are among the strongest beneficiaries of legal AI. Lynn Pinker Hurst and Schwegmann adopted Harvey across drafting, research, deposition preparation, and internal memos, and its lawyers report saving more than eight hours per lawyer each week. Managing Partner Chris Schwegmann has described the effect as amplifying the firm's judgment and sharpening its insight, where the tool speeds the response while the lawyers decide what wins the case. The same pattern shows up across many firms. According to the report, Perspectives on Legal AI's Power Users , the heaviest Harvey users at law firms save far more time each month than average users. One defining trait of a power user is the habit of probing the weaknesses in a proposed line of argument. That habit is the litigator's core move, which is part of why the technology compounds in litigation specifically. The more a team uses it to test arguments, the more it gets back. The gain in law firm productivity sits in where the reclaimed hours go. A deposition outline pulled from thousands of pages of transcripts, or a first draft of a motion built from the record, are the tasks that once consumed a junior lawyer's week. When a team spends less time on that assembly, those hours move to the parts of a case that reward experience. That means shaping the theory, weighing settlement, and preparing a witness. In IP litigation, where the technical detail is heavy and the schedules are unforgiving, that shift adds up to real money over the life of a matter. Who Owns the Argument When AI Drafts it? The answer is simple and worth stating plainly. The litigator owns the argument. The job of any AI tool is to reach a review-ready draft faster, using sources the lawyer can open and check. That traceability is what makes the speed safe to rely on. Sound governance backs this up. According to The Legal AI Governance Imperative in Practice , legal teams take on responsibility for reviewing and verifying the accuracy of the outputs from AI that they use. That governance exists to preserve professional independence and judgment while the tools carry the mechanical work. Professional duties point the same way. A lawyer's duty of competence now includes an understanding of the benefits and risks of relevant technology, reflected in ABA Model Rule 1.1 Comment 8 . That duty does not pause because a draft was produced quickly. Using AI well means understanding what it produced well enough to stand behind it. The same holds for the duties that govern what reaches the court. A lawyer's obligations of candor to the tribunal and supervision over work product apply no matter how a draft was created. An output that no one has checked has no place in a filing. So the discipline is concrete. Every AI-generated summary, chronology, or counterargument is treated as a first draft that a qualified lawyer reviews before it is filed or relied on. The measure of a good legal AI tool in this setting is whether its factual and legal assertions trace back to sources a lawyer can verify. An argument a litigator cannot check is an argument they cannot responsibly make. Winning IP Litigation With a Lawyer in the Lead IP litigation begins with a dense complaint and a deadline, and the earliest work is comprehension and response before strategy. The teams that handle that opening well close the distance between a complaint landing and a working counterargument. From there, they turn to the technical record and map the claims and the chronology the argument will rest on. Across all of that, the work stays the lawyer's. Legal AI can carry the reading, the legal drafting , and the structuring, while a qualified litigator reviews every output, checks it against the record, and decides what belongs in the case. Used that way, the technology speeds the response while keeping professional judgment with the lawyer. This is where Harvey fits into IP litigation. Harvey summarizes and analyzes an IP complaint and generates counterarguments a litigator refines and pressure-tests, so the team reaches the judgment work faster while keeping full control of the argument. For litigation groups and in-house IP teams facing dense filings and tight deadlines, that is the difference between reacting and getting ahead. See how Harvey works for IP litigation in a demo. Request a Demo Unable to load form. Please try again. Try Again Thank you! We'll be in touch shortly. Frequently Asked Questions What types of disputes fall under IP litigation? IP litigation covers patent, trademark, copyright, and trade secret disputes. Within those categories, the most common claims involve infringement, challenges to the validity of a right, and the misappropriation of a trade secret. The technical subject matter varies widely, but the core question is usually whether a protected right exists and whether it was violated. Where are IP cases heard? Most IP cases are filed in federal district court, and patent validity is often litigated separately before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board. Certain import-related patent disputes are heard at the International Trade Commission, and patent appeals go to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. What is a claim chart and why does it matter? A claim chart maps each element of an asserted patent claim against an accused product or a prior-art reference. It matters because it structures both the infringement argument and the invalidity defense, letting each side see exactly where a claim is met or missing. How long does IP litigation take? It depends on the forum and the type of right, but patent cases in particular can run for years and carry significant cost through discovery, claim construction, and expert work. Parties often weigh an early resolution against the expense and time of a full trial. Can AI help with IP litigation? Yes, within limits. Alongside summarizing a complaint, drafting counterarguments, and building a chronology, AI for legal questions can help a team research the issues, provided a qualified lawyer reviews every answer before relying on it. Its role is to speed the reading and drafting so litigators can spend more time on judgment. blogs.title: How Much of the Change Management Journey Does the Vendor Own?
blogs.author: Shadi
blogs.description: A conversation with Jerry Levine (Leah), Colin Levy (Malbek) and Rich Robinson (Epiq) Change management is an essential part of getting buy-in and ROI from legal technology investments. The gap between promise and outcome is already showing up in the numbers: legal AI adoption reached 78% in 2026, up from just 23% in 2023, yet […] The post How Much of the Change Management Journey Does the Vendor Own? appeared first on CLOC .
blogs.content: A conversation with Jerry Levine (Leah), Colin Levy (Malbek) and Rich Robinson (Epiq) Change management is an essential part of getting buy-in and ROI from legal technology investments. The gap between promise and outcome is already showing up in the numbers: legal AI adoption reached 78% in 2026 , up from just 23% in 2023, yet actual time savings from these tools have averaged 18.3% against a median vendor projection of 41% , according to research from the Legal Stack. Clearly, more change management is needed to support ROI expectations. But where does “vendor support” end and organizational change management begin? What is it reasonable for buyers to expect from a vendor, and what requires wider, enterprise change? We put the questions to three leaders who sit in different seats – a CLM platform, an e-discovery managed-services provider, and a legal AI company – and let them talk it through. What follows is an edited version of that conversation. No vendor can own transformation on behalf of the customer RICH ROBINSON (Epiq): I think the best vendors help organizations navigate change. What they can’t do is own transformation on behalf of the customer. We can provide the methodology, training, coaching, governance, and measurement. The organization still has to bring the leadership, accountability, and willingness to work differently. In my experience, the implementations that hold up are the ones where both sides share ownership of the journey. JERRY LEVINE (Leah): That’s a useful distinction to draw out, because my role isn’t what Rich just described, and I think buyers often assume every vendor is offering some version of it. Someone in a role like Rich’s delivers a change management program as part of what Epiq delivers. My role is different. I get adoption questions constantly, usually from a GC asking how to get people using the tool. I’ll talk it through with them. What I offer is guidance. You need someone internally, often externally too, who owns that work. COLIN LEVY (Malbek): I’d put myself closer to Jerry on that spectrum than to Rich. Malbek is a software vendor, not a managed-services business. Buyers want a partner now, not just a system. In my experience, that shows up as co-building the product with the customer, and staying in the relationship well past the sale. None of that is change management. It’s what separates a good vendor from one who shows up for the sale and disappears. If neither side has the resources, bring in a third party RICH: That’s why I think it’s important that whoever is running the selection and deployment process goes in with eyes open. You have to be honest about your own resources and about your vendor’s resources. Change management is critical to adoption. If neither side has the acumen or the bandwidth for it, my advice is to hire a third-party implementation partner rather than hope the gap closes on its own. JERRY: That gap is where things fall apart in practice. A customer comes back and asks how to get adoption going, and the honest answer depends on questions that often don’t have consistent answers inside the same organization. What have you done so far? Who’s driving this, and who just signed off on it? If leadership is pushing AI initiatives from the top down without knowing why, those initiatives are going to keep failing, and it won’t be the tool to blame. The “easy button” myth, and its mirror image on the vendor side RICH: I see this from both sides now that I’ve moved to the vendor side. Too many buyers treat these tools as an “easy button.” They’re not thinking about the time it takes to implement and deploy them, and especially the time it takes to get lawyers to change how they work. From the vendor’s side, there’s a mirror-image problem: a feeling that adoption should be a “no-brainer.” So hesitation reads as friction, not a real concern. Add a market full of shiny things, and buyers freeze up choosing between them. The purchase ends up being treated as the finish line, when the real work is only just getting started. COLIN: That “no-brainer” instinct is something I actively coach my own sales team out of. You can’t assume a good product sells itself, or walk in thinking, why wouldn’t you buy this? That doesn’t land well. You have to build the relationship first: understand who you’re actually talking to, their internal politics, their team, their specific pressures, not just the size of the deal. That takes time, and I’ll admit it’s a real tension for vendors who are also being measured on quarterly numbers. But skipping that step is how change management ends up as an afterthought instead of part of the deal. RICH: If I had one piece of advice for both sides, it is to treat each other as a consultative partner. What a buyer says they need isn’t always what will solve their problem, and the seller has to be willing to listen long enough to get to what will. That’s what a real partnership looks like. Where they landed The three legal tech leaders don’t sell the same thing, and they don’t play the same role in a customer’s rollout. Rich delivers change management as a service, Jerry and Colin operate more as advisors, helping without owning the program directly. Three points held across all three seats: A vendor hands off the framework of training, methodology, coaching, and governance, but not the leadership, accountability, or directive to change. That must come from inside the organization. Guidance and ownership are different things, and buyers should ask a vendor directly which one they’re getting. If neither side has real change management capability, that’s a gap to close before the contract is signed. None of that makes “how much change management does the vendor own?” a simple question. It does make it a fair one to ask before signing, not after the rollout stalls. Jerry Levine CLOC Board Member Chief Evangelist & General Counsel, Leah Transforming legal through technology, trust, and human-centered innovation As a CLOC Board Member and longtime contributor to the legal operations community, Jerry Levine champions innovation, communication, and collaboration as the cornerstones of transformation. For more than five years, he has helped shape CLOC’s mission—participating in multiple CGI events, supporting member engagement, and advancing the profession’s adoption of legal technology worldwide. In his role as Chief Evangelist and General Counsel at Leah (formerly ContractPodAi), Jerry brings both legal and business expertise to help teams work smarter through digital transformation and AI. Previously a global general counsel at Amelia (IPsoft), he implemented Leah’s own solution in-house before joining the company to lead thought leadership and client advocacy from the inside out. Recognized by Legal 500 as one of the Top USA General Counsel, Jerry is a vocal advocate for what he calls “Legal Ops 3.0”—a movement focused on earning stakeholder trust through transparency, communication, and practical innovation. Beyond his professional life, Jerry is a Certified Sake Professional, frequent legal tech speaker, and avid traveler who enjoys exploring new cultures and ideas that challenge convention. His curiosity and global outlook continue to shape his work as a connector, educator, and champion for the future of legal operations. Jerry Levine CLOC Board Member Chief Evangelist & General Counsel, Leah Colin Levy CLOC Board Member General Counsel, Malbek Bridging people and technology to help legal professionals unlock meaningful change As a CLOC Board Member, Colin Levy is driven by a simple mission: to help legal professionals understand and embrace technology to make their work more effective, accessible, and human. He believes CLOC plays a vital role in uniting the legal tech ecosystem and helping professionals navigate it with confidence. Colin serves as General Counsel at Malbek, a leading contract lifecycle management company, where he combines legal strategy with innovation to advance the practice of law through technology. He also teaches as an Adjunct Professor at Albany Law School, focusing on technology and law practice management, and regularly contributes thought leadership through writing, speaking, and mentoring. A published author and recognized leader in legal technology, Colin wrote The Legal Tech Ecosystem, co-authored CLM for Dummies, and edited the Handbook of Legal Tech. His work has been featured in Above the Law, Today’s General Counsel, and other leading publications. Named to the Fastcase 50 for innovation in law, Colin also advises startups, judges the American Legal Technology Awards, and champions accessibility and education in legal tech. Colin Levy CLOC Board Member General Counsel, Malbek Richard Robinson CLOC Board Member Director of Client Success, Epiq Bridging innovation and community to empower practical impact in legal operations Rich has been an active member and contributor to CLOC for nearly a decade, helping shape conversations at the intersection of legal operations, data, and technology. He is passionate about advancing CLOC’s mission as a unifying force for innovation, bringing together professionals, ideas, and tools that help the legal industry evolve with purpose and efficiency. Rich’s career began in the IT department of a Boston law firm and evolved through diverse leadership roles in legal operations and technology at JCPenney, Toyota Motor North America, and now Epiq. A founding board member of the ACEDS and Law Rocks chapters in Dallas, Rich has also served on the inaugural Education Advisory Committee for CLOC. As an architect with Legal Data Intelligence (LDA) and a frequent speaker at eDiscovery and Legal Operations conferences nationwide, he continues to shape how organizations apply AI and data analytics to modern legal practice. Rich believes in pragmatic innovation—leading with transparency, collaboration, and continuous improvement. He’s committed to developing teams that balance technical fluency with human connection, and to mentoring the next generation of legal operations leaders. Outside of work, Rich is the creator of Legal Power Skills, a content and speaking series dedicated to upskilling legal professionals in communication, collaboration, emotional intelligence, and adaptability—core traits he believes define the future of effective legal leadership. Richard Robinson CLOC Board Member Director of Client Success, Epiq The post How Much of the Change Management Journey Does the Vendor Own? appeared first on CLOC .

blogs.title: Raise your hand to lead with CLOC in 2027
blogs.author: Shadi
blogs.description: A few weeks ago, I spoke on a panel about how to get on a board and what it takes to stay there. It was the last session on the last day of the conference, when most attendees had already left for the airport, but my room was full. That full room told me people […] The post Raise your hand to lead with CLOC in 2027 appeared first on CLOC .
blogs.content: A few weeks ago, I spoke on a panel about how to get on a board and what it takes to stay there. It was the last session on the last day of the conference, when most attendees had already left for the airport, but my room was full. That full room told me people want to lead. They have skills and passion, and they want to give back to the communities that have given them so much. Many of them haven’t found where to put that energy yet. In our latest member survey, nearly 9 in 10 members said they want to help shape CLOC, and nearly 30% want a volunteer leadership role. This month, CLOC is giving them that place with the largest volunteer recruitment in our history. More seats at the table than ever before From today through October 31, CLOC is accepting applications for councils, committees and group leadership roles, plus nominations for three open Board seats. We have never offered this many opportunities at once. Three of the councils are new. The first is the Technology & Innovation Council, because AI is moving fast and no one has perfected it, whatever some may claim. Our more than 6,500 members deserve trusted guidance on how AI can benefit them and which red flags to watch for. We’re also building the Professional Advancement & Leadership Development Council because of a question I hear all the time: “Laura, how did you get here?” People want to know which courses to take and who to have coffee with. I expect to join that council myself. The third, the Global Advisory Council, will bring what members see in their own legal markets into CLOC’s plans. We also don’t have all the answers, and I love that. If you see a need among our members, tell us. Some of the best ideas for CLOC’s future will come from the people who raise their hands this month. We’re listening. Who should apply We want applications from across our ecosystem: law firms, in-house teams, academia, government, students and every industry we support. We want senior leaders and people just starting out. If you’re curious, that’s enough to apply. If you’re thinking, “I don’t have enough experience to contribute,” let me tell you a story. A while back, a young student told me she didn’t think she had enough wisdom to share with our Inclusion & Social Impact Council. I told her, “Can you just get in here, please? Let’s figure this out.” She joined, and she told us about the financial hurdles that kept people from attending the CLOC Global Institute (CGI). Her story led us to set aside funding to help people attend the event, and that funding became our Community Access Program (CAP). At CGI this year, so many recipients came up to me, thanking me for the chance to be in this space, and it all started with one student who raised her hand. What we’re looking for Above all, we’re looking for passion for legal operations and for the people who will come after us. Tell us how you would invest in CLOC and what you’d leave for others to build on. Some councils, such as Technology & Innovation, will be led by subject-matter experts, because our members rely on that guidance. Those councils will still have room for people who are eager to learn. A small group of us, myself included, will read every application. If a leadership role isn’t the right fit this time, we’ll look for a place for you on a committee. What it takes Like me, you have a day job that has to come first, so we’ve designed these roles to avoid a heavy lift. Time: Plan on at least two hours a month, possibly a bit more at the start while each group sets its strategy. Format: Meetings are remote, and each council and committee decides how often to meet. Recognition: In May, we plan to bring our volunteer leaders and committee members together at CGI in Las Vegas to celebrate what they’ve built. Support: If life gets heavy, your fellow volunteers and CLOC staff will step in. If you make the investment, we’ll help you succeed. Manager approval: Please get your manager’s approval before applying, so you can commit with confidence. One application covers every council, committee and group leadership role, and you can raise your hand for as many as interest you. Why I give my time I started volunteering young, as a candy striper in a pediatric ward, and I’ve been caring for people my whole life. None of this feels like work to me. We do it out of love for people and passion for this profession. I see that same spirit across CLOC, from our staff to the largest, strongest Board we’ve had. Through CLOC Cares, we’ve volunteered at food banks and shelters in the cities that host CGI. The people who join us as volunteer leaders will teach others what they’ve learned and help build the next generation of legal ops professionals and good human beings, shaped by expertise you can’t buy. Many of them will go on to lead in their own communities, and we will prepare them for that. I’ve been blessed with so much, and giving back is my privilege. I invite you to do the same. Three open Board seats Last year, we opened Board seats to members beyond core legal operations roles. Our Board now includes other voices from across the legal ecosystem, and their perspectives make our decisions stronger. This year, three directors who are legal operations professionals finish their terms on December 31. We’re looking for legal operations professionals to fill those three seats, so the Board keeps a strong practitioner voice alongside those other perspectives. Board nominations use their own form and election process. You can nominate yourself or a colleague by October 31. Learn more and apply here . Applications are open through October 31. Have questions first? Join our informational webinar on October 14 at 1 PM ET. The post Raise your hand to lead with CLOC in 2027 appeared first on CLOC .

blogs.title: Why Legal Operations Is Finally Getting Its Own Credential, And Why That’s Overdue
blogs.author: marcela.valencia@cloc.org
blogs.description: Ten years ago, legal operations wasn’t a job title most people could define with confidence — including, often, the people doing the job. CLOC is now building something that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago: a formal certification for legal operations professionals, the Legal Operations Certified Professional (LOCP). As a board member and liaison […] The post Why Legal Operations Is Finally Getting Its Own Credential, And Why That’s Overdue appeared first on CLOC .
blogs.content: Ten years ago, legal operations wasn’t a job title most people could define with confidence — including, often, the people doing the job. CLOC is now building something that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago: a formal certification for legal operations professionals, the Legal Operations Certified Professional ( LOCP ) . As a board member and liaison to the advisory committee overseeing this effort, I want to explain why we’re doing this now, how it’s taking shape, and why it matters to how legal departments run. A Profession That’s Outgrown its Own Definition Problem Anyone who has worked in legal ops knows the challenge: the role looks completely different depending on where you sit. A team of one supporting a mid-size company’s legal department has a different day-to-day than someone overseeing a department of 50 or more inside a global enterprise. That variability, among others, has made legal ops notoriously hard to define, and even harder to measure or hire for with confidence. When I started in legal operations, CLOC was about five years old and my GC at the time was looking to transform the legal department, and “legal operations” was the pathway to help operationalize his initiative. But when I discussed my role as a team of one with other legal operations professionals across the country, what I did, I discovered, was different from others in larger corporations. What was consistent among all legal operations professionals are the skills required in order to perform the work. That’s the gap this credential aims to close. The foundation is the CLOC Core 12 , the competency framework CLOC introduced to define what a legal operations professional does, regardless of company size, industry, or where that person sits organizationally. The LOCP will be grounded in the Core 12, so candidates have a real, defined standard to work toward. Earning your LOCP will mean demonstrating your judgment against real scenarios. We’re building the assessment now through a formal job task analysis and standard-setting process, working with practitioners across the field to make sure it reflects the work as it’s done. The goal is to have the first candidates begin that process at CGI in Las Vegas in May 2027. Independent Expertise, Built in From the Start We’ve brought in KaWest Partners and Assessment Systems Corporation, certification and psychometric specialists who’ve built credential programs for other professions, to guide the job task analysis, standard-setting, and validation work now underway alongside our Certification Advisory Committee. Having the best team of specialists in the certification space ensures that this certification means something to not only the examinees but to employers and the overall profession as a whole. Over time, governance of the certification will transition to an independent Certification Board, separate from CLOC’s own Board of Directors, the same kind of separation programs like the PMP or CAE rely on to protect against bias in how standards are set and exams are scored. Ethics and AI as core competencies Ethics isn’t an afterthought here. Whether inside a law firm, in-house, or inside legal tech companies, lawyers operate under model rules of professional responsibility, and legal ops professionals working alongside them need that same grounding. AI is the harder one, because it won’t hold still long enough to test. Capturing it in a static exam is akin to chasing a cat; it doesn’t sit still. So we won’t try to freeze a snapshot of today’s tools into the test. AI sits inside the broader legal tech competency, and the credential itself will be designed to evolve as the technology and the skills required around it shift, with regular recalibration of exam content over time. The Case for Standardization In a recent global CLOC member survey, 53% of respondents flagged credentialing as a high-value addition to their career trajectory, and notably, that wasn’t even a yes/no question we asked directly. Members raised it unprompted. That demand has been consistent for years, echoed in conversations at the board level and across the community, and bringing it to fruition has taken close to two years of work. From conversations, to committee formation, and bringing in consulting and psychometric expertise to get from that feedback to an eventual launch. The early response has reflected this desire in the CLOC community for a formal certification. Since the announcement last week, many people had already reached out expressing interest, through LinkedIn, email, texts. That’s a real signal of pent-up demand, particularly among “team of one” legal ops professionals who are often the least-resourced and most vocal about wanting a standardized way to demonstrate their expertise. What’s Next We’re still building this and we’re building it deliberately. CLOC is targeting the CLOC Global Institute in May 2027 in Las Vegas as the milestone where the first professionals will be taking the exam, meaning the full arc from curriculum to credential could take under a year for early candidates. Long-term, I’d like to see the LOCP carry the same recognition in our field that a PMP carries in project management, a CP for paralegals, or a CPA in accounting. That’s an ambitious bar. But CLOC is 11 years old this year, mature enough as a community to build this the right way, and this certification is where that maturity shows. blogs.title: Legal Operations Is Splitting Into Specialties. Is Your Hiring Keeping Up?
blogs.author: marcela.valencia@cloc.org
blogs.description: Ten years ago, a company that wanted help running its legal department in a more organized way hired “a legal operations person.” That title told a hiring manager most of what they needed to know. The job covered day-to-day needs, such as contracts, outside counsel spend, and basic technology support, all handled by one person […] The post Legal Operations Is Splitting Into Specialties. Is Your Hiring Keeping Up? appeared first on CLOC .
blogs.content: Ten years ago, a company that wanted help running its legal department in a more organized way hired “a legal operations person.” That title told a hiring manager most of what they needed to know. The job covered day-to-day needs, such as contracts, outside counsel spend, and basic technology support, all handled by one person under one job description. But legal operations has matured, and it has evolved from a single generalist role into a profession with distinct disciplines, each requiring its own skill set and its own kind of hire. What used to be one job title now describes a family of roles, and a company that treats it as one role risks hiring the wrong person for the work it actually needs. Where the Branches Are Forming Outside counsel and financial management. This stream covers the full relationship with outside counsel. For example, it encompasses which firms to hire for which matters, how money is spent, and how the department decides between insourcing and outsourcing work. But this is about more than money. It’s about the partnership that a company builds with its law firms. It’s about translating the work into data that helps to inform future decisions about those firms. People in this lane build the data and the relationships that let a legal department negotiate from a position of knowledge instead of habit. Contract and document management. This is where it all began, if I am honest. For most of us, “operations” used to really mean contract management. But how we create, negotiate and manage our contracts and other documents looks markedly different today. What used to be called knowledge management now looks more like document intelligence. Older tools mainly stored documents and we relied on user input to capture the metadata that made them searchable. The newer generation of tools now reads contracts and surfaces what’s inside them. Which means our contract and document professionals have an entire new set of information and data to analyze, organize and utilize. Technology. Two distinct paths have opened here. One road leads legal operations professionals into legal tech companies themselves, whether they be Legal AI, Workflow Management, or specific to a specialized area such as contracts or spend. Or, lets face it, one of the 700-odd legal tech companies that seem to appear on an almost daily basis. These companies are (smartly) tapping into the deep experience these professionals have building and running legal operations for in-house legal departments to create and market products built for people doing that same job. Legal operations knowledge has become as invaluable to the companies building the tools as the departments buying them. And these companies recognize that having internal resources that speak the language is the force multiplier that will propel them to success. The second path is the legal engineer, a role that gained attention as a buzzword and has been a topic of conversation and controversy of late. Legal Engineering sits at the intersection of law, technology, data, process design, and AI and is usually tasked with designing the systems that translate legal work into scalable processes and technology. A legal engineer may (among other things) be designing legal workflows that automate routine legal work, building or configuring legal technology solutions, such as contract lifecycle management (CLM), document automation, matter management, or AI tools, or translating legal requirements into technical specifications. Companies hiring for legal engineers look for candidates with data backgrounds, which has turned this into a data role that happens to sit inside a legal department. But really savvy companies recognize that there are some amazing unicorns out there who have both the legal background and data skills. Strategy and innovation. This lane is emerging and, arguably, sits above the others and truthfully the skill runs through them all. It draws on the data from all of the systems we employ, and asks broader questions: is the department spending its time and money in the smartest way, and is technology changing how legal work gets done instead of simply sitting on top of an old outdated process? For example, that can mean building an intake system or creating a legal front door. It can also mean giving business leaders a dashboard they can use on their own to make decisions. Because business partners at these companies are starting to see legal as a function that adds value alongside managing risk, it’s becoming more important for lawyers to understand how to use data to drive decision making. A good legal operations strategist can be the team member who helps to structure a legal data intelligence program to support that. Law firms. Corporate legal departments are not the only place where legal operations roles are becoming more varied. Law firms have begun creating senior roles, such as director of AI and Innovation, at compensation levels that draw people who have spent their careers in-house. For the first time maybe ever, I am seeing in-house lawyers moving to law firms because they can command large salaries, work with huge budgets and truthfully, in some ways we are seeing law firms outpace in-house departments in innovation. That sentence itself would have been unheard of a few years ago and deserves a closer look on its own, but it is worth mentioning here because it is yet another indicator of just how far the legal operations world has grown and the impact it has had on the entire legal ecosystem. It Matters Who You Hire, and When Organic evolution of the field into specialties is a sign of a maturing profession, but it introduces risk. Companies new to legal operations often will start a search without knowing which of these lanes they need to fill first. The result is a job description that tries to cover every stream at once, or one built around an outdated version of the role. Either way, it makes it harder to find the right person for what the team actually needs. The fix starts before the job posting gets written. A department first needs to know what it is trying to achieve and what its goals actually are, since the lane worth hiring for depends entirely on that answer. It is always very apparent to me when reading a job posting which companies have done the analysis and answered the question “What is the problem I am solving for?” From there, the question shifts to sequencing. Few departments need every specialty at once, so the more useful question is where it makes sense to start, and which gap is costing the department the most right now. Skipping that step is what produces the scattered job descriptions that try to say “here’s everything I want this person to do” without a clear sense of what the role actually is. That kind of posting is hard to hire against and even harder for a candidate to answer honestly. And most importantly, will result in the wrong hire for the wrong job. Where CLOC Comes In This scenario is a place where the CLOC community can make a difference. Leaders across the organization take calls and answer messages every day from companies that are early in building out legal operations and are not sure what to hire for. They may ask for a second read of a job description, or a sense check on whether a role is realistic for the market. That kind of guidance, drawn from people who have watched this field split into these lanes as it happened, is what a professional community is for. Tapping into the collective experience and knowledge base of those who live in this world day in and day out can make the difference between a successful Legal Operations strategy and one that fizzles out because the directives weren’t clear and the candidate couldn’t execute. The shape of legal operations will keep changing. What stays constant is knowing that when you take the time to define what you need, and what will drive the biggest impact for your department, it will steer you to the lane you are hiring for, and having a place to ask when you are not sure, is what turns a hire into the right hire. The post Legal Operations Is Splitting Into Specialties. Is Your Hiring Keeping Up? appeared first on CLOC .

blogs.content: Insights Why Legal Entity Management is More Than a Register Legal entity management involves recurring governance work. Learn how teams compare filing requirements, review bylaws, and prepare shareholder resolutions. by Harvey Team • Sep 14, 2026 A director’s resignation from a holding company and two subsidiaries can trigger different filing requirements in every jurisdiction where those entities are incorporated. In one jurisdiction that means a filing within 14 days. In another it means a board resolution, a certified translation, and a form the company secretary has not touched since last year. None of it is difficult on its own. But all of it has to be right, and it has to be right in five places at once. Now consider a group with 40 subsidiaries across a dozen jurisdictions that runs this loop constantly, through director changes, share transfers, annual returns, and the occasional restructuring. The register shows what exists and when the next filing falls due. It cannot read the articles of a Spanish subsidiary and tell you how this year's annual return differs from the German subsidiary down the list. Someone has to open the documents, compare them, and reason through what each jurisdiction wants. That reading is the quiet, recurring cost of running a multi-entity group. Miss a step and the cost lands quickly. An entity can lose good standing, which can stall a financing or a sale until it is cured. Directors and officers can carry personal exposure for late or inaccurate filings. A deal team can ask for a clean picture of the group on a Friday and find that three subsidiaries are mid-correction. The work of keeping every entity current and consistent is unglamorous, and it protects the whole organization from problems that surface at the worst possible moment. This article is about the gap between the register and the reasoning behind it, and how in-house teams are closing it. Legal Entity Management in Plain Terms Legal entity management is the ongoing work of keeping a company's legal entities in good standing. It means maintaining accurate records of directors, officers, shareholders, and governing documents for each entity, and meeting the statutory filing obligations in every jurisdiction where the group operates. In practice, that work runs on two tracks. The first is the record itself: the current list of who sits on each board, who holds the shares, which entity owns which, and when each filing is due. The second is the set of governing documents behind every entry: the articles of association, bylaws, constitutions, shareholder agreements, and past filings that define how each entity is actually run. Keeping the record current is demanding but well understood. It means tracking statutory deadlines, filing annual returns on time, updating director and officer details after every change, and maintaining the beneficial-ownership registers that a growing number of jurisdictions now require. Company administrators and corporate-services teams own most of this, working alongside legal operations and local counsel in each jurisdiction where the group holds entities. The discipline sounds procedural, and much of it is. The judgment shows up on the second track, in reading and reconciling the documents behind the record. Where the Entity Register Reaches its Limit An entity management platform holds the entity list, the ownership structure, the document files, and the filing calendar, and it reminds you when something is due. For a group with hundreds of entities, that record is the difference between order and chaos, and no serious legal team should run without one. Its job ends at the record. The platform can tell you that an annual return is due for a subsidiary next month. It cannot open that subsidiary's articles and tell you what this year's return has to contain in that jurisdiction, or how that differs from the subsidiary incorporated next door. The platform keeps the register current. The legal question sits one layer down, in the governing documents behind each line of that register. Consider what happens when a rule changes. A jurisdiction introduces a new beneficial-ownership requirement, and the platform can flag that a filing is now due for every entity there. It cannot tell you which of those entities already satisfy the requirement in their existing articles, which need a fresh resolution, and which raise a question the local rule leaves open. That reading is a person's job, and it repeats every time a regime shifts. This is where the real measure of complexity hides. Teams tend to size an entity portfolio by counting entities. The work, though, scales with the number of legal regimes and languages the portfolio spans, because that is the reasoning surface. A group of 60 subsidiaries sitting in three jurisdictions is far lighter to run than 30 subsidiaries spread across 20. The rows look similar. The reasoning does not. According to The Accelerating Impact of Legal AI , most in-house teams and firms deploying Harvey's agents are putting them to work on contracting, compliance, and regulatory tasks, the same recurring, rules-driven texture as entity obligations. The pattern is telling. The work moving to legal AI first is the high-volume reasoning that used to sit in a queue, waiting for a lawyer to find time. Does Multi-Jurisdiction Compliance Scale With Entity Count? Each subsidiary is its own small legal world. It has its own filing calendar, its own conventions for how articles and constitutions are drafted, its own regulators, and often its own working language. A group with 60 subsidiaries across 15 jurisdictions is really 15 sets of rules to hold in view, refreshed every time a rule changes in any one of them. That creates a specific kind of reasoning work. Someone has to compare how an annual return differs across jurisdictions and flag where the obligations diverge. Someone has to check that the articles of association and constitutions across subsidiaries still line up where the group needs them to, and note where local law has pulled them apart. And someone has to work with governing documents that arrive in several languages, holding the meaning steady across each translation. The divergence is rarely dramatic, and that is what makes it costly. One jurisdiction wants an annual return that confirms the current directors and registered office. Another wants updated articles filed whenever the share capital changes. A third treats a late confirmation statement as a criminal matter for the officers. Holding all of that straight across a portfolio, and spotting the one subsidiary where the rule quietly changed this year, is the work that fills a corporate-services team's calendar. This is the work a reasoning layer can take on. For example, Harvey can run the legal research to compare filing requirements across the jurisdictions a group operates in, and summarize what an annual return calls for in each. It can read governing documents in several languages and hold the analysis consistent across them, so a change in one subsidiary can be checked against its siblings without a separate manual review for each. Consider Talanx , one of Europe's largest insurance groups, which brings brands such as HDI and Hannover Re together across 175 countries. Its legal team uses Harvey to review 100-page foreign court decisions in minutes and to produce consistent outputs across jurisdictions, with multilingual contracts and translations part of the daily routine. On one recurring review tied to a new regulatory regime, the team cut the work from about two hours to 15 minutes. Over a single year, that discipline saved more than 400 hours of external consultant time. Across all of this, Harvey produces a first pass that a qualified lawyer reviews before the team relies on it. Harvey reads, compares, and summarizes the documents, and the register remains the group's book of record. Who Reads the Articles of Association Across Every Subsidiary? The register points to the documents. The documents hold the answers. A single subsidiary can carry a stack of bylaws, articles, shareholder agreements, and historic filings that no one has read in full in years. The answer to a live question, who can sign what a quorum requires, whether a transfer needs consent, usually sits somewhere inside them. The reading work has a few recurring shapes. A team needs to turn a subsidiary's governance documents into a short, usable summary. It needs the current director and officer list pulled from corporate registries or the latest filings. It needs legal document comparison across subsidiaries, reading the articles or constitutions to see where they diverge. And it needs dense bylaws turned into plain-language guidance, sometimes in another language so a local team can use it. Harvey does this reading work directly. It summarizes governance documents into a brief a lawyer can scan, extracts director and officer details from filings, and compares constitutions across subsidiaries to surface the differences that matter. Deutsche Telekom , the telecommunications group operating across many jurisdictions, identified around 50 priority uses for Harvey out of roughly 400 it reviewed, among them legal text analysis, contract comparison, and document translation. Its lawyers describe Harvey as one place to analyze, compare, draft, and translate dense material that once meant opening a dozen files by hand. Extraction is worth pausing on, because director and officer records drift more than teams expect. People resign, boards reshuffle, and a registry filing lands months after the meeting that prompted it. Pulling the current list straight from the filings gives a team firmer ground than a field someone updated by hand. It is often the difference between a clean group picture and an awkward correction in the middle of a deal, where AI for due diligence can expose a stale record in minutes. The same reading turns a dense set of bylaws into plain-language guidance a business team can act on without a lawyer decoding every clause. Summarizing and extracting are exactly the kind of output a team will act on, so the review discipline holds here too. Harvey produces the summary, the list, or the comparison, and a qualified lawyer checks it against the source before anyone relies on it. Harvey does the reading and the drafting, and the register and the underlying filings stay the record. Bringing Corporate Entity Work In-House For years, the cost of understanding each jurisdiction's rules made outside counsel the default for even routine entity steps. If confirming what a Dutch annual filing requires meant hours of research or a call to a local firm, sending the whole task out was the rational choice. When that research gets faster and cheaper, the make-or-buy line moves, and more of the work comes back in-house. What a team can produce in-house grows accordingly. First-pass comparisons of filing obligations across jurisdictions, plain-language summaries of governance documents, and drafts of the recurring work product itself all become in-house tasks. A team can draft template shareholder resolutions from its own approved exemplars in Harvey, then route them to a qualified lawyer to review and finalize before they are used. This does not pull everything in-house, and it should not. Novel local-law questions, contentious matters, and anything that turns on a judgment call a regulator might test still belong with specialist counsel. What changes is the long tail of routine work — the confirmations, comparisons, and first drafts that were sent out mainly because checking them in-house was slow. The shift shows up in the research. According to The New Economics of In-House Legal , more than a third of in-house teams report bringing work back in-house that they used to send to outside counsel. Most point to reduced external spend as a reason they justify their investment in Harvey, individual users report saving four to eight hours a week, and headcount stays flat even as the work absorbed grows. The economics move quietly, one recurring task at a time. Repsol , the global energy group, runs a legal division across 12 jurisdictions and reached 96% adoption of Harvey among its lawyers. With that reach, the team has taken corporate matters in-house that it would once have sent outside, doing the research and first drafts internally and reserving outside firms for the judgment calls that warrant them. None of this removes the lawyer or the filing. Harvey does the reasoning and produces the draft, a qualified lawyer reviews it, and the filing itself stays with the team, the registered agent, or local counsel. The judgment call is still a lawyer's to make. Deploying a Reasoning Layer Over the Register The workable model is straightforward. Keep the entity platform or register as the book of record. Add a reasoning layer over it for the document and obligation work. Hold a firm review discipline over everything that reasoning layer produces. Each part has a clear job, and the boundaries between them are what keep the arrangement trustworthy. Starting is a matter of picking one task and proving it. Choose the recurring, high-volume work that hurts most, annual-return comparison across jurisdictions, say, or the filings that follow a director change, and run it through the reasoning layer. Check the output against the register and the source documents. When it holds up on the task you know best, extend it to the next one. The boundary is worth stating plainly. The register stays the record. The reasoning layer reads, compares, summarizes, and drafts. A qualified lawyer reviews the output before anyone relies on it. That review reflects a lawyer's duties of competence and supervision, and the guidance in ABA Model Rule 1.1 Comment 8 that competence now includes understanding the benefits and risks of the technology a lawyer uses. Running this work through one reasoning layer has a second benefit. Because the analysis, the comparisons, and the drafts pass through a single place, leadership gets a consistent and auditable view of how the group's entity obligations are handled across jurisdictions. That visibility is hard to get when the same work is scattered across local firms and inboxes. That single path also feeds the group's legal knowledge management , leaving a record of what was reviewed and when that an auditor or a board committee can rely on. The Work Behind the Register An entity register does an essential job. It keeps an accurate list of directors, officers, shareholders, and governing documents, and it tracks when each filing is due. The legal work sits one layer down, in reading, comparing, and drafting against those documents across every jurisdiction the group touches. That reading is what turns a current record into answers a team can act on. The volume of that work rises with the number of jurisdictions and languages a group operates in, well past what an entity count suggests. Teams that treat the reasoning as the real work handle recurring filing and governance work with more consistency and a clearer view of the whole group. They get there by holding a lawyer's review over everything the analysis produces. The register tells them what they have. The reasoning tells them what to do about it. Harvey is the reasoning layer that sits over the register. It summarizes governing documents, extracts director and officer details, compares articles and filing requirements across subsidiaries, and drafts the recurring work product for a qualified lawyer to review and finalize. If your organization is carrying a growing portfolio of entities across jurisdictions, book a demo to see how Harvey handles the reasoning behind your register. Request a Demo Unable to load form. Please try again. Try Again Thank you! We'll be in touch shortly. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between entity management software and legal entity management? Entity management software is the record. It stores the entity list, ownership structure, documents, and filing deadlines, and it reminds you when something is due. Legal entity management is the wider discipline that includes the legal reasoning on the documents behind that record, such as comparing filing requirements across jurisdictions and reading the articles behind each entity. The software keeps the register, and the discipline covers the judgment the register cannot. Can AI file annual returns or maintain the entity register? No. The filing itself stays with your team, a registered agent, or the relevant registry, and the register remains your book of record. AI can take on the reasoning and drafting around those steps, such as comparing what each jurisdiction's return requires or preparing a first draft. A qualified lawyer reviews that work before anyone relies on it. How does Harvey handle governing documents in multiple languages? Harvey can read and summarize governing documents in several languages and keep its analysis consistent across them, so articles in one subsidiary can be compared against siblings drafted in another language. A qualified lawyer should review the summary or comparison before the team relies on it. Does using AI for entity work create compliance risk? The risk comes from relying on output without checking it, which is why a qualified lawyer reviews everything the tool produces before it is used. Handled that way, the practice sits comfortably within a lawyer's duties of competence and supervision, including the expectation in ABA Model Rule 1.1 Comment 8 that competent lawyers understand the technology they use. Verification discipline is what keeps AI-assisted entity work sound. Next Up What Legal Workflows Can In-House Teams Automate? Learn More Resources RESOURCES Customer Stories Resource Hub Blog What's New Pricing Events & Webinars Guides Legal AI Assistant Guide AI Contract Review Guide Legal Matter Management Guide Contract Guides Learn More Company Company About Us Careers Newsroom Learn More Sign In Book a Demo Product Solutions Resources Company Sign in Book a Demo BLOG Industry Insights Entrust’s Binta Balogun on AI, Time, and the In-House Lawyer’s Job Last updated: August 12, 2026 Written by: Daniel Lewis, J.D. , Global CEO In-house legal teams are navigating the same pressure: more work, higher stakes, and a profession that's changing faster than most organizations can keep up with. In this series, LegalOn CEO Daniel Lewis sits down with in-house legal professionals to talk workload, tools, trade-offs—and what it actually means to be a lawyer today. Ask Binta Balogun what excites her about AI, and she doesn’t start with big predictions about the legal profession. She starts with time. As product and regulatory counsel at Entrust, Binta works in the kind of environment where legal questions are rarely neat. They sit inside product launches, customer demands, regulatory expectations, internal processes, and commercial pressure. The work isn’t just about knowing the law. It’s knowing what the business is trying to do, where the risk is real, and where a lawyer can help people move forward. That’s why the practical promise of AI matters to her. Not because it can “replace” a lawyer, but because it can take on some of the work that slows lawyers down: pulling together a first cut of research, summarizing long documents, comparing provisions, cleaning up drafts, or helping get from a blank page to something usable. "AI doesn’t make the lawyer less important. It makes the lawyer's real job harder to avoid." For Binta, who is also a mother of two, those hours aren’t theoretical. The minutes spent wrestling with admin, formatting, repeat questions, or first-pass document work are minutes taken from deeper legal thinking, better business conversations, or simply getting home with a little more left in the tank. What This Means for the Junior Lawyer Binta is especially interested in what legal AI means for junior lawyers. Much of early legal training has always involved repetition: reviewing documents, checking clauses, producing first drafts, searching for the right precedent. Some of that work builds discipline. Some of it is just grind. AI may change the balance. A junior lawyer who can use these tools may get to the real questions faster: What matters here? What is missing? What would I recommend, and why? The risk, of course, is that speed can create a false sense of competence. Binta’s point isn’t that trainees can skip learning the craft. It’s that the craft may need to be taught more deliberately, with less time spent on mechanical work and more time spent developing judgment. The In-House Advantage Her view of the in-house role is similarly practical. The lawyers who will be most valuable are the ones who understand the product roadmap, the customer pressure, the regulatory backdrop, and the commercial trade-offs—not the ones who sit outside the business and review things at the end. If a tool can help with the first draft, the summary, or the issue spot, then the lawyer’s value has to show up somewhere else. In context, prioritization, judgment, and trust. In knowing when a risk is material and when it is not. In helping a product team see around corners. In giving advice that can actually be used. For Binta, that’s the real opportunity. AI doesn’t make the lawyer less important. It makes the lawyer’s real job harder to avoid. ‍ Binta Balogun is a product and regulatory lawyer at Entrust. blogs.author: Anita Gorney
blogs.description: The questions legal teams should ask to understand how AI providers protect data, disclose tradeoffs, and maintain trust as their products evolve.
blogs.content: Insights Evaluating Legal AI Providers Across Trust, Privacy, and Security The questions legal teams should ask to understand how AI providers protect data, disclose tradeoffs, and maintain trust as their products evolve. by Anita Gorney • Sep 14, 2026 Law firms and in-house legal teams evaluating legal AI providers face a different set of questions than most enterprise software buyers. Lawyers must ensure the confidentiality and protection of their client’s data at the same time while also keeping up with the pace of change. Therefore, one of the most crucial questions that buyers and innovation officers must ask is: can their legal AI provider innovate at the speed that AI demands whilst still prioritizing and keeping their customers’ trust, security, and privacy? An example from a couple months ago illustrates why this matters. When Anthropic released Claude Fable 5, it also announced that the model required additional safety measures. Unlike Anthropic's zero data retention (“ZDR”) offering for many of its other models, Claude Fable 5 requires 30-day data retention and permits limited review by Anthropic's safety team for interactions flagged by its safety systems. That left us with a decision. Should we delay adopting one of the most capable models available because it didn't support ZDR? Or should we make it available while being completely transparent about the change in data handling? We chose the latter. Harvey made Claude Fable 5 available as an optional model, clearly and very publicly, disclosing that it goes against our standard practice of offering models with ZDR. We allowed customers to decide whether the additional capabilities justified that tradeoff for their use case. What we didn't do was incorporate a model with weaker data protections without telling anyone. That should never be an option. This scenario got me thinking about how other providers handle moments where there is a tension between innovation, speed, and data protection, and whether they're as forthcoming. Not all of them are, especially when it comes to: The potential for government access to customer data; Data localization commitments and whether true localization can actually be achieved; How legal data is sourced; Whether ZDR commitments continue to apply as AI products evolve beyond simple chat interfaces into long-horizon agents and long-running workflows. The rest of this post is a practical guide for legal teams, CIOs, procurement leaders, and security teams evaluating legal AI providers, offering specific questions to ask and red flags to watch for. A Practical Checklist for Evaluating Legal AI Providers The checklist below walks through key questions to ask across data sourcing and IP, data localization, ZDR, subprocessors and supply chain, and governance and accountability. Why Transparency Matters More as Legal AI Evolves When we talk about customer trust, we're talking about more than just the privacy and security of our customers' data. We're building a company around the idea that our customers trust us to be honest, transparent, and to not brush difficult topics under the rug. That's the real differentiator: Does your AI provider proactively communicate with you and give you the information you need to make informed decisions? Are they willing to address the difficult topics other providers won't talk about? In a recent subprocessor update, we proactively addressed the issue of prompt caching and how it works with zero data retention (ZDR), which is something a lot of providers stay quiet about. That update is available for our customers to read here . Looking ahead, buyers should evaluate not just a provider's current commitments, but how they communicate and adapt as AI continues to evolve. The question worth asking: Is transparency their north star? Trust is a Crucial Part of the Platform For legal organizations, evaluating an AI platform is not simply a question of product quality or model performance. The real test is how a provider makes decisions when trust, privacy, governance, and compliance create constraints on what is possible. Rather than avoiding those constraints, the strongest solutions make deliberate choices, explain them clearly, and remain accountable as technology evolves. These issues are complex, evolving, and rarely black and white. We do not claim to have solved every challenge. But we do believe legal AI providers should be willing to confront difficult questions directly and be transparent and accountable in their response. The easier path would be to ignore them, but that path only leads to a damaging loss of trust for the industry as a whole.
